Part 1 of 17
What ML Actually Is
Rules vs examples, paradigms, framing, baselines, when not to use ML

1.1 Rules vs examples — what ML actually trades ⭐

Machine learning replaces explicit rules with examples plus a loss function. Every other property of ML systems — including all of their failure modes — follows from that single substitution.

When you write a rule, you own the logic. You can read it, test it clause by clause, explain it to a regulator, and change it on a Tuesday afternoon. When you fit a model, you no longer own the logic — you own the data, the loss, and the evaluation, and the logic is inferred from those three things. That is a genuinely good trade when the rule is complex, unknown, or changes faster than you could rewrite it. It is a terrible trade when the rule is simple, known and stable.

What you give up, concretely

PropertyHand-written ruleFitted model
Where the logic livesIn code you wroteIn parameters inferred from data
AuditabilityRead itApproximate it post-hoc (Part 14)
Behaviour on new inputsDefined by the ruleUnknown — this is the whole reason validation exists
Failure modeYou wrote the wrong ruleYou collected the wrong data, or chose the wrong loss, or measured the wrong thing
Cost to changeEdit and deployRetrain, revalidate, redeploy, re-monitor
Scales withYour understandingYour data

Two axes that get asked as follow-ups

Online vs batch learning. Batch learning fits on a fixed dataset and is redeployed on a schedule; online learning updates continuously from a stream. Almost all production classical ML is batch-trained and served online — meaning the model is refitted nightly or weekly but answers requests in real time. Saying “we'd use online learning to keep it fresh” is usually the wrong answer, because continuous updating makes incidents unreproducible, is hard to validate, and is vulnerable to feedback loops (§15.7).

Transductive vs inductive. Inductive learning produces a function that generalises to rows you have never seen — this is what almost everything in this guide does. Transductive learning only produces labels for a specific known set of unlabelled rows, with no reusable function: label propagation and some graph methods work this way. The distinction matters the moment someone asks “how do you score a new customer?” and your method has no answer.

The framing that makes you sound senior

When asked “what is machine learning?”, most candidates define it. Better: define it as a trade. “It's learning a function from examples instead of specifying it — you trade explicit, auditable rules for data, a loss function and an evaluation procedure. That's the right trade when the rule is genuinely unknown or too complex to write, and the wrong one otherwise, which is why the first question I ask on any project is whether a rule would do.”

Likely interview questions
ConceptualWhat is machine learning, in one or two sentences?

Learning a function from examples plus a loss function, instead of specifying that function as explicit rules. The trade is that you stop owning the logic and start owning the data, the loss and the evaluation — which is why validation and monitoring are structural requirements rather than nice-to-haves. Define it as a trade rather than a category and the rest of the interview follows more naturally.

ConceptualOnline vs batch learning — which would you use in production and why?

Almost always batch-trained, online-served: refit on a schedule, answer requests in real time. True online learning updates from a stream, which sounds attractive but makes incidents unreproducible, is very hard to validate before it affects users, and amplifies feedback loops — a fraud model that learns continuously from its own accepted transactions drifts in a direction nobody chose (§15.7). Online learning earns its place with genuinely non-stationary, high-volume, low-stakes problems (ad ranking, some recommendations), not with credit or claims.

GotchaTransductive vs inductive — why would anyone care?

Inductive learning gives you a reusable function that scores rows you have never seen; transductive learning gives you labels for a specific fixed set and nothing more. Label propagation over a graph is transductive: add a new node and you re-run the whole thing. It matters the moment the system has to score a new customer at request time — a transductive method has no answer to that, and discovering it after choosing the method is expensive.

1.2 The five learning paradigms

Naming the paradigm is the first move in any design answer, because it determines what data you need, what it costs, and what could possibly go wrong.

ParadigmYou supplyIt learnsReal problemThe hard part
SupervisedFeatures + labelsf: x → yCredit default, claim severity, churn, fraudGetting labels, and getting them at the right time
UnsupervisedFeatures onlyStructure — clusters, components, densitySegmentation, anomaly detection, compressionEvaluation — there is no ground truth to score against
Semi-supervisedFew labels + much unlabelled dataf: x → y, propagatedFraud where only confirmed cases are labelledConfirmation bias — the model reinforces its own errors
Self-supervisedUnlabelled data + a pretext taskRepresentationsAll modern pretraining; increasingly tabular too (§16.1)Designing a pretext task whose solution is useful
ReinforcementAn environment + a rewardA policy π: s → aBidding, inventory, routing, pricing under feedbackYou need an environment — and reward design is notoriously fragile

The distinctions that trip people up

Self-supervised is not unsupervised. Both start from unlabelled data, but self-supervised learning manufactures labels from the data itself — mask a token and predict it, corrupt a column and reconstruct it — and then trains with ordinary supervised machinery. The output is a representation, not a clustering. That distinction matters in 2026 because it is the mechanism behind tabular foundation models (§16.1).

Semi-supervised is not “just use the unlabelled data”. Its methods — self-training, label propagation, co-training — all rest on an assumption (that the decision boundary lies in a low-density region, or that the data has cluster structure aligned with the labels). When that assumption fails, pseudo-labelling makes things actively worse because the model trains on its own confident mistakes.

Reinforcement learning needs an environment, and you probably don't have one. The most common bad answer in a case interview is proposing RL for a problem where you can only observe historical logs of a policy you did not control. That is offline RL or, more usefully, a causal inference problem (§16.4) — and framing it that way instead is a strong signal.

Likely interview questions
Very commonSupervised vs unsupervised vs reinforcement learning — with a real example of each.

Supervised: features plus labels → a mapping. Predicting credit default from application data. Unsupervised: features only → structure. Customer segmentation, or anomaly detection where you have no confirmed anomalies. Reinforcement: an environment and a reward → a policy. Real-time bid optimisation, inventory replenishment. Add for credit: self-supervised (a pretext task manufactures the labels — the basis of all pretraining) and semi-supervised (a few labels plus lots of unlabelled data, which is the realistic fraud situation).

GotchaIs self-supervised learning just unsupervised learning with a new name?

No. Both start from unlabelled data, but self-supervised learning creates labels from the data itself via a pretext task — mask and predict, corrupt and reconstruct — then trains with ordinary supervised machinery. The output is a representation you then fine-tune, not a clustering or density estimate. It matters on tabular data now because it is the mechanism behind TabPFN-style models (§16.1), which are pretrained on synthetic data and applied in-context.

DesignA stakeholder asks for reinforcement learning to optimise pricing. How do you respond?

Ask what environment we would train in. RL needs to interact — take an action, observe the consequence, repeat — and if all we have is a log of prices someone else set, we have observational data from an unknown policy, not an environment. That is either offline RL (hard, data-hungry, easy to get wrong) or, far more usefully, a causal inference problem: estimating price elasticity with confounding by the historical pricing policy (§16.4). Proposing a geo experiment or a DML approach instead is the stronger answer, and it is usually also the cheaper one.

ConceptualWhen does semi-supervised learning hurt rather than help?

When its underlying assumption fails — that the decision boundary lies in a low-density region, or that cluster structure aligns with the labels. Pseudo-labelling then trains the model on its own confident mistakes, which reinforces them: the classic confirmation-bias failure. Guard against it by holding out a clean, human-labelled validation set that never receives pseudo-labels, and by adding pseudo-labels gradually with a confidence threshold rather than all at once.

1.3 Prediction vs inference vs decision ⭐

Three different projects, three different methods, three different ways to be wrong — and they are constantly conflated, including by the people commissioning the work.

“We want to understand churn” is not a specification. It could mean any of three things, and each one changes the model, the validation, the metric and the deliverable.

How to tell which one you're being asked for

Listen for the verb. “Predict”, “score”, “flag”, “rank” ⇒ prediction. “Understand”, “explain”, “which factors drive”, “how much does X affect Y” ⇒ inference. “Who should we target / offer / approve / intervene on” ⇒ decision. Then say which one you heard, out loud, and confirm it — because if the stakeholder wanted a decision and you deliver a prediction, the project will be judged a failure for reasons nobody will be able to articulate.

Feature importance is not a cause

A model can be highly accurate while assigning importance to a feature that has no causal effect at all — it may be a proxy, a collider, or a consequence of the target. “num_support_tickets is the top driver of churn, so let's reduce support tickets” is an inference claim made from a prediction model, and it is usually wrong. If someone will act on the explanation, you need a causal design, not a SHAP plot (Part 14, §16.4).

Likely interview questions
Very commonWhat's the difference between prediction and inference, and why does it matter?

Prediction asks “what will happen?” and is judged on out-of-sample accuracy; correlation is sufficient because you never intervene. Inference asks “why?” or “how much does X affect Y?” and is judged on identifiability and correct uncertainty; it needs assumptions to hold and often prefers a simpler, well-specified model over a more accurate one. It matters because the methods diverge: a GBM with SHAP is excellent for the first and inadmissible as evidence for the second. And there is a third — decision — which needs a causal quantity, not either of the first two.

GotchaYour churn model is 0.88 AUC. The business wants to know what causes churn. What do you say?

That the model is not evidence of causes and I'd be misleading them if I read it that way. A predictive model happily uses proxies, consequences of the target, and features that are only correlated through a confounder — num_collection_calls predicts default beautifully and reducing collection calls will not reduce default. To answer “what causes churn” I'd need a causal design: an experiment where possible, or an identification strategy with the assumptions stated (§16.4). What I can offer immediately from the predictive model is a hypothesis list worth testing, which is genuinely useful as long as it is labelled as that.

DesignHow do you tell which of the three a stakeholder is actually asking for?

Ask what happens the day after the model ships — specifically, what action does someone take, and on which rows? If nobody acts and the output is a report, it's inference. If a system consumes the score and treats rows differently, it's prediction feeding a decision, and then I need to know the action's cost and whether it plausibly changes the outcome — which is what turns it into an uplift problem. Listening for the verb helps too: “predict/score/flag” vs “understand/explain” vs “target/offer/approve”.

1.4 The ML lifecycle

The loop is not linear, it closes, and the box everyone practises is the smallest one in it.

The three things to write down before any fit()

  • The target metric — and specifically, the metric at the operating point you will deploy, not a threshold-free summary (Part 12).
  • The baseline it must beat — including the existing business rule, which is the real bar (§1.6).
  • The decision it feeds — because if you cannot state the decision, you cannot choose the metric, and you will optimise something arbitrary.

Interviewers who ask “how would you know the project succeeded?” are checking whether you do this. The answer they want is not a metric name; it is evidence that success was defined before the modelling started.

Likely interview questions
ConceptualWalk me through the ML lifecycle. Where does the time actually go?

Problem framing → data collection → EDA and deciding the split → feature engineering → baseline then model → validation → deployment → monitoring → retraining, which loops back into re-framing. The time goes overwhelmingly into data and validation, not modelling — the modelling box is the one everyone practises and the smallest one in the loop. Two things worth adding unprompted: the loop closes (monitoring changes the problem definition, not just the weights), and the offline metric is a proxy whose link to the business outcome is an assumption you test.

DesignHow would you know the project succeeded?

By having defined it beforehand: a target metric measured at the deployed operating point, a baseline it must beat (including the current business rule), and the decision it feeds. Then success is the business quantity that decision moves — cases prevented, hours saved, margin protected — measured against that baseline, ideally with an experiment. And an operational half: is it monitored, is it maintainable, can it be rolled back, does the team trust it.

GotchaWhat is the offline/online metric gap?

Your offline metric is a proxy for a business outcome, and the mapping is an assumption. A model with better AUC can lose an A/B test — because the improvement was in a score region users never see, because the score distribution shifted under a fixed threshold, or because the business metric depends on something you never optimised (diversity, latency, fairness of exposure). Manage it by stating the assumed link explicitly, validating it against historical launches, and shipping through shadow → canary → A/B with guardrails (§15.7–15.8).

1.5 Framing a problem correctly ⭐

Choosing the target variable is the highest-leverage decision in the whole project, and the one most often made in thirty seconds.

Take “predict churn”. It is not a specification. Churn could be a cancelled subscription, ninety days of inactivity, a downgrade, or a support ticket asking how to close an account. Each definition produces a different label, a different base rate, a different model — and, crucially, a different set of customers you would act on.

The five decisions inside “the target”

DecisionThe questionConsequence of getting it wrong
DefinitionWhat event exactly counts?You optimise for something the business does not care about
Unit of predictionCustomer? Session? Transaction? Customer-month?Determines your splitting strategy — get it wrong and you get group leakage (§3.6)
HorizonWithin 30 days? 90? Ever?“Ever” is unlearnable and unactionable; too short and the base rate collapses
Decision windowHow long does the team need to act?A prediction that arrives after the action window is worthless
Data latencyWhen does each feature actually become available?You build features from data that will not exist at prediction time — temporal leakage

The same business problem, framed four ways

FramingTargetWhat it buysWhat it costs
ClassificationWill this customer churn in 30 days?Simple, calibratable, thresholdableLoses timing information entirely
Regression / survivalWhen will they churn?Timing for the intervention calendar; handles censoring (§10.3)Harder to evaluate and to explain
RankingWho are the top 500 at risk?Matches a fixed outreach capacity exactlyScores stop being probabilities, so expected value breaks
Uplift / CATEWho will churn only if we do nothing?The correct target for a retention offerNeeds experimental data; harder to validate (§16.5)
Cost asymmetry, in the units the business uses

“What does a false positive cost versus a false negative?” is the question that turns a metric argument into a business conversation. A wrongly-blocked legitimate payment costs a lost sale plus a support contact; a missed fraud costs the transaction value plus a chargeback fee plus scheme penalties. Once those are numbers, the threshold (§12.7) stops being a matter of taste and becomes arithmetic — and you can defend it to someone who does not know what a threshold is.

Likely interview questions
Very common⭐ How do you choose the target variable and prediction horizon for a churn model?

Work backwards from the decision. Ask what action the model triggers and how long that action needs — if retention needs 30 days to run a campaign, the target is “churns within 30 days”, not “ever churns”. Then define churn concretely (cancellation? 90 days inactive? downgrade?) and check the base rate under each definition, because that determines whether the problem is even learnable. Pin the unit of prediction — customer, or customer-month — because it fixes your splitting strategy. Add a data-latency gap so every feature is knowable at prediction time. And close with the framing caveat: if the decision is who gets a retention offer, churn is the wrong target and you want uplift.

DesignWhy does the unit of prediction matter so much?

Because it determines the split, and the split determines whether any number you report is meaningful. If the unit is a transaction but rows are nested inside customers, a random split puts the same customer on both sides — the model learns to recognise the customer rather than the pattern, and validation looks excellent right up until it meets a new customer. It also determines what a “positive” means (one churned customer, or twelve churned customer-months?) and therefore the base rate and the metric.

DesignSame business problem, four framings — when would you pick each?

Classification when a yes/no decision at a threshold is enough and you want calibrated probabilities. Survival when timing matters and some customers simply have not churned yet — censoring makes binary labels biased. Ranking when capacity is fixed ("we can call 500 people"), though you then lose probability semantics. Uplift when you are choosing who to treat rather than who to watch. Saying “these are four different targets, and the right one depends on the action” is worth more than any one of them.

GotchaWhat's wrong with defining churn as "ever cancels"?

Three things. It is unactionable — you cannot intervene on an event with no time bound. It is unlearnable in practice, because the features that predict a cancellation next week are different from those predicting one in three years, and the model averages them into mush. And it creates a censoring problem: customers still active are labelled 0 when they may simply not have churned yet, which biases the model toward whatever tenure distribution your snapshot happens to have.

1.6 Baselines you must always report

A model without a baseline is an unfalsifiable claim. Reporting baselines is nearly free, and forgetting them is one of the most visible junior tells there is.

interactive What does your model actually have to beat?
—majority-class accuracy
—your model's accuracy
—accuracy gained
—AP vs base-rate AP

All computed from 4,000 simulated rows. Drag the base rate to 3% and watch the majority-class baseline hit 97% accuracy while your model gains almost nothing on that metric — even though its average precision is many times the baseline. This is the accuracy trap in §12.1, encountered before you have written any model code, which is exactly when it should be encountered.

The five baselines, and what each one tells you

BaselineWhat it isWhat it tells you
Majority / meanAlways predict the majority class or the training meanThe floor. On a 99:1 problem it scores 99% accuracy — which is the whole argument of §12.1
Previous valueNaive or seasonal-naive forecastThe one that embarrasses time-series models most often (§10.6)
The existing ruleWhatever the business does todayThe real bar. If you can't beat it, the project's value is negative
Random-but-calibratedPredict the base rate for everyoneAnchors intuition for log loss and Brier — and it is the correct AP baseline
Strong simple modelLogistic regression or a small GBM on obvious featuresUsually reaches 90–95% of the final performance in 2% of the effort
The finding is allowed to be “don't ship it”

If the complex model doesn't beat those baselines by a margin that justifies its serving cost, its retraining cost and its risk, that is the result — report it. Candidates who volunteer this are describing a real project; candidates who can't imagine it are describing a tutorial. The corollary is that a strong simple baseline should be built first, not last, because it also tells you whether the problem is learnable at all before you spend three weeks on features.

Likely interview questions
Very commonWhat baselines would you report before any model?

Majority class or mean; the previous value / seasonal-naive for time series; the existing business rule, which is the real bar; a random-but-calibrated predictor to anchor log loss and to give the correct average-precision baseline; and a strong simple model — logistic regression or a small GBM on obvious features. Then the sentence that matters: if the complex model doesn't beat these by enough to justify its cost and risk, that is the finding, and I'd report it.

GotchaWhy is "the existing business rule" the most important baseline?

Because it is what the model actually replaces, so it is what the project's value is measured against. Beating a majority-class baseline proves nothing if the current hand-written rule already beats it by more. It is also the baseline most often skipped, because it takes work to reconstruct and it sometimes produces an uncomfortable answer — which is precisely why an interviewer asking about it is testing your honesty as much as your method.

ConceptualWhat's the right baseline for average precision?

The base rate — a random ranker achieves an average precision equal to the positive class proportion, not 0.5. That is why an AP of 0.30 can be excellent (on a 2% base rate it is 15× lift) or poor (on a 40% base rate it is worse than random). Always report AP alongside the base rate, or report lift over it, otherwise the number is uninterpretable. Contrast with ROC-AUC, whose random baseline is always 0.5 regardless of imbalance — which is precisely the flattery described in §12.3.

1.7 When not to use ML ⭐⭐

The strongest senior signal in this entire part, and it takes one sentence: most candidates answer “when you don't have data”, and the full answer has four branches — three of which are about consequences rather than data volume.

Two more reasons to say no that candidates rarely mention

The feedback loop makes evaluation impossible. If the model's decisions determine the data you will next observe, and you have no exploration traffic, you cannot measure whether it works (§15.7). Shipping into that situation is shipping something you can never evaluate.

The cost of being wrong is not symmetric with the cost of being right. If a correct prediction saves £5 and an incorrect one costs £5,000, you need precision so high that a rule with a human reviewer will usually beat an ML system on expected value — and will be defensible in a way the model is not.

How to deliver this in an interview

Do not wait to be asked. When given a case, spend the first thirty seconds on it: “Before designing this — is there a rule that would do? Do we have labels, or a path to them? Is an unexplainable error acceptable here? And is there enough data for the effect size we're chasing? Assuming yes to all four, here's how I'd approach it…” It costs half a minute and it reframes you from someone who builds models into someone who decides whether to.

Likely interview questions
Very common⭐ When would you not use machine learning?

Four branches. (1) The rule is stable and writable — ship the rule; it's auditable, free, and never drifts. (2) You have no labels and no path to getting them — reframe as unsupervised, buy labels, or instrument now and model later. (3) An unexplainable error is unacceptable — use a deterministic system, or ML with a human in the loop. (4) The data is too small for the effect size you're chasing — a GLM, a statistical estimate or a lookup table will beat an under-trained model. Two more worth adding: when a feedback loop makes evaluation impossible without exploration traffic, and when cost asymmetry is so extreme that a rule plus a human reviewer wins on expected value.

DesignGive a concrete example where a rule beats a model.

“Flag every transaction above £10,000 to a payee first seen today.” It is auditable, instant, has no training data requirement, cannot drift, and a compliance officer can sign it off. A model might catch marginally more, but it would need labels, monitoring, retraining, an explanation layer and a fairness review — and the regulator would still ask why a specific transaction was flagged. In regulated screening the rule is often the correct engineering answer, with ML used to rank the alert queue the rule generates rather than to replace it.

Gotcha“We don't have labels but we have lots of data — can't we just use unsupervised learning?”

Sometimes, but check what you'd do with the output. Unsupervised methods give you structure, not answers, and you cannot evaluate them against the thing you actually care about — a clustering that looks beautiful may have nothing to do with churn. If the goal is genuinely exploratory (segmentation for a marketing team to interpret), it's fine. If the goal is a prediction, unsupervised learning is a way of postponing the labelling problem, not solving it. The better answer is often: label 500 rows properly, use active learning to spend the next 500 well (§10.1), and get a supervised baseline you can actually measure.

DesignHow does cost asymmetry change the build-or-rule decision?

It changes the precision you need, which changes whether any achievable model is viable. If a correct catch saves £5 and a false positive costs £5,000, the break-even precision is above 99.9% — no model on a noisy problem will hit that, so the viable design is a high-recall cheap filter plus human review, where the ML system's job is to rank the queue rather than to decide. Working that arithmetic out loud, before proposing an architecture, is one of the clearest senior signals available in a case interview.

Part 2 of 17
The Mathematical Toolkit
Linear algebra, optimization, Bayes, MLE/MAP, distance, the curse of dimensionality

2.1 Linear algebra

You will not be asked to prove anything. You will be asked what an eigenvector has to do with PCA, and what multicollinearity does to a coefficient — and both answers live here.

ObjectWhat it means hereWhere it shows up
Dot productProjection / unnormalised similarityEvery linear model; cosine similarity; kernels (§6.6)
Matrix × vectorA linear map — rotate, scale, projectXw is “apply the model to every row at once”
Norms L1, L2, L∞How you measure “size”Lasso, Ridge, robustness, distance metrics (§2.6)
Rank / linear independenceHow much unique information the columns carryMulticollinearity; XᵀX singular ⇒ no unique solution
Eigenvectors & eigenvaluesDirections unchanged by the map, and how much they stretchPCA is literally this (§9.6); convergence of iterative methods
SVDX = UΣVᵀ — any matrix, factoredPCA, TruncatedSVD/LSA, pseudo-inverse, numerically stable least squares
Positive semi-definiteNon-negative curvature: vᵀAv ≥ 0Covariance matrices; valid kernels; Hessians at a minimum
Condition numberHow much the output amplifies input errorWhy you don't invert XᵀX (§5.1)

The one derivative you should be able to write

Least squares in matrix form is L(w) = (Xw − y)ᵀ(Xw − y). Its gradient is ∂L/∂w = 2Xᵀ(Xw − y). Set that to zero and you get XᵀXw = Xᵀy — the normal equations, and therefore w = (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy whenever XᵀX is invertible. Everything in §5.1 follows from those three lines, including why nobody actually computes the inverse.

Likely interview questions
ConceptualWhat do eigenvectors have to do with PCA?

PCA looks for the directions of maximum variance in centred data. Variance along a unit direction v is vᵀΣv, and maximising that subject to ‖v‖=1 gives exactly the eigenvector of the covariance matrix Σ with the largest eigenvalue — and the eigenvalue is the variance along it. Equivalently, they are the right singular vectors of the centred data matrix, which is how it's actually computed (SVD is numerically better than forming Σ). Details in §9.6.

ConceptualWhy does anyone care whether a matrix is positive semi-definite?

Three places. A covariance matrix must be PSD, so an estimate that isn't signals a numerical or sampling problem. A kernel must produce a PSD Gram matrix (Mercer's condition) or it doesn't correspond to an inner product in any feature space and the SVM's convexity guarantee evaporates (§6.6). And a Hessian that is PSD everywhere means the function is convex, which is what gives you a unique global minimum (§2.2).

DebugYour linear model's coefficients flip sign when you refit on a slightly different sample. What's happening?

Almost certainly multicollinearity. Correlated columns make XᵀX ill-conditioned, so the loss surface has a long flat valley in which many coefficient combinations fit almost equally well — small sample changes move the optimum a long way along that valley. Diagnose with a correlation matrix, the condition number, or VIF = 1/(1−R²ⱼ) above ~5–10. Note it damages interpretation and stability, usually not predictive accuracy. Fix by dropping one, combining them, or using Ridge, which re-conditions the problem directly.

2.2 Calculus & optimization ⭐

One idea does most of the work — follow the negative gradient. Two follow-ups separate candidates: convexity, and why XGBoost bothers with second derivatives.

interactive Gradient descent — watch the learning rate decide everything
—final loss
—distance to optimum
—condition number
—behaviour

Real gradient descent on a real quadratic. Three experiments. η too small — it crawls and never arrives in the step budget. η too large — it oscillates across the valley or diverges outright. Conditioning 20:1 with a moderate η — it zig-zags, because the gradient points across the valley rather than along it. That last one is the reason you scale features before any gradient-based model (§3.4).

Convexity: what it actually buys you

A convex function has one basin: every local minimum is the global minimum. That is a guarantee about the answer, not about speed. Its practical consequence is reproducibility — with a convex loss, the optimiser's starting point does not change the result, so “I get a different model every run” is alarming for logistic regression and completely expected for k-means or a neural net.

The optimiser zoo, and where each one appears

MethodThe updateWhere you meet it
Batch gradient descentFull-dataset gradient — exact, slowTextbook derivations; small problems
SGD / mini-batchNoisy gradient per sample or batchSGDClassifier, out-of-core training; the noise itself regularizes
Momentum / AdamVelocity plus per-parameter step sizesNeural nets; rarely needed in classical ML
Newton / second-orderΔ = −H⁻¹g — uses curvatureXGBoost: gradients and Hessians give the exact optimal leaf value in one step (§8.6). Also IRLS for logistic regression
Coordinate descentOptimise one coefficient at a timeHow Lasso is actually fitted — the soft-threshold step is what produces exact zeros (§5.6)
Lagrange multipliersConstrained optimisation via the dualThe SVM dual, and where the kernel enters (§6.6)
Why second-order, in one sentence

The gradient tells you which way is downhill; the Hessian tells you how the slope is changing, so you can jump straight to the bottom of a quadratic approximation instead of taking a fixed-size step. XGBoost exploits this: expanding the loss to second order gives a closed form for the optimal leaf weight, w*ⱼ = −Gⱼ/(Hⱼ + λ), and a matching split-gain formula — which is why it needs no learning-rate tuning within a tree and why λ appears naturally as regularization rather than being bolted on.

Likely interview questions
ConceptualWhy does convexity matter, and which of your models are convex?

Convexity guarantees that any local minimum is global, so the optimiser's starting point doesn't change the answer — you get reproducibility, and you can trust that a converged fit is the best fit. Convex: linear regression, Ridge, Lasso, logistic regression, linear SVM (all with their standard losses). Non-convex: decision trees (the split search is combinatorial), k-means, GMM/EM, neural nets. Practical consequence: n_init and seeds matter for the second group; different results across runs of logistic regression indicate a bug.

Very commonExplain gradient descent and how you'd choose the learning rate.

Repeatedly step in the direction of the negative gradient: w ← w − η∇L(w). Too small and it crawls, wasting budget and possibly stopping short; too large and it oscillates across the valley or diverges. In practice: use a schedule (decay, or one-cycle), monitor the loss curve rather than picking blind, and — most importantly for classical ML — scale your features first, because a badly conditioned surface makes the gradient point across the valley instead of along it, and no single learning rate works well for all directions.

Deep diveWhy does XGBoost use second-order gradients?

Expanding the loss to second order around the current predictions gives a quadratic in each leaf's output, which can be minimised in closed form: w*ⱼ = −Gⱼ/(Hⱼ + λ), where G and H are the summed gradients and Hessians in that leaf. That yields a principled split-gain formula ½[G_L²/(H_L+λ) + G_R²/(H_R+λ) − G²/(H+λ)] − γ, so the tree structure is chosen by the same objective the model optimises rather than by a proxy impurity measure. It also means the regularization terms λ and γ fall out of the derivation instead of being bolted on afterwards.

GotchaHow is Lasso actually fitted, given the L1 term isn't differentiable at zero?

By coordinate descent: cycle through coefficients, optimising one at a time with the others fixed. For each, the update has a closed form — the soft-thresholding operator S(ρ, λ) = sign(ρ)·max(|ρ|−λ, 0) — and that max(·, 0) is exactly what sets coefficients to precisely zero rather than merely small. So the sparsity isn't an artefact of a tolerance; it comes out of the optimiser's update rule. Sub-gradient methods also work but converge more slowly and don't give exact zeros as cleanly.

2.3 Probability & the base-rate fallacy ⭐

One worked example here transfers directly to fraud, screening and every imbalanced problem in Part 12 — which is why interviewers keep asking it.

The vocabulary, with the trap attached

  • Sensitivity = recall = TPR, specificity = 1 − FPR. These are properties of the test and do not depend on prevalence.
  • Precision (PPV) depends on prevalence — which is exactly why it changes when your model meets production traffic with a different base rate than your training sample.
  • Independence vs conditional independence. Two features can be dependent overall and independent given the class — the assumption Naive Bayes makes (§6.2). They can also be independent overall and dependent given a third variable, which is what a collider is, and conditioning on one is a classic way to manufacture a spurious association.
Base rates move, and your precision moves with them

A model validated on a 10%-positive sample and deployed into 2%-positive traffic will have far worse precision than you measured, even though nothing about the model changed — sensitivity and specificity held, but PPV is a function of prevalence. This is prior/label drift (§15.5), and the response is usually to re-threshold rather than retrain. Knowing that distinction is worth a lot in a production interview.

Likely interview questions
Very commonA test is 99% sensitive and 95% specific for a disease with 1% prevalence. You test positive. What's the probability you have it?

About 17%. Work it in counts, not fractions — it's faster and less error-prone. In 10,000 people: 100 sick, of whom 99 test positive; 9,900 healthy, of whom 5% = 495 test positive. So 594 positives, 99 real ⇒ 99/594 ≈ 16.7%. The lesson to state: with a rare condition, false positives from the huge negative population swamp the true positives, so a highly accurate test still fires wrongly most of the time. That is precision under imbalance, and it's the same arithmetic as a fraud alert queue.

GotchaYour model's precision dropped in production but sensitivity and specificity are unchanged. What happened?

The base rate fell. Sensitivity and specificity are properties of the classifier and don't depend on prevalence; precision does. If positives went from 10% to 2% of traffic, the same FPR now generates far more false positives relative to true ones, so PPV collapses without the model changing at all. This is prior/label drift, and the right response is usually to re-threshold (§12.7) rather than retrain — retraining fixes nothing if the relationship P(y|x) is stable.

ConceptualIndependence vs conditional independence — why does the distinction matter?

Because models make claims about one and not the other. Naive Bayes assumes features are independent given the class — not marginally — which is why it can work on obviously correlated features (§6.2). And the reverse case matters for causal reasoning: two independent variables can become dependent when you condition on a common effect (a collider), so adding a control variable can create a spurious association rather than removing one. That's the standard trap in §16.4.

2.4 Maximum likelihood & MAP — the bridge ⭐

The highest-value few minutes in this part. Every loss function you use is a maximum-likelihood statement in disguise, and every regularizer is a prior.

Maximum likelihood asks: which parameters make the observed data most probable? Write down an assumption about the noise, take the log, flip the sign, and a familiar loss falls out. This is not a coincidence or an analogy — it is a derivation, and being able to run it is what turns “we use MSE” into “we are assuming Gaussian noise, which is why outliers hurt us so much.”

What this buys you in an interview

Three answers become one idea. Why does MSE punish outliers so hard? Because it assumes Gaussian noise, whose tails are thin, so a large residual is enormously improbable and the fit contorts to explain it. Why use log loss instead of accuracy? Because log loss is the Bernoulli likelihood — a proper scoring rule, minimised by the true probability. What does α actually control in Ridge? The ratio σ²/τ² — how tight your prior belief is that coefficients are near zero, relative to the noise. Saying any one of those unprompted lands well.

Likely interview questions
Deep dive⭐ Show that Ridge is MAP estimation with a Gaussian prior.

With Gaussian noise the likelihood is p(y|X,w) ∝ exp(−‖y−Xw‖²/2σ²). Put a Gaussian prior p(w) ∝ exp(−‖w‖²/2τ²). The posterior is proportional to their product, so taking −log gives ‖y−Xw‖²/2σ² + ‖w‖²/2τ². Maximising the posterior means minimising that, which is exactly the Ridge objective with α = σ²/τ². Swap the Gaussian prior for a Laplace prior exp(−‖w‖₁/b) and the penalty becomes ‖w‖₁ — Lasso. A tighter prior (small τ) means stronger regularization, which gives α an interpretation rather than leaving it as a knob.

ConceptualWhy is least squares the "right" loss for regression?

It isn't, universally — it's the right loss if you believe the noise is Gaussian, because then minimising squared error is maximum likelihood. That framing tells you when it's wrong: heavy-tailed or contaminated noise makes the Gaussian assumption bad, and a single outlier will drag the fit a long way, which is why Huber (Gaussian centre, Laplace tails) or MAE exist. It also explains the deeper fact that MSE recovers the conditional mean while MAE recovers the median — different summaries of the same conditional distribution.

ConceptualWhat's the difference between MLE and MAP?

MLE maximises p(data | parameters); MAP maximises p(parameters | data) ∝ p(data|parameters)·p(parameters). The only difference is the prior, and in log space a prior is exactly a penalty term. So MAP = MLE + regularization, and as data grows the likelihood dominates and the two converge — which is the formal version of "regularization matters most when you have little data". Neither is fully Bayesian: both return a point estimate rather than a posterior distribution.

2.5 The statistics you actually use

Not hypothesis testing for its own sake — the statistics of comparing two models honestly and of not being fooled by a subgroup.

The two resampling tools that do the real work

  • The bootstrap. Resample your evaluation set with replacement, recompute the metric, repeat 1,000 times, take percentiles. That gives a confidence interval for any metric — including ones with no closed-form standard error, like AUC or a business KPI. For comparing two models, bootstrap the difference, resampling paired (same indices for both models), or your interval will be far too wide.
  • The permutation test. Shuffle the labels (or the model assignment) many times and see how often you'd see a difference this large by chance. Assumption-light, and it directly answers "could this gap be noise?"
What a p-value is not

It is not the probability the hypothesis is true, not the probability the result was chance, and not a measure of effect size. It is the probability of data at least this extreme under the null. If you evaluated forty model variants, several will clear p < 0.05 by construction — so report effect sizes with confidence intervals and correct for multiple comparisons. And note the sample-size trap in both directions: with a million rows, a meaningless difference is “significant”; with two hundred, a large real effect is not.

Likely interview questions
Very commonWhat is a p-value, and what is it not?

It's the probability of observing data at least as extreme as yours assuming the null hypothesis is true. It is not P(hypothesis is true), not P(result was chance), and not an effect size. Two practical consequences: with enough data any trivial difference becomes significant, so always report the effect size and a confidence interval; and if you tested many variants, some will pass by construction, so correct for multiple comparisons or treat the winner as a hypothesis to confirm rather than a result.

Very commonHow would you test whether model B is genuinely better than model A?

Paired comparison on the same folds or the same test rows — never independent samples, because that throws away the pairing and inflates the variance. Then a bootstrap confidence interval on the difference (resample indices once and score both models on the same resample), or a paired permutation test. If comparing across CV folds, note that plain t-tests are anti-conservative because training sets overlap, so use the corrected resampled t-test. And finish with practical significance: a 0.002 AUC gain that costs 10× the latency is not an improvement.

GotchaWhat is Simpson's paradox and when have you seen it in ML?

A trend present in every subgroup reverses or vanishes when the groups are pooled, because the groups differ in both exposure and baseline. In ML you meet it as: a model that beats the incumbent overall while losing on every segment (the mix changed); an A/B test where treatment wins overall but loses on both mobile and desktop — which is nearly always a sample-ratio mismatch bug rather than a real effect; and univariate feature screening that reverses sign once you condition. The fix is to condition on the confounder or randomise, and to always look at slices (§11.6).

2.6 Distance & similarity

Every distance-based method inherits two properties from its metric: it is meaningless without scaling, and it degrades in high dimensions.

MetricFormula / ideaUse it whenWatch out
Euclidean (L2)√Σ(xᵢ−yᵢ)²Continuous, comparable scalesDominated by the largest-variance feature if unscaled
Manhattan (L1)Σ|xᵢ−yᵢ|High dimensions, grid-like dataOften more robust than L2 when p is large
MinkowskiThe L_p familyTuning p as a hyperparameterRarely worth the search
Mahalanobis√((x−y)ᵀΣ⁻¹(x−y))Correlated features — it whitens by the covarianceNeeds a well-conditioned Σ estimate; fails when p ≈ n
CosineAngle, not magnitudeDirection matters, length doesn't (text, embeddings)Identical to L2 on unit-normed vectors
Jaccard / HammingSet overlap / bit differencesBinary vectors, sets, categorical codesIgnores counts entirely
GowerPer-feature normalised, then averagedMixed numeric + categorical rowsThe pragmatic answer for clustering real tabular data
The Mahalanobis intuition worth having

Euclidean distance treats a 1-unit move in every direction as equally surprising. Mahalanobis asks “how many standard deviations is this, accounting for how the features co-vary?” — so a point that is far along the axis of natural variation is not unusual, while a point that breaks the correlation structure is. That is exactly why it is a good multivariate outlier detector (§3.3), and why it reduces to plain Euclidean distance when Σ is the identity, i.e. after whitening.

Likely interview questions
ConceptualWhen would you use Mahalanobis distance over Euclidean?

When features are correlated and on different scales. Mahalanobis normalises by the covariance matrix, so it measures distance in units of natural variation — a point far along the main axis of the data isn't unusual, while one that violates the correlation structure is. That makes it a good multivariate outlier score. The cost: you need a stable estimate of Σ and its inverse, which fails when p is close to n or features are collinear — use a shrinkage estimator or fall back to a robust method like Isolation Forest.

PracticalHow do you compute distance for a table with both numeric and categorical columns?

Gower distance is the standard answer: compute a per-feature distance in [0,1] — normalised absolute difference for numeric, 0/1 mismatch for categorical, Jaccard for sets — then average (optionally weighted). Alternatives: one-hot the categoricals and use Euclidean, which implicitly weights a category by how many levels it has and is usually worse; or embed everything and use cosine. And the honest option: on tabular data, prefer a tree-based method that needs no metric at all.

2.7 The curse of dimensionality ⭐

Not a slogan — a measurable phenomenon, with a specific mechanism and a specific list of victims.

interactive Distance concentration, measured
—mean distance
—relative spread (σ/μ)
—d_near / d_far
—is kNN meaningful?

Real uniform points, real pairwise Euclidean distances. Drag p from 2 to 100 and watch the histogram collapse into a spike while d_near/d_far climbs toward 1. When that ratio approaches 1, “nearest neighbour” has stopped carrying information — every point is about the same distance from every other. Note that adding samples barely helps: the cure for the curse is fewer dimensions, not more rows.

Three distinct effects, often conflated

EffectMechanismWho suffers
Distance concentrationRelative spread of pairwise distances → 0, so near and far become indistinguishablekNN, k-means, DBSCAN, RBF-SVM, LOF
Empty spaceVolume grows exponentially; a fixed sample covers a vanishing fraction of it, so every region is sparseAny local method; density estimation
Capacity / overfittingMore features ⇒ more ways to fit noise ⇒ more varianceEverything, including trees — this is the one that matters most in practice

The third is why “more features can't hurt” is a trap answer (§17.16), and it applies even to models that are immune to the first two. A gradient boosting model is fine with distance concentration and still degrades if you hand it a thousand noisy columns — because each one gives the split search another chance to find a spurious threshold.

Why trees mostly escape it

A tree never computes a distance. It asks “is feature j above threshold t?” — a one-dimensional question at every node — so distance concentration and empty space simply don't apply. What does apply is the capacity effect, plus a subtler one: with many irrelevant features, random feature subsampling (max_features) starts picking mostly noise columns at each split, which weakens Random Forest specifically. That's a good argument for feature selection even on tree models (§13.5).

Likely interview questions
Very commonWhat is the curse of dimensionality and which models suffer most?

Three things bundled under one name. Distance concentration: as p grows, pairwise distances converge to a common value, so nearest and farthest neighbours become nearly equidistant and "local" stops meaning anything. Empty space: volume grows exponentially while your sample doesn't, so every neighbourhood is sparse. Capacity: more features means more ways to fit noise, hence more variance. The first two hit kNN, k-means, DBSCAN and RBF-SVM hardest; trees and tree ensembles escape them because they only ever ask one-dimensional threshold questions — but they still suffer the third.

GotchaDoes adding more training rows fix the curse of dimensionality?

Barely, for the geometric part. The volume of the space grows exponentially in p while your sample grows linearly, so to maintain the same density you'd need exponentially more data — which is why distance concentration persists across any realistic n (the widget above lets you verify this). More rows do help the capacity/overfitting effect. The real fixes are dimensionality reduction (PCA, §9.6), feature selection (§13.5), using a model that doesn't rely on distance, or embedding into a lower-dimensional space where the structure is genuinely lower-dimensional.

DebugYour kNN model works well on 8 features and collapses on 80. Why?

Distance concentration, most likely combined with irrelevant features diluting the metric. In 80 dimensions the distance between a point and its true nearest neighbour is nearly the same as to a random point, so the "neighbourhood" is arbitrary — and every irrelevant feature adds noise to the distance without adding signal. KD-trees and ball-trees won't save you either; above roughly 15–20 dimensions they degrade to brute-force scanning. Fixes: aggressive feature selection, a supervised metric (LDA projection, metric learning), PCA first, or switch to a tree ensemble that doesn't use a distance at all.

Part 3 of 17
Data Before Models
EDA, missingness, scaling, encoding, splitting, and the four kinds of leakage

3.1 EDA that earns its time

EDA is not a gallery of histograms. Its job is to answer three questions, and once they are answered you should stop and start modelling.

The checks worth automating

CheckWhat it catches
Row count vs distinct ID countNesting — the single most important fact for your split
Exact and near-duplicate rowsData-pipeline double-loads; the group-leakage source people forget
Cardinality per columnIDs masquerading as features; categorical columns that will explode under one-hot
Null rate per column, over timeA column that became all-null in March — the most common production incident (§15.5)
Target rate over timeDefinition drift, and whether a time split will even be comparable
Correlation with target, sortedThe top of this list is where leakage hides (§3.7)
Mutual informationNon-linear association that correlation misses entirely
Look at the target's timestamp, not just its value

The single most useful EDA question that nobody asks: when was each column recorded, relative to the target? A column that is populated only after the outcome — a closure date, a collection-call count, a resolution code — will dominate your model and will not exist at prediction time. Building a small table of column → when it becomes available takes an hour and prevents the most expensive class of mistake in this guide.

Likely interview questions
ConceptualWhat do you actually look for in EDA?

Three questions, then stop. What is a row? — nesting, duplicates, IDs posing as features, because this determines the split. What is the target? — base rate, skew, label noise, and critically when it was recorded. How will I split? — time index, groups, distribution shift over time, feature latency. Distributions, correlations and mutual information are inputs to those questions, not an end in themselves. I'd also automate null-rate-over-time and cardinality checks, because those become my production data-quality monitors later.

DebugOne feature has 0.94 correlation with the target. What do you do?

Celebrate cautiously and then investigate, because that is far more likely to be leakage than signal. I'd ask: what is this column, and when is it populated relative to the outcome? Is it a consequence of the target (a closure date, a collection flag), an ID proxy, or an aggregate computed over the full period including the future? Then I'd check whether the score collapses under a time-based split. Only after those three checks would I treat it as a genuine predictor — and even then I'd confirm it will exist at prediction time.

3.2 Missing data ⭐

The taxonomy is examinable, the indicator column is the trick nobody mentions, and the pipeline rule is non-negotiable.

The strategies, and what each one costs

StrategyWhat it doesCost
Listwise deletionDrop rows with any NaNUnbiased only under MCAR; can destroy most of your data, and biases everything under MAR/MNAR
Mean / median / modeConstant fillShrinks variance, distorts correlations, and asserts a certainty you don't have
kNN imputationFill from similar rowsNeeds a distance, so needs scaling; expensive; degrades in high dimensions (§2.7)
MICE / iterativeModel each column from the others, cyclingPrincipled under MAR; slow; must be fitted on the training fold only
Indicator columnadd_indicator=TrueAlmost free; use it alongside any of the above
Native handlingXGBoost/LightGBM learn a default direction per split; sklearn's HistGradientBoosting* takes NaN directlyUsually the best answer on tabular data — no imputation step to get wrong, and the model learns where missing values belong
Imputation is model-fitting

A median is a statistic learned from data. Computing it over the whole dataset before splitting leaks test information into training — the same class of error as scaling before splitting. Imputers belong inside the Pipeline, and the pipeline is fitted inside the CV loop. This is not pedantry: with a small validation set and a skewed column, whole-dataset imputation can move the CV score by a noticeable margin.

Likely interview questions
Very commonMCAR / MAR / MNAR — define them and say which is dangerous.

MCAR: missingness independent of everything observed and unobserved — deletion is unbiased, imputation is fine, and it's rare. MAR: missingness depends on observed variables (income missing more often among younger applicants) — model-based imputation like MICE is principled; this is the realistic common case. MNAR: missingness depends on the unobserved value itself (high earners decline to state income) — the dangerous one, because no imputation can recover it from the data alone. You either model the mechanism explicitly or flag the limitation. In all three cases add a missingness indicator.

PracticalHow do you impute, and where in the pipeline does imputation live?

On tabular data my first choice is often no imputation — let XGBoost/LightGBM learn a default direction for NaN, or use HistGradientBoosting, which handles it natively and usually beats hand-imputation. Otherwise: median/mode as a baseline (noting it shrinks variance), iterative/MICE under MAR, always with add_indicator=True. Wherever it happens, it lives inside the Pipeline and is fitted on the training fold only — a median is a statistic learned from data, so computing it over the whole dataset is train-test contamination.

GotchaWhy can missingness itself be a useful feature?

Because the fact that a value is absent often carries signal — an applicant who declines to state income, a customer with no support history, a device that reports no location. Under MNAR the missingness pattern is precisely what encodes the hidden value, so imputing it away destroys information. Add a was_missing indicator; it costs one column and is frequently one of the biggest single wins. Caveat worth adding: if missingness is an artefact of a system rather than the subject (a logging bug), the indicator will encode your pipeline's history and may not generalise.

DebugA column is 60% missing. Drop it or keep it?

Check three things before deciding. Is the missingness informative? Compare the target rate for missing vs present — if it differs, the indicator alone may be valuable even if the values aren't. Is it missing at random over time? A column that was fully populated until March and empty since is a pipeline break, not a data property, and the fix is upstream. Will it exist at serve time? If it's 60% missing in training and 99% missing in production, it's a liability. Often the right answer is: drop the values, keep the indicator.

3.3 Outliers & robustness

Detection is easy and mostly irrelevant. The judgement call is what the point is.

Before you touch an outlier, answer one question: is this a data error (a negative age, a misplaced decimal point), a rare but real event (a genuine £400,000 transaction), or exactly the thing you are trying to predict (fraud, equipment failure, a large claim)? Removing outliers from a fraud dataset is removing the positive class — and it happens more often than you would think, because the cleaning script ran before anyone looked at what it was deleting.

DetectionAssumptionHandlingWhen
z-score > 3Roughly Gaussian, univariateRemoveConfirmed data errors only
IQR fence (1.5×)Distribution-free, univariateClip / winsorizeHeavy tails you want bounded without deleting rows
MahalanobisMultivariate GaussianTransform (log, Yeo-Johnson)Skew rather than true outliers
Isolation ForestAnomalies are easy to isolateUse a robust modelThe default answer — trees, Huber loss, quantile regression
LOFLocal density variesRobust scaling (median/MAD)Clusters of differing density
Robust by construction beats robust by cleaning

Trees split on order, not magnitude, so a value of 10⁹ is just “the largest one” — they barely notice outliers. Huber loss is quadratic near zero and linear in the tails, so a single extreme residual has bounded influence. Quantile regression ignores magnitude entirely. Reaching for a robust loss is usually a better answer than deleting rows, because deletion is irreversible, unauditable, and silently changes what your metric means.

Likely interview questions
ConceptualHow do you handle outliers?

First classify them: data error, rare but real, or the thing I'm predicting. Errors get fixed or removed with a documented rule. Rare-but-real values get clipped or transformed if they're destabilising a linear model, or left alone if I'm using a tree. And if they are the target — fraud, failure, large claims — removing them is removing the positive class, which is a mistake I'd flag loudly. My default is to prefer a robust model or loss (trees, Huber, quantile) over cleaning, because cleaning is irreversible and changes what the metric means.

GotchaShould you remove outliers before fitting a gradient boosting model?

Usually no. Trees split on rank order, so an extreme value is simply "the largest" and has bounded influence on the split search — unlike a linear model, where one point can pivot the whole fit. The exception is the target: with squared loss, an extreme y value does distort the fit, because the gradient is proportional to the residual. There the answer is a robust objective (Huber, quantile, or a log-transformed target) rather than deleting rows.

3.4 Scaling & transformation ⭐

“Which models need scaling?” is asked in almost every interview, and the reason matters more than the list.

The transformer menu

TransformerWhat it doesReach for it when
StandardScalerZero mean, unit varianceDefault for roughly symmetric features
MinMaxScalerSquash to [0,1]Bounded inputs; very sensitive to outliers
RobustScalerMedian and IQROutliers you're keeping
MaxAbsScalerDivide by max |x|Sparse matrices — it preserves zeros, which StandardScaler destroys
QuantileTransformerMap to a uniform/normal distributionWild distributions; destroys linear relationships, so be deliberate
PowerTransformerYeo-Johnson / Box-CoxSkew, when you want to stay roughly interpretable (Box-Cox needs positive values)
NormalizerScales each row to unit normRarely what you want — it's for direction-only comparisons, not feature scaling
Log-transforming the target changes the loss

Fitting on log(y) and minimising MSE means you are optimising relative error, and exp(ŷ) gives you back the conditional median, not the mean — so summing predictions across rows will systematically under-shoot the total. That is often exactly what you wanted, but say it out loud, remember to invert before reporting error in the target's units, and if you need unbiased sums, use a Gamma or Tweedie GLM with a log link instead (§5.8), which models the same multiplicative structure without the retransformation bias.

Likely interview questions
Very commonWhich models need feature scaling and which don't — and why?

Need it: anything that measures distance (kNN, k-means, DBSCAN, RBF-SVM), maximises variance (PCA), or penalises coefficient magnitude (Ridge, Lasso, regularized logistic), plus neural nets for gradient conditioning. Don't: trees and every tree ensemble, because a split is a threshold on rank order and a monotone transform can't change which side of it a value falls on. Unregularized OLS doesn't need it either — the coefficient absorbs the units — but the moment a penalty appears, it does, because otherwise you're regularizing by choice of measurement unit.

GotchaYou have a sparse matrix. Which scaler?

MaxAbsScaler, or StandardScaler(with_mean=False). The reason: subtracting a mean turns every structural zero into a non-zero, which destroys sparsity and can blow up memory by orders of magnitude — on a large TF-IDF matrix that's the difference between fitting in RAM and not. MaxAbsScaler divides by the maximum absolute value per column, so zeros stay zeros and the data stays sparse.

DebugSomeone scaled the whole dataset then split. What's wrong, and how bad is it?

That's train-test contamination: the scaler's mean and variance were computed using validation rows, so information about them leaked into training. How bad depends — with a large balanced dataset the effect is small; with a small validation set, a skewed column, or a transformer that learns more (QuantileTransformer, PCA, target encoding) it can be substantial and produce a CV score that simply doesn't reproduce. The fix is structural rather than a judgement call: split first, put the scaler inside a Pipeline, and let cross-validation refit it per fold.

3.5 Categorical encoding ⭐

One-hot is the safe default, native handling is the modern default, and target encoding is the most common source of subtle leakage in the whole field.

EncodingDimensionsGood forDanger
One-hotk (or k−1)Low cardinality, linear modelsExplodes on high cardinality; dummy trap for linear models with an intercept
Ordinal1Genuinely ordered categories; treesImposes a false order on linear models — “Paris = 3” means nothing
Frequency / count1Cheap signal from popularityCollides distinct categories that happen to share a count
Hashingfixed dStreaming, unbounded vocabulariesCollisions; no inverse ⇒ no interpretability
Target / mean1High cardinality with real signalLeaks unless cross-fitted — see below
Native0CatBoost, LightGBM, HistGradientBoosting*Usually the best answer — no manual step to get wrong
Likely interview questions
Very commonWhat is target encoding and how do you do it without leaking?

Replace a category with a statistic of the target within it. Done naively it uses the row's own label, so the feature contains the target — CV soars, production collapses, and a category seen once becomes literally its own label. Do it out-of-fold / cross-fitted (each fold's encoding computed from the other folds), smoothed toward the global mean by count (n·ȳ_c + m·ȳ)/(n+m), with an explicit unknown bucket for serve-time categories — and all of it inside the pipeline. CatBoost's ordered target statistics solve it structurally by using only rows preceding each row in a random permutation.

DesignHow do you handle a categorical column with 50,000 levels?

One-hot is out — it creates 50,000 sparse, weak columns. In order of preference: native handling (CatBoost, LightGBM categorical splits, HistGradientBoosting) which is least likely to go wrong; cross-fitted target encoding with smoothing; frequency/count encoding as a cheap partial signal; hashing if the vocabulary is unbounded or streaming; and often the best one — group by a business hierarchy (merchant → merchant category → sector), which usually beats any statistical trick because it encodes real domain structure. I'd also add an unknown bucket, because at serve time you will see levels that weren't in training.

GotchaWhat's the dummy variable trap?

With an intercept term, k one-hot columns for a k-level categorical are perfectly collinear — they sum to 1 everywhere, which is exactly the intercept — so XᵀX is singular and the coefficients aren't uniquely identified. Drop one level (drop='first') for linear models with an intercept. It's harmless for trees and for regularized linear models, where the penalty breaks the tie — though it makes the coefficients harder to interpret, since they're now relative to an implicit baseline.

3.6 Splitting — where careers are made or lost ⭐⭐

One rule covers every case: your split must simulate how the model will actually be used. Random splits are the default and they are wrong more often than people think.

interactive Split strategy visualiser — watch the leak appear

60 rows · 12 customers × 5 rows each · ordered in time left-to-right, top-to-bottom. The contaminated customers count is exact: it is the number of customers whose rows land in more than one fold, meaning the model has seen that customer's other rows while being evaluated on them.

Pick the splitter from the structure in your data

StructureThe right splitterWhat goes wrong without it
None — rows are independentKFold—
Imbalanced classesStratifiedKFoldA fold with no positives; wild fold-to-fold variance
Rows nested in entitiesGroupKFold, StratifiedGroupKFoldGroup leakage — the model recognises the customer, not the pattern
Temporal orderTimeSeriesSplit + gapPredicting the past from the future; drift invisible until production
Both group and timeTime split, then verify groups don't straddle the boundaryThe realistic case, and the one people skip
Feature reporting latencyPurge + embargo around the boundaryFeatures built from data that wasn't available at prediction time
Spatial correlationSpatial blocking (split by region/tile)Neighbouring locations on both sides — the geospatial version of group leakage
Deduplicate before you split, not after

Near-duplicate rows are the group-leakage source people forget, because they don't look like groups. The same document scraped from two sources, an augmented copy, a record re-imported after a pipeline retry — split randomly and copies land on both sides, so the model is evaluated on rows it has effectively memorised. Dedupe first, using a key that reflects the real entity rather than an exact hash, then split.

Likely interview questions
Very commonWhen is a random split wrong? Give three cases.

(1) Grouped rows — many transactions per customer; a random split lets the model recognise the customer rather than the pattern, so use GroupKFold. (2) Temporal data — a random split trains on the future to predict the past and hides drift entirely; use TimeSeriesSplit with a gap. (3) Near-duplicates — deduplicate before splitting, or copies straddle the boundary. A fourth if they want more: spatial correlation, where neighbouring locations are effectively the same observation. The governing rule: your split must simulate how the model will be used.

ConceptualIs stratification a substitute for grouping?

No — they're orthogonal. Stratification balances the class distribution across folds; grouping ensures an entity appears in only one fold. You can have perfectly stratified folds that are riddled with group leakage, which the widget above demonstrates directly. When you need both, StratifiedGroupKFold approximates them jointly — approximately, because you can't always satisfy both exactly, and the fold-to-fold class balance will be less even as a result. Report the spread.

DesignHow do you validate when rows are grouped by customer AND ordered in time?

Time takes precedence, because that's what production looks like: train on everything before t, test after. Then verify no customer straddles the boundary in a way that matters — if a customer has rows on both sides, the model has seen their history, which may or may not be realistic depending on whether production scores existing customers or only new ones. Match the split to the deployment: for “score existing customers monthly”, straddling is fine and realistic; for “score new applicants”, it's leakage. Add a purge/embargo gap for feature latency either way.

GotchaHow many times can you look at the test set?

Once. Every additional look is a selection you haven't accounted for — if you evaluate ten variants on the test set and ship the best, that score is optimistically biased for exactly the reason nested CV exists (§11.3). In practice: do all development against cross-validation on the training data, and touch the test set at the end to produce the number you report. If you've already burned it, say so and treat the number as an upper bound rather than pretending.

3.7 Data leakage — the most examinable topic in ML ⭐⭐

If you learn one thing from this part, learn the four kinds, their shared symptom, and the one structural fix that prevents most of them.

interactive Leakage simulator — the CV score you'd have reported

A real simulation, not a mock-up: 800 rows are generated with a genuinely weak signal, each enabled leak adds a component to the validation-time score that was computed using the validation labels, and both AUCs are computed exactly by the Mann-Whitney rank formula. The production score never sees those channels — which is precisely what happens when the pipeline is refitted on training data alone.

The structural fix, stated precisely

Everything learned from data goes inside a Pipeline, and the pipeline is fitted inside the cross-validation loop. “Learned from data” is broader than people expect: a scaler's mean, an imputer's median, an encoder's category list, a feature selector's chosen subset, a resampler's synthetic points, PCA's components, a target encoder's per-category statistics. If any of those is computed before the split, validation information has entered training. That single rule prevents kind 2 entirely and makes kinds 3 and 4 much harder to commit by accident.

Likely interview questions
Very common⭐ What is data leakage? Name four distinct kinds.

Information available at training time that will not be available at prediction time. Target leakage: a feature that is a consequence of the target or recorded after it (account_closed_date, num_collection_calls). Train-test contamination: scaling, imputing, encoding, selecting features or resampling before the split. Temporal leakage: features computed over the whole period, or from the future. Group leakage: the same entity or a near-duplicate on both sides. Symptom in all four: an implausibly good validation score that collapses in production. Structural fix: everything learned from data goes inside a Pipeline, fitted inside the CV loop — plus a split that mimics deployment.

DebugYour model gets 0.99 AUC on validation and 0.62 in production. Walk me through your diagnosis.

That gap is leakage until proven otherwise. In order: (1) Sort feature importances and ask what the top feature is and when it's populated relative to the outcome — target leakage is the most common and most dramatic. (2) Check whether any transform was fitted outside the pipeline. (3) Re-run with a time-based split and see whether the score falls to the production level; if it does, you have temporal leakage or drift. (4) Check for duplicate IDs or near-duplicate rows across the split. (5) Only then consider non-leakage explanations: training/serving skew (§15.4), a base-rate shift, or a threshold that was never re-tuned.

GotchaIs it leakage to use the full dataset to decide which features to engineer?

Strictly, yes — and it's the kind everyone commits. Every time you look at a plot of feature-vs-target on the full data and decide to add an interaction, you've used validation information to make a modelling decision. It's rarely as damaging as fitting a transformer on all the data, but it's why held-out test sets get optimistic over a long project, and it's the reason for the “touch the test set once” discipline. The practical mitigation: do exploratory work on the training split only, and keep a genuinely untouched holdout for the final number.

ConceptualGive an example of temporal leakage that isn't obvious.

A "customer average order value" feature computed once, over the entire history, and joined onto every training row. For a row in January it silently includes orders from November — the future relative to that prediction. The model learns to rely on information it will never have at serve time, so validation looks strong and production doesn't. It's insidious because the feature looks perfectly reasonable and there's no timestamp in the column name. The fix is an as-of join against a time-versioned feature history (§13.7), which is the core reason feature stores exist.

3.8 Auditing someone else's pipeline

A very common practical exercise: you're handed a notebook with a suspiciously good score and asked what's wrong with it. Here is the checklist, in the order that finds problems fastest.

#CheckWhat it catches
1Is the split the first data operation? Scroll to the top and find it.Train-test contamination — the most common and easiest to spot
2Search for fit_transform and .fit( outside a PipelineScalers, imputers, encoders, selectors, SMOTE fitted on everything
3Sort feature importances. What is the top feature, and when is it recorded?Target leakage — usually one dominant, suspicious column
4Re-run with a time-based splitTemporal leakage and drift — the score should not collapse
5Check for duplicate IDs / near-duplicate rows across the splitGroup leakage
6Compare the CV score's variance across foldsVery low variance on a hard problem is itself suspicious
7Ask what the base rate and the majority baseline areAn impressive-looking accuracy that a constant predictor matches
8Look for the test set being used more than onceOptimistic selection bias (§11.3)
The drop tells you which kind

The most informative single diagnostic is comparing random CV against grouped CV against time-series CV. If grouped is much lower, you have group leakage. If time-series is much lower, you have temporal leakage or genuine drift — and distinguishing those two takes one more step: check whether the relationship changed (concept drift) or just the inputs (§15.5). If all three agree, your leak is either target leakage or contamination, and steps 1–3 will find it.

Likely interview questions
DebuggingHow would you detect leakage in someone else's notebook in five minutes?

Five checks in order. (1) Is the split the first data operation? (2) Search for fit_transform outside a pipeline. (3) Sort feature importances and ask what the top feature is and when it was recorded. (4) Re-run with a time-based split and see how far the score falls. (5) Check for duplicate IDs across train and test. Two bonus signals: unusually low variance across folds on a hard problem, and a single feature that reaches >0.90 AUC on its own. Those five catch the overwhelming majority of real leakage.

DebuggingRandom CV gives 0.91, grouped CV gives 0.68. What does that tell you?

Group leakage, and it's severe. Under random splitting the model is being evaluated on rows from entities it has already seen, so it can memorise entity-level idiosyncrasies rather than learning a transferable pattern — 0.68 is its actual ability to generalise to a new customer. Which number is right depends on deployment: if production only ever scores existing customers with history, 0.91 might be the honest estimate; if it scores new applicants, 0.68 is. That question — which population does production see? — is the one to ask before deciding.

Part 4 of 17
The Learning Problem
Loss functions, ERM, bias-variance, L1 vs L2, over- and underfitting

4.1 Loss functions ⭐

The loss defines what “best” means. Choosing MSE when the business cares about the median is a framing error, not a tuning error — and no amount of hyperparameter search will fix it.

§2.4 established that every common loss is a maximum-likelihood statement. This section is the practical consequence: each loss recovers a different summary of the conditional distribution, and you should pick the one the business acts on.

LossRecoversUse whenFailure mode
MSE / squaredThe conditional meanLarge errors are disproportionately bad; noise is roughly GaussianOne outlier drags the whole fit
MAE / absoluteThe conditional medianOutliers you can't clean; "typical error" is the business quantityNot differentiable at 0 (rarely a real issue); predictions can be less smooth
HuberMean, robustlyBoth — quadratic near zero, linear in the tails; δ sets the elbowOne more hyperparameter to choose
Pinball / quantileThe τ-th quantilePrediction intervals; asymmetric costs (stock-out vs overstock)Quantiles fitted separately can cross — check monotonicity
Log lossCalibrated probabilitiesAny time the probability itself is used downstreamPunishes confident mistakes very hard — which is usually the point
HingeA marginSVMsNo probability comes out of it
FocalEmphasis on hard examplesExtreme imbalance where easy negatives swamp the gradientAdds two hyperparameters; often threshold tuning is enough (§12.9)
Why we optimise log loss instead of accuracy

Accuracy is a step function of the parameters — flat almost everywhere, with a jump where a prediction flips. It has no useful gradient, so there is nothing for an optimiser to follow.
