Log loss is differentiable, convex in the linear model's parameters, and a proper scoring rule: it is minimised by the true probability, which is why it is the correct surrogate when you need probabilities rather than just a ranking. Brier score is the other proper rule you should be able to name.

Likely interview questions
ConceptualWhat does the loss function actually decide?

What "best" means. MSE recovers the conditional mean, MAE the median, pinball loss at τ the τ-th quantile, log loss calibrated probabilities. So "which loss?" is really "which summary of the conditional distribution does the business act on?" On a right-skewed target those summaries differ materially — optimising MSE when someone will act on a typical value is a framing error no amount of tuning will fix.

Very commonWhy do we optimise log loss rather than accuracy directly?

Accuracy is a step function of the parameters — flat everywhere with jumps where predictions flip — so it has no useful gradient and can't be optimised directly by gradient methods. Log loss is differentiable, convex in the linear model's parameters, and a proper scoring rule (minimised by the true probability), which is why it gives you well-behaved probabilities rather than just a ranking. It's also the Bernoulli likelihood, so it has a principled derivation rather than being a convenient surrogate.

DesignYour forecast is used to set inventory. Stock-outs cost 4× more than overstock. Which loss?

Pinball loss at τ = 0.8, because the optimal service level under those costs is c_under/(c_under + c_over) = 4/5. That fits the 80th percentile rather than the mean, so you deliberately over-forecast — which is exactly right when under-forecasting is four times worse. Using MSE here would give you the conditional mean and systematically under-stock. I'd also report coverage (what fraction of actuals fall below the forecast) to confirm the quantile is honest, and check that quantiles fitted at several τ don't cross.

GotchaWhen is Huber loss the right choice over MAE?

When you want robustness to outliers without giving up the efficiency of squared error on the bulk of the data. MAE treats a residual of 0.1 and 0.2 as equally informative per unit, so it can converge more slowly and produce less stable fits; Huber is quadratic within δ (efficient, like MSE) and linear outside it (bounded influence, like MAE). Practically: use Huber when most residuals are small and well-behaved but a handful are extreme. The cost is choosing δ, which is often set from a robust scale estimate like the MAD.

4.2 Empirical risk minimization & generalization

You minimise error on the sample you have and hope it transfers. Everything about validation exists because that hope needs checking.

The quantity you want to minimise is the true risk — expected loss over the real data distribution. You cannot compute it, so you minimise the empirical risk — average loss on your sample — and rely on the two converging. That convergence needs the sample to be representative (the i.i.d. assumption) and the hypothesis class not to be so flexible that it can fit any sample perfectly.

Where the i.i.d. assumption actually breaks

ViolationReal exampleConsequence
Not independentMany rows per customer; sequential observationsEffective sample size is far smaller than n; CV is optimistic (§3.6)
Not identically distributed over timePrices, fraud patterns, user mix all driftYesterday's risk estimate doesn't bound tomorrow's (§15.5)
Sampling biasOnly approved applicants have outcomesYou estimate risk on a selected population — the reject-inference problem (§15.7)
FeedbackThe model's decisions change who you observeThe distribution is no longer exogenous at all
Likely interview questions
ConceptualWhat is empirical risk minimization, and what does it assume?

You want to minimise true risk — expected loss over the real distribution — but you can't compute it, so you minimise empirical risk on your sample and rely on the two converging. That relies on the sample being i.i.d. from the deployment distribution and the hypothesis class being constrained enough that fitting the sample means something. Both assumptions break routinely in practice: rows nested in customers aren't independent, distributions drift over time, and selection bias means you only observe outcomes for a filtered population. Each break is why a specific validation technique exists.

ConceptualWhat is the "no free lunch" theorem and what does it imply practically?

Averaged over all possible problems, no algorithm outperforms any other — superiority comes entirely from assumptions matching the problem structure. Practically: there is no universally best model, which is exactly why benchmarking is a step in the process rather than a formality, and why "always use XGBoost" is a well-calibrated heuristic about the distribution of real tabular problems rather than a theorem. It also justifies spending effort on the inductive bias — feature engineering, monotonic constraints, the right loss — rather than only on the algorithm.

ModernWhat is double descent, and does it matter for tabular ML?

Beyond the classical U-curve, test error can rise to a peak near the interpolation threshold (roughly where parameters ≈ samples) and then fall again as capacity grows further — well documented in over-parameterised models. It matters for tabular ML mostly as a fact you should know rather than one you'll exploit: with regularized GBMs on structured data you're firmly in the classical regime, and early stopping keeps you there. Mentioning it shows currency; claiming the U-curve is obsolete would show the opposite.

4.3 Bias, variance and the decomposition ⭐⭐

Be able to write E[(y − f̂)²] = Bias² + Variance + σ², and — more importantly — to diagnose which term you are suffering from using two numbers you already have.

interactive Fit a polynomial and watch the decomposition move
—train MSE
—validation MSE
—gap (val − train)
—diagnosis

Real least-squares fits, solved by Gaussian elimination on the normal equations with inputs mapped to [−1,1] for conditioning. Try: degree 1 (both errors high and close — bias). Degree 12 with 20 points (train ≈ 0, validation explodes — variance). Then raise the training points to 80 and watch the variance problem shrink while the bias problem at degree 1 does not move at all.

The decomposition, term by term

Bias² Error from wrong assumptions
Means
The model class cannot represent the true function, no matter how much data you give it. A straight line fitted to a curve.
Symptom
Training error is high, and validation error is close to it.
Fix
More capacity (deeper trees, higher degree, more boosting rounds), better features, weaker regularization. More data will not help.
Variance Sensitivity to the particular sample
Means
Refit on a different sample from the same distribution and you get a noticeably different function. The model is fitting noise.
Symptom
Training error is low and validation error is far above it.
Fix
More data, more regularization, less capacity, bagging (which attacks variance directly), feature selection.
σ² Irreducible noise
Means
Two identical rows can have different outcomes. Includes genuine randomness and label noise.
Symptom
A floor your validation error never goes below, no matter what you do.
If you beat it
You are memorising noise, or you have leakage. A model that beats the label-noise rate is not learning (§16.7).
The subtlety worth adding

The decomposition is exact for squared loss and only heuristic for others — there is no equally clean bias-variance split for log loss or 0-1 loss (several competing definitions exist, and they disagree). Saying that takes four seconds and shows you know it as a theorem rather than a slogan.

Likely interview questions
Very common⭐ Explain the bias-variance trade-off. Write the decomposition.

E[(y − f̂(x))²] = Bias[f̂]² + Var[f̂] + σ². Bias is error from wrong assumptions — the model class can't represent the truth. Variance is sensitivity to the particular training sample. σ² is irreducible noise. Diagnosis from two numbers: both errors high and close ⇒ bias; train low and validation far above ⇒ variance. Levers: complexity, regularization strength, feature count, tree depth, k, ensemble size. The one-liner they're listening for: bagging reduces variance, boosting reduces bias. And the credit-earning caveat: the decomposition is exact only for squared loss.

DebugTrain MSE 0.02, validation MSE 0.31. What's wrong and what do you do?

High variance — a gap that large means the model is fitting sample-specific noise. In order of what I'd try: more regularization (raise alpha, lower max_depth, raise min_samples_leaf), fewer features if many are noisy, bagging or a larger ensemble, and more data if it's obtainable — a learning curve tells me whether that will help. What I would not do is add capacity. And before any of it, I'd check for leakage in reverse: a gap this large sometimes means the validation set is genuinely different (a time or group boundary), not that the model is overfitting.

ConceptualWhich knobs move bias and which move variance?

Toward less bias, more variance: deeper trees, more leaves, higher polynomial degree, smaller k in kNN, larger C in SVM, more boosting rounds, more features. Toward less variance, more bias: stronger L1/L2, shallower trees, larger min_samples_leaf, larger k, smaller C, early stopping, feature selection. Two special cases worth naming: bagging reduces variance with almost no bias cost (which is why n_estimators in a Random Forest isn't a regularization knob), and more data reduces variance without touching bias at all.

GotchaDoes the bias-variance decomposition apply to classification?

Not cleanly. The exact additive decomposition Bias² + Var + σ² holds for squared loss. For 0-1 loss and log loss there are several proposed decompositions (Kong-Dietterich, Domingos, James) and they don't agree — variance can even reduce error on the wrong side of a boundary. The intuition transfers perfectly and is what interviewers want; the mathematics doesn't. Saying that explicitly is a small, cheap signal that you learned it properly.

4.4 L1 vs L2 regularization ⭐⭐

One of the three most-asked questions in classical ML. The complete answer has a geometric half, a probabilistic half and a practical half — give all three and the question is finished.

interactive Ridge vs Lasso on correlated features — sweep α
—Ridge · exact zeros
—Lasso · exact zeros
—Ridge · val MSE
—Lasso · val MSE

Genuinely fitted: Ridge by solving (XᵀX + αI)w = Xᵀy directly, Lasso by cyclic coordinate descent with the soft-threshold operator. Eight standardised features — x₀…x₃ carry signal (x₂ and x₃ are 0.97-correlated with each other), x₄…x₇ are pure noise. Push α up and watch Ridge shrink everything smoothly while Lasso sets coefficients to exactly zero, killing noise first — and then, revealingly, dropping one of the correlated pair rather than splitting the credit.

The geometric half

The probabilistic half

From §2.4: Ridge is MAP with a Gaussian prior on the coefficients, Lasso is MAP with a Laplace prior. The Laplace density has a sharp spike at zero, so the posterior mode genuinely lands there — the sparsity is not an artefact of the optimiser but a consequence of the prior. This also gives α a meaning: it is σ²/τ², the ratio of noise variance to prior variance, i.e. how strongly you believe coefficients are near zero relative to how noisy the data is.

The practical half

L2 / RidgeL1 / LassoElastic Net
Effect on coefficientsShrinks smoothly, never exactly zeroDrives some to exactly zeroBoth
Feature selectionNoYes, automaticallyYes, in groups
Correlated featuresShrinks them together; handles collinearity wellPicks one arbitrarily, zeroes the rest — unstable across refitsKeeps the group together — this is why it exists
When p > nFineSelects at most n featuresNo such limit
Closed formYes — (XᵀX + αI)⁻¹XᵀyNo — coordinate descentNo
Reach for it whenMany small effects; collinearity; you want stabilityYou believe few features matter and want a sparse modelCorrelated groups, or you don't know which of the above
Standardise before you regularize

The penalty α‖w‖ treats every coefficient on the same footing. If income is in pounds and age in years, their coefficients live on wildly different scales and the penalty falls almost entirely on one of them — you are regularizing by choice of measurement unit. Always standardise inside the pipeline, and note that the intercept is conventionally left unpenalised (there's no reason to shrink the baseline toward zero).

Likely interview questions
Very common⭐ L1 vs L2 — what does each do, and why does L1 produce exact zeros?

L2/Ridge shrinks coefficients smoothly, handles multicollinearity by re-conditioning XᵀX + αI, and never reaches exactly zero. L1/Lasso drives coefficients to exactly zero, so it does feature selection. Three reasons for the zeros: Geometric — the L1 constraint region is a diamond whose corners lie on the axes, and elliptical loss contours generically first touch it at a corner. Probabilistic — Lasso is MAP with a Laplace prior, whose density spikes at zero, so the posterior mode lands there. Algorithmic — coordinate descent's soft-thresholding update literally contains a max(·, 0). Then the practical caveat: Lasso is unstable with correlated features, and Elastic Net fixes that.

Very commonWhy must you standardise features before regularizing?

The penalty is on coefficient magnitude, and magnitude depends on the feature's units. Income in pounds and age in years produce coefficients orders of magnitude apart, so the penalty lands almost entirely on one feature — you'd be regularizing by choice of measurement unit rather than by any belief about importance. Standardise inside the pipeline so it's refitted per fold, and leave the intercept unpenalised. Note this is exactly why unregularized OLS doesn't need scaling: the coefficient absorbs the units and nothing compares across features.

ConceptualWhen would you use Elastic Net over Lasso?

With groups of correlated features. Lasso picks one essentially arbitrarily and zeroes the rest, and picks a different one on a slightly different sample — fine for prediction, bad for stability and interpretation, and confusing for anyone who has to explain the model. Elastic Net's L2 component makes correlated coefficients shrink together so the group survives or dies as a unit. Also when p > n: Lasso can select at most n features by construction; Elastic Net has no such cap. The cost is a second hyperparameter (l1_ratio).

GotchaDoes regularization change the bias-variance balance? In which direction?

It adds bias to remove variance. The penalty pulls coefficients away from their unbiased least-squares values — so the estimator is deliberately biased — but it shrinks the variance more than the bias grows, over a useful range of α. That's the whole trade, and it's why there's an optimal α rather than "more is better": push α too far and bias dominates, which is visible in the widget above as validation MSE turning back upward. Worth adding: Ridge can beat OLS in MSE even when OLS is unbiased, which is a nice concrete demonstration that unbiasedness is not the goal.

4.5 Regularization beyond penalties

“Name three regularization techniques that aren't a penalty term” is a common follow-up, and it separates people who learned the concept from people who learned the formula.

KindExamplesMechanism
PenaltyL1, L2, Elastic Net, group lassoAdds a cost for coefficient magnitude
Structuralmax_depth, min_samples_leaf, num_leaves, max_features, polynomial degreeLimits the hypothesis space directly — the model literally cannot express complex functions
StochasticRow subsampling, column subsampling, bagging, dropoutDecorrelates and injects noise, so no single pattern can be relied on
Implicit / early stoppingStop boosting when validation stops improvingHalts before the model reaches full capacity. In boosting, early stopping ≈ shrinkage — they trade off against each other
DataMore data, augmentation, noise injection, label smoothingRaises the bar for memorisation — the same pattern must hold across more cases
ConstraintMonotonic constraints, interaction constraints, non-negativityEncodes domain knowledge as a hard restriction; strong regularizer and a compliance tool (§8.6)
EnsemblingAveraging several modelsVariance reduction without a bias cost (§8.1)
Monotonic constraints are underrated as regularization

Most people know them as a compliance feature — “risk must not decrease as debt rises”. They are also one of the strongest regularizers available on tabular data, because they eliminate an enormous fraction of the hypothesis space using genuine domain knowledge rather than a generic penalty. On small or noisy datasets they frequently improve held-out performance, not just interpretability, and they make the model far more robust to drift. Mentioning that dual role is a strong signal.

Likely interview questions
ConceptualName three regularization techniques that aren't a penalty term.

Structural: tree depth, min_samples_leaf, num_leaves, max_features — these limit the hypothesis space directly. Stochastic: row and column subsampling, bagging, dropout — inject noise so no single pattern can be relied on. Implicit: early stopping, which halts before full capacity is reached and in boosting is approximately equivalent to shrinkage. Two more if they want them: constraints (monotonic and interaction constraints, which are strong regularizers as well as compliance tools) and more data, which raises the bar for memorisation.

ConceptualWhy is early stopping considered regularization?

Because it limits the effective capacity the model reaches. In boosting, each round adds capacity and moves the fit further from the initial constant prediction; stopping early leaves the model closer to that simple starting point, which is functionally the same as shrinking coefficients toward zero. There's a formal correspondence for gradient descent on a linear model: the number of steps and the L2 penalty trade off almost exactly. Practically it means learning rate and number of rounds are not independent knobs — halve the learning rate and you'll need roughly twice the rounds for the same effective complexity.

4.6 Overfitting & underfitting in practice ⭐

The question is never “what is overfitting”. It is “how do you know which one you have, and will more data help?” — and learning curves answer both.

Reading a learning curve, precisely

ShapeReadingAction
Both curves converged, above targetHigh biasMore capacity, better features, less regularization. Not more data
Large gap, still narrowingHigh variance, data-limitedMore data will help; also more regularization or bagging
Large gap, flatHigh variance, capacity-limitedMore data won't close it — reduce capacity or regularize
Both converged at targetYou're doneShip it; spend effort on serving and monitoring
Validation below trainingUsually a bugCheck for leakage in reverse, a mis-stratified split, or a regularizer active only at train time
Validation erratic across sizesValidation set too smallUse CV rather than a single hold-out; report the spread
Label noise sets a ceiling

If 8% of your labels are wrong, no model can be more than ~92% right on that measurement — and a model that beats the noise rate is memorising the noise, not learning. Before blaming the algorithm, audit 200 random labels. This is the practical face of the data-centric argument in §16.7, and it is why “we'll fix it with a better model” is a trap answer (§17.16).

Likely interview questions
Very commonOverfitting vs underfitting — how do you diagnose which one you have?

Two numbers. Training error high and validation error close to it ⇒ high bias / underfitting: add capacity, add features, reduce regularization. Training error low and validation error far above ⇒ high variance / overfitting: more data, more regularization, less capacity, bagging. Then confirm with a learning curve, which also answers the follow-up about whether more data will help. One caution: a huge gap can also mean the validation set is genuinely different — a time or group boundary — rather than the model overfitting, so check the split before concluding.

Very commonWill more data help? How do you know?

Plot a learning curve — training and validation error against training-set size. If both have converged and sit above your target, you have a bias problem and more data will do nothing: change the model, the features, or the regularization. If a substantial gap is still narrowing as size grows, more data will help, and you can extrapolate roughly how much you'd need. The compact statement: more data fixes variance, not bias. And it's worth costing: if 2× the data buys 0.005 AUC, that's a business decision, not a modelling one.

DebuggingValidation error is lower than training error. What's going on?

Almost always a bug or an artefact, not good news. Common causes: regularization active only at training time (dropout, or noise injection) so training loss is measured on a handicapped model; a validation split that's easier — mis-stratified, or a time period with lower base rate; leakage in the other direction, where validation rows appeared in training; or simply a validation set too small to be stable. I'd check the split composition first, then whether training loss is being measured with the regularizer applied.

GotchaYour model hits 99% accuracy on a task humans do at 92%. Good news?

No — that's a red flag. If human agreement is 92%, the labels themselves contain roughly 8% noise, which sets a ceiling: a model that beats it isn't learning the concept, it's memorising the specific noise pattern in your labels. The likely explanations are leakage (§3.7) or test-set contamination. I'd check the label-generation process, measure inter-annotator agreement properly, and audit 200 random cases where the model and the label disagree — that audit usually explains it within an hour.

4.7 Discriminative vs generative

A clean conceptual axis that interviewers use to test whether you understand models rather than remember them.

Likely interview questions
ConceptualDiscriminative vs generative — an example and a trade-off.

Discriminative models P(y|x) directly: logistic regression, SVM, trees, GBMs. Generative models the joint P(x,y) and derives the posterior by Bayes' rule: Naive Bayes, LDA/QDA, GMM, HMM. Generative imposes more structure so it needs less data, handles missing features naturally, and can sample; discriminative typically wins on accuracy with enough data because all its capacity goes into the boundary rather than into modelling the inputs. Same axis as HMM vs CRF in sequence labelling.

Deep diveIs there a case where a generative model beats a discriminative one on the same data?

Yes, in the small-sample regime. The classic result (Ng & Jordan) compares Naive Bayes with logistic regression on the same features: Naive Bayes has higher asymptotic error because its independence assumption is wrong, but it converges to that error much faster — so with few training examples it wins, and the discriminative model overtakes it only once there's enough data. That's the practical version of "more structure means less data needed". It also explains why generative methods persist in domains where labelled data is genuinely scarce.

Part 5 of 17
Linear Models
Every assumption and what breaks, diagnostics, VIF, logistic, GLMs, quantile regression

5.1 The model, and how it is actually fitted ⭐

Everyone can write y = Xw + ε. The interview is in the three follow-ups: how it's solved, why nobody solves it that way, and what “linear” actually constrains.

From loss to normal equations

Minimise L(w) = (Xw − y)ᵀ(Xw − y). The gradient is 2Xᵀ(Xw − y); setting it to zero gives the normal equations XᵀXw = Xᵀy, hence w = (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy when XᵀX is invertible. Geometrically, Xŵ is the orthogonal projection of y onto the column space of X — which is why the residual is perpendicular to every column, and therefore why residuals always sum to zero when you include an intercept.

Why nobody computes the inverse

Problem with (XᵀX)⁻¹ConsequenceWhat's used instead
Singular under perfect collinearityNo unique solution — the inverse doesn't existSVD / pseudo-inverse returns the minimum-norm solution
Cost is O(p³) plus O(np²) to form XᵀXProhibitive for large pQR decomposition, or iterative methods for huge problems
Forming XᵀX squares the condition numberYou lose roughly half your significant digits before you startQR or SVD on X directly — which is what lstsq does

Scikit-learn's LinearRegression calls scipy.linalg.lstsq, which uses an SVD-based driver. So the closed form is the right thing to derive and the wrong thing to implement — and saying exactly that is the complete answer.

“Linear” means linear in the parameters

A very common misunderstanding. y = w₀ + w₁x + w₂x² + w₃log(x) + w₄(x₁·x₂) is still a linear model — it is linear in w, which is all the maths requires. What is not linear is y = w₀·x^w₁. This matters practically: you can fit curves, interactions and splines with ordinary least squares simply by expanding the feature matrix, which is exactly what PolynomialFeatures and SplineTransformer do.

Likely interview questions
Very commonDerive the normal equation, and say why you'd avoid computing (XᵀX)⁻¹.

Minimise (Xw−y)ᵀ(Xw−y); the gradient is 2Xᵀ(Xw−y); setting it to zero gives XᵀXw = Xᵀy, so w = (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy. Three reasons not to compute it that way: it's singular under perfect collinearity; it costs O(p³); and critically, forming XᵀX squares the condition number, so you lose roughly half your significant digits before solving. Use QR or SVD on X directly — which is what lstsq, and therefore sklearn, actually does.

ConceptualIs a model with x² and log(x) terms still a linear model?

Yes. "Linear" refers to linearity in the parameters, not the features — y = w₀ + w₁x + w₂x² + w₃log(x) is linear in w, which is all least squares needs. That's why you can fit arbitrary curves, interactions and splines by expanding the design matrix and still use OLS. A genuinely non-linear model would be something like y = w₀·x^{w₁}, where a parameter appears in an exponent.

Deep diveWhat's the geometric interpretation of least squares?

Xŵ is the orthogonal projection of y onto the column space of X — the closest point in the space your features can reach. The residual vector is therefore perpendicular to every column of X, which is exactly what the normal equations Xᵀ(y − Xŵ) = 0 state. Two immediate consequences: residuals sum to zero whenever an intercept is included (since the intercept is a column of ones), and residuals are uncorrelated with every fitted feature — which is why a pattern in a residual plot always signals a missing structure rather than a fitting failure.

5.2 The assumptions, one by one ⭐⭐

“State the assumptions of linear regression” is asked constantly and answered badly. Here is each one with what it means, what breaks when it fails, how you detect it, and what you do about it — which is the answer that finishes the question.

interactive Break an assumption and watch the residual plot
—fitted slope (true = 2.00)
—reported std. error
—R²
—what's damaged

Real OLS on real generated data. The point of the middle panel: the residual-vs-fitted plot has a distinct signature for each violation, which is why it is the first plot you draw. Note also what the numbers do — some violations bias the coefficient, others leave the coefficient fine and corrupt only the standard error. Knowing which is which is the substance of this section.

The five assumptions

A1 Linearity — the relationship really is linear in the parameters
Means
E[y|X] = Xw. The conditional mean is a linear combination of your features (which may themselves be non-linear transforms).
What breaks
Biased predictions and biased coefficients. This is the only violation that makes the model wrong rather than merely inefficient — you are estimating the best linear approximation to something that isn't linear, and it will be systematically off in whole regions of the feature space.
Detect
Residual vs fitted plot showing curvature; partial-residual (component-plus-residual) plots per feature; a RESET test; or simply comparing against a GBM — if a tree model beats your linear one by a lot, you're missing structure.
Fix
Add polynomial terms, splines (SplineTransformer — usually better behaved than high-degree polynomials), interactions, or transform the target. Or accept it and use a non-linear model.
A2 Independence of errors — no autocorrelation or clustering
Means
Cov(εᵢ, εⱼ) = 0 for i ≠ j. Each observation contributes independent information.
What breaks
Coefficients stay unbiased, but standard errors are badly wrong — usually far too small, because your effective sample size is much less than n. Every p-value and confidence interval is then overconfident. In ML terms: your cross-validation is optimistic for exactly the same reason (§3.6).
Detect
Residuals plotted in time order showing runs or waves; the Durbin-Watson statistic (≈2 is fine, <1.5 or >2.5 suspicious); an ACF plot of residuals; or knowing structurally that rows are nested (many rows per customer).
Fix
Cluster-robust standard errors; add lag features or model the time structure explicitly; use a mixed-effects model for nesting; and for ML purposes, GroupKFold or TimeSeriesSplit.
A3 Homoscedasticity — constant error variance
Means
Var(ε|X) = σ², the same everywhere. Errors on large predictions are no bigger than errors on small ones.
What breaks
Coefficients stay unbiased but inefficient (no longer minimum-variance), and standard errors are wrong — so inference is unreliable. Prediction intervals are also wrong, being too wide where variance is low and too narrow where it is high, which is often exactly where the expensive mistakes are.
Detect
The classic fan or cone shape in the residual-vs-fitted plot; a scale-location plot (√|standardised residual| vs fitted) with a rising trend; Breusch-Pagan or White's test.
Fix
Robust (heteroscedasticity-consistent) standard errors — HC3 — if you only need valid inference; a log or Box-Cox transform of the target; weighted least squares if you know the variance structure; or a GLM with a variance function that matches (Gamma or Tweedie, §5.8), which is usually the principled answer when variance grows with the mean.
A4 Normality of errors — only needed for inference
Means
ε ~ N(0, σ²). Note this is about the residuals, not about y or the features — a very common confusion.
What breaks
Nothing, for prediction. Gauss-Markov gives you BLUE (best linear unbiased estimator) without it. Normality is needed for exact t- and F-tests and confidence intervals in small samples — and by the CLT even that requirement fades as n grows. This is the assumption most candidates over-weight.
Detect
Q-Q plot of residuals (points off the diagonal in the tails), a histogram, Shapiro-Wilk — though with large n every normality test rejects, so read the plot rather than the p-value.
Fix
Usually do nothing if you only care about prediction. If you need inference: transform the target, use bootstrap confidence intervals (assumption-free), or switch to a GLM with the right family. Heavy tails often really mean outliers (A5) or a missing feature (A1).
A5 No perfect multicollinearity — and no high leverage you haven't noticed
Means
No feature is an exact linear combination of the others, so XᵀX is invertible and the coefficients are identified.
What breaks
Perfect collinearity: no unique solution at all. Near-collinearity: coefficients remain unbiased but their variance explodes — signs flip between refits, magnitudes swing wildly, and individual t-tests become insignificant while the model as a whole is highly significant. Predictions are usually fine; interpretation is destroyed.
Detect
VIF = 1/(1−R²ⱼ) above ~5–10; correlation matrix; the condition number of X; the tell-tale pattern of a high overall F-statistic with no individually significant coefficients (§5.4).
Fix
Drop one of the pair, combine them into a ratio or index, use PCA, or use Ridge — which re-conditions the problem directly by adding αI. Also check leverage and Cook's distance for single points with outsized influence (§5.3).
The two facts that separate a strong answer

(1) Normality is for inference, not prediction. If you're building a predictive model and someone asks whether your residuals are normal, the correct answer is that it doesn't affect the prediction — it affects the p-values you probably aren't using. (2) Only violated linearity biases the coefficients. Autocorrelation and heteroscedasticity leave the estimates unbiased and corrupt the uncertainty. Knowing which failures cost you accuracy and which cost you only inference is the substance of the question, and almost nobody separates them.

The one nobody lists: exogeneity

Strictly, the assumption that makes OLS unbiased is E[ε|X] = 0 — the errors are uncorrelated with the features. Omitted-variable bias, measurement error in a feature, and simultaneity all violate it, and no residual plot will reveal it because the residuals are orthogonal to X by construction. It is invisible to diagnostics and only addressable by design — which is precisely the gap that instrumental variables and the rest of §16.4 exist to fill. Mentioning it marks you out.

Likely interview questions
Very common⭐ State the assumptions of linear regression and what breaks when each fails.

Linearity — fails ⇒ biased predictions and coefficients, visible as curvature in the residual plot; fix with splines, polynomials, interactions, or a non-linear model. Independent errors — fails with time or clustered data ⇒ coefficients unbiased but standard errors far too small; detect with residuals in time order or Durbin-Watson; fix with cluster-robust SEs, lag features, or GroupKFold/TimeSeriesSplit for ML. Homoscedasticity — fails ⇒ unbiased but inefficient, wrong SEs and wrong prediction intervals; detect via a fan shape or Breusch-Pagan; fix with robust SEs, a log transform, WLS, or a GLM with the right variance function. Normality of residuals — needed only for exact inference in small samples, not for prediction; detect with a Q-Q plot; usually do nothing, or bootstrap. No perfect multicollinearity — fails ⇒ no unique solution; near-failure inflates coefficient variance so signs flip; detect with VIF > 5–10; fix by dropping, combining, or using Ridge. And the one people miss: exogeneity, E[ε|X]=0, which is what actually makes OLS unbiased and is invisible to every diagnostic.

GotchaDo the residuals need to be normally distributed?

Only if you need exact inference — t-tests, F-tests and confidence intervals in small samples. For prediction it doesn't matter at all: Gauss-Markov gives you the best linear unbiased estimator using only linearity, exogeneity, homoscedasticity and no perfect collinearity — normality is nowhere in it. And by the CLT, even the inference requirement fades as n grows. Two clarifications worth adding: the assumption is about the residuals, not y or the features; and heavy-tailed residuals usually signal an outlier or a missing feature rather than a genuine distributional problem.

DebuggingYour residual plot shows a clear fan shape. What is it, and does it matter?

Heteroscedasticity — error variance grows with the fitted value, which is extremely common for positive, right-skewed targets like spend or claim amounts. Consequences: coefficients stay unbiased, but they're no longer minimum-variance and the standard errors are wrong, so inference is unreliable — and prediction intervals are too narrow exactly where the values are largest. Fixes in order of preference: a GLM with a matching variance function (Gamma or Tweedie with a log link) since variance genuinely scales with the mean; a log transform of the target; robust HC3 standard errors if I only need valid inference; or weighted least squares if I know the variance structure.

DebuggingResiduals show a clear wave pattern when plotted in time order. What's the problem?

Autocorrelation — the errors aren't independent, so consecutive observations carry overlapping information. The coefficients remain unbiased, but the effective sample size is much smaller than n, so standard errors are far too small and everything looks more significant than it is. Confirm with Durbin-Watson (≈2 fine, <1.5 suspicious) or an ACF plot of residuals. Fix by modelling the time structure (lags, seasonal terms), using cluster/HAC-robust standard errors, or — for the ML version of the same problem — switching from random CV to TimeSeriesSplit with a gap, because a random split is optimistic for exactly this reason.

Deep diveWhich assumption violations bias the coefficients, and which only affect inference?

Bias the coefficients: violated linearity (you're fitting the wrong functional form) and violated exogeneity (E[ε|X] ≠ 0 — omitted variables, measurement error, simultaneity). Leave coefficients unbiased but corrupt inference: heteroscedasticity and autocorrelation, both of which make standard errors wrong while the point estimates stay centred on the truth. Neither, exactly: non-normal residuals, which affect only small-sample exact tests. Multicollinearity is its own case — unbiased but enormously high variance, so individual coefficients become unreliable while predictions stay fine. Separating these four cases is what makes the answer sound like you've used the model rather than read about it.

5.3 Residual diagnostics ⭐

Four plots, each with a distinct signature. Being able to name the plot and what a bad one looks like is the practical half of §5.2.

Likely interview questions
PracticalWhich diagnostic plots do you look at, and what does each tell you?

Residuals vs fitted — the first one: curvature means non-linearity, a fan means heteroscedasticity, random scatter means you're fine. Scale-location (√|standardised residual| vs fitted) — the cleanest heteroscedasticity signal, because it removes the sign. Normal Q-Q — tails off the diagonal mean non-normal residuals, which matters for inference only. Residuals vs leverage with Cook's distance — finds single points that are moving the whole fit. For time-structured data I'd add residuals plotted in time order, which is the only way to see autocorrelation.

ConceptualWhat's the difference between leverage, outlier and influence?

An outlier has a large residual — it's far from the fitted line in the y direction. Leverage measures how unusual a point's features are (the hat-matrix diagonal h_ii) — it's about x, not y, and it quantifies the potential to move the fit. Influence is the actual effect: how much the fit changes if you delete the point. A high-leverage point that follows the trend has little influence; a high-leverage point with a large residual has enormous influence. Cook's distance combines both, which is why it's the practical number — flag anything above roughly 4/n, and investigate rather than automatically delete.

5.4 Multicollinearity & VIF ⭐

The assumption violation with the most counter-intuitive consequences: your predictions are fine, your coefficients are nonsense, and your F-test disagrees with all your t-tests.

The tell-tale signature

SymptomWhy it happens
High overall F-statistic, no individually significant coefficientsThe features jointly explain a lot; individually none is identifiable, because another feature can substitute for it
Coefficient signs flip when you add or remove a featureThe loss surface is a flat valley — many coefficient combinations fit almost equally well (§2.1)
Enormous standard errorsVar(β̂ⱼ) = σ²/((1−R²ⱼ)·Σ(xⱼ−x̄ⱼ)²) — the (1−R²ⱼ) in the denominator is the VIF
Coefficients change wildly between CV foldsSame cause; and it's a good practical detector even without computing VIF
A coefficient with an economically implausible signClassic with correlated pairs: one absorbs the effect and pushes the other negative

VIF for feature j is 1/(1 − R²ⱼ), where R²ⱼ comes from regressing xⱼ on all the other features. It is literally the factor by which that coefficient's variance is inflated relative to an uncorrelated world. VIF = 10 means R²ⱼ = 0.9 and the standard error is √10 ≈ 3.2× larger. Rules of thumb: > 5 worth a look, > 10 a problem — but these are conventions, not thresholds.

Does it matter? Ask what the model is for

For prediction, multicollinearity is usually a non-issue: the fitted values are stable even when the individual coefficients aren't, because the correlated features move together in new data too. For inference or explanation it's fatal — you cannot say “a one-unit increase in X raises y by β” when X never moves alone in your data. So the correct answer to “does multicollinearity hurt?” is “it depends what you're using the model for”, and then give both halves. One caveat for prediction: if the correlation structure changes in production, unstable coefficients become unstable predictions.

Likely interview questions
Very commonWhat is multicollinearity, how do you detect it, and does it hurt predictions or interpretation?

Two or more features carrying near-identical information, so XᵀX becomes ill-conditioned and the loss surface has a long flat valley. Detect: correlation matrix, condition number, and VIF = 1/(1−R²ⱼ) above ~5–10 — plus the signature of a high overall F-statistic with no individually significant coefficients, and signs that flip between refits. Does it hurt? It inflates coefficient variance, so it destroys interpretation and stability while usually leaving predictions fine — the correlated features move together in new data too. Caveat: if the correlation structure changes in production, the predictions become unstable as well. Fixes: drop one, combine into a ratio, PCA, or Ridge, which re-conditions the problem by adding αI.

GotchaYour F-test is highly significant but no coefficient is. What's going on?

The classic multicollinearity signature. The F-test asks whether the features jointly explain variance — they do. Each t-test asks whether a feature adds anything given all the others — and when two features are near-duplicates, neither adds anything the other doesn't already provide, so both look insignificant. The information is there; it just can't be attributed. Check VIFs, and note this is a good example of why you should never do feature selection by dropping individually-insignificant coefficients one at a time.

DesignWould you use VIF on a gradient boosting model?

Not for the same reason. Trees don't solve a linear system, so there's no coefficient variance to inflate and no numerical instability — a GBM handles correlated features without complaint. But correlation still matters for interpretation: permutation importance and SHAP both split credit unpredictably between correlated features, so two genuinely important features can each look unimportant (§14.3). So I'd compute correlations to inform how I read the explanations, and potentially drop redundant features for latency and stability reasons — not because the model needs it.

5.5 R², adjusted R² and friends

A metric everybody quotes and few can criticise. Three facts about it are commonly asked and commonly missed.

FactWhyWhat to do instead
R² never decreases when you add a featureAdding a column can only enlarge the space the fit is chosen from, so RSS can't rise — and least squares will exploit chance correlation to do slightly better even with pure noiseAdjusted R², which penalises p: 1 − (1−R²)(n−1)/(n−p−1), or a held-out score
Test-set R² can be negativeIt's 1 − SS_res/SS_tot using the training mean as the baseline; a model worse than predicting that mean scores below zeroReport it anyway — a negative test R² is a useful, loud signal
R² is not comparable across datasetsIt depends on the variance of y in that sample. A high-noise target caps R² regardless of model qualityCompare models on the same data; use RMSE in target units for communication
Anscombe's quartet, in one sentence

Four datasets with identical means, variances, correlations, regression lines and R² — and radically different shapes, one of which is entirely driven by a single outlier. It is the canonical argument for plotting your data before trusting any summary statistic, and it's a nice thing to name if a discussion of R² starts going in circles.

Likely interview questions
Very commonWhy does R² always increase when you add a feature? What do you use instead?

An extra column can only enlarge the space the fit is chosen from, so the residual sum of squares cannot increase — and with a column of pure noise, least squares will still exploit chance correlation to reduce RSS slightly. Use adjusted R², which penalises the parameter count, or better, a held-out score. Two follow-on facts worth volunteering: test R² can be negative (a model worse than predicting the training mean), and R² is not comparable across datasets because it depends on the variance of y in that particular sample.

GotchaModel A has R² = 0.85 on dataset 1, model B has R² = 0.45 on dataset 2. Which is better?

Unanswerable as posed. R² measures the fraction of that dataset's variance explained, so it's bounded by how much of the target is predictable in the first place — a noisy target caps R² no matter how good the model is. Dataset 2 might simply be harder. To compare, I'd need both models on the same data, or a scale-free comparison against a shared baseline — which is exactly what MASE does for forecasting (§10.6) and what "lift over baseline" does generally.

5.6 Ridge, Lasso and Elastic Net in practice ⭐

The theory is in §4.4. This is what the coefficient paths look like, how you choose α, and the practicalities that come up.

PracticalityDetail
Standardise firstNon-negotiable — otherwise the penalty is applied in arbitrary units (§4.4). The intercept is not penalised.
sklearn's alphaLarger = more regularization for Ridge/Lasso. But LogisticRegression uses C = 1/alpha, so smaller C = more regularization — an inverted convention that catches people out.
Lasso pathFitted by coordinate descent; lars_path gives the exact piecewise-linear path if you want to see where each feature enters.
Ridge with p > nWorks fine — the penalty makes the problem well-posed even when XᵀX is rank-deficient. Lasso caps out at n selected features.
Group LassoZeroes whole groups of coefficients together — the right tool when one categorical's dummies should enter or leave as a unit.
Likely interview questions
PracticalHow do you choose α?

Cross-validation over a log-spaced grid — RidgeCV, LassoCV, ElasticNetCV do this efficiently, and Lasso's path algorithms make it nearly free. Then apply the one-standard-error rule: pick the most regularized model whose CV error is within one SE of the minimum, which costs almost nothing in accuracy and buys a simpler, more stable model. Two cautions: the CV must be inside a pipeline with the scaler, and if you tune α and then report that same CV score, it's optimistically biased (§11.3).

GotchaIn sklearn, does a larger C mean more or less regularization?

Less. LogisticRegression and SVC use C as the inverse regularization strength, so small C means a strong penalty — the opposite convention to alpha in Ridge and Lasso, where larger means more. It's a genuine API inconsistency inherited from libsvm, and getting it backwards in a tuning grid is a common and embarrassing bug that produces a search over exactly the wrong region.

ConceptualYou have 5,000 features and 300 rows. Which regularizer?

p ≫ n, so unregularized OLS has no unique solution at all and something must constrain it. If I believe few features matter, Lasso — but note it can select at most n = 300 features by construction, and it will pick unstably among correlated ones. If I believe many small effects, Ridge, which handles p > n gracefully and keeps everything. In practice I'd start with Elastic Net, which spans both and keeps correlated groups together, and I'd cross-validate l1_ratio alongside α. I'd also be honest that with 300 rows the CV estimate itself will be noisy, so I'd use repeated CV and report the spread.

5.7 Logistic regression ⭐⭐

The interpretability and calibration baseline. Credit scoring runs on it for reasons you should be able to state — and the coefficient interpretation is the thing people most often fumble.

interactive Log-odds → odds ratio → probability
—odds ratio exp(β)
—log-odds z
—probability σ(z)
—dp/dx at this point

The point this makes better than any sentence: a logistic coefficient is constant in log-odds and wildly non-constant in probability. Drag x to the tails and watch dp/dx collapse toward zero while the odds ratio never moves. That is why “a one-unit increase raises the probability by β” is wrong and “multiplies the odds by exp(β)” is right.

The pipeline, and where each term attaches

Why it survives in regulated industries

Three concrete reasons, worth having ready. (1) Each coefficient is a defensible, monotone, sign-interpretable contribution you can put in an adverse-action notice. (2) It is nearly calibrated out of the box when well-regularized, because log loss is a proper scoring rule and it optimises exactly that — so predict_proba can be used in an expected-value calculation with far less anxiety than a GBM's (§12.8). (3) It is trivial to monitor: coefficient drift is directly inspectable, and the model has no capacity to encode exotic interactions you haven't sanctioned.

Likely interview questions
Very common⭐ Interpret a logistic regression coefficient. What is an odds ratio?

A one-unit increase in x raises the log-odds by β, equivalently multiplies the odds by exp(β) — the odds ratio. β = 0.4 ⇒ odds ×1.49, a 49% increase in odds. The effect on the probability is not constant: it's β·p(1−p), maximal near p = 0.5 and vanishing in the tails. That's the distinction people fumble — "raises the probability by 0.4" is simply wrong. Standardise features first if you want to compare coefficient magnitudes, and remember sklearn's C is the inverse penalty strength.

Very commonWhy can't you use MSE as the loss for logistic regression?

Two reasons. Composed with a sigmoid, squared error is non-convex in the parameters, so gradient descent has no guarantee of reaching the global optimum. And log loss is the negative log-likelihood of the Bernoulli model — the MLE, and a proper scoring rule — so it produces well-behaved probabilities and has a principled derivation rather than being an arbitrary choice. There's a practical third: MSE barely penalises a confidently wrong prediction (the gradient vanishes as the sigmoid saturates), which is exactly the error you most want punished.

ConceptualHow is logistic regression fitted, given there's no closed form?

Iteratively. The classic statistical method is IRLS (iteratively reweighted least squares) — a Newton method, since the log-likelihood's Hessian is available in closed form. Modern libraries use quasi-Newton solvers (lbfgs, the sklearn default) or coordinate descent (liblinear, and saga for L1/elastic-net at scale). Because the loss is convex, all of them reach the same optimum — so different solvers changing your coefficients materially means a convergence failure or an under-tuned max_iter, not a modelling choice.

DesignMulti-class: one-vs-rest or multinomial?

Multinomial (softmax) by default. It optimises a single joint likelihood so the probabilities are normalised across classes and are usually better calibrated; OvR fits k independent binary models whose outputs must then be normalised post hoc, which distorts them. OvR is worth considering when you want independent per-class thresholds — for instance, when each class feeds a separate downstream decision with its own cost — or when classes are genuinely not mutually exclusive, in which case you actually want multi-label (§10.2) rather than either.

GotchaYour logistic regression fails to converge and one coefficient is enormous. Why?

Almost certainly perfect (or quasi-perfect) separation — some feature or combination separates the classes exactly. The MLE then doesn't exist: the likelihood keeps improving as the coefficient goes to infinity, so the optimiser marches off and never converges. Causes: a leaked feature (§3.7), a categorical level that appears with only one class, or simply very few rows. Fixes: add regularization (any L2 penalty makes the solution finite and is why sklearn regularizes by default), use Firth's penalised likelihood, or merge/drop the offending level. Worth flagging that a perfectly separating feature is itself a leakage alarm.

5.8 GLMs — link functions and families ⭐

A GLM is a linear model plus two choices: a distribution for the target and a link function. Knowing which pair to reach for is one of the clearest practical signals available.

Target looks likeFamilyLinkVariance functionReal example
Continuous, symmetricGaussianidentityσ² (constant)Ordinary linear regression
BinaryBernoullilogitμ(1−μ)Default, churn, click
CountsPoissonlogμClaims per policy-year, visits per month
Counts, over-dispersedNegative binomiallogμ + μ²/kThe realistic version of the above (variance > mean)
Positive, right-skewedGammalogμ²Claim severity, time-to-repair, spend
Zero-inflated positiveTweedie (1<p<2)logμᵖInsurance pure premium — most policies claim £0, a few claim a lot
Proportions in (0,1)Betalogitμ(1−μ)/(1+φ)Rates and shares that aren't counts
You don't have to give up trees to keep the right loss

XGBoost and LightGBM both ship Poisson, Gamma and Tweedie objectives, and sklearn has PoissonRegressor, GammaRegressor and TweedieRegressor plus HistGradientBoostingRegressor(loss="poisson"). So the choice of distributional family is genuinely independent of the choice between a linear model and a GBM — and using a GBM with a squared-error loss on a claims target is leaving accuracy on the table for no reason.

Likely interview questions
Very commonWhen would you reach for a GLM — Poisson or Tweedie — instead of linear regression?

When you know the target's distribution and it isn't Gaussian. Poisson (log link) for counts; negative binomial when counts are over-dispersed (variance > mean, which is the usual real case); Gamma for positive right-skewed amounts like claim severity; Tweedie for zero-inflated positive targets like insurance pure premium. You get non-negative predictions, a correct variance function (so heteroscedasticity is handled by design rather than patched), multiplicative effects, and coefficients a regulator will accept. And you don't have to give up trees — XGBoost, LightGBM and sklearn's HistGB all support these objectives.

DesignWhy does insurance pricing use Tweedie rather than modelling claims directly?

Because pure premium — expected cost per policy — has a point mass at zero (most policies never claim) and a heavy right tail (a few claim a lot). A Gaussian model predicts negative premiums and fits the tail terribly. Tweedie with 1 < p < 2 is exactly a compound Poisson-Gamma: a Poisson number of Gamma-distributed claims, which is the actual data-generating process. The alternative — and it's a good answer too — is to decompose into frequency × severity: a Poisson model for claim count and a Gamma model for size, multiplied. That's more interpretable and lets you diagnose which component is driving a change.

ConceptualWhat does the link function actually do?

Two things. It maps the unbounded linear predictor Xw onto the target's valid range — a log link forces positive predictions, a logit link forces (0,1) — so the model can't produce impossible values. And it determines whether effects are additive or multiplicative: with a log link, a coefficient means "multiplies the expected value by exp(β)", which is usually the right structure for rates, counts and amounts. The canonical link for each family (logit for Bernoulli, log for Poisson) also gives nicer mathematical properties, though you're not obliged to use it.

5.9 Quantile & robust regression

Two more members of the linear family that solve problems the standard version cannot: asymmetric costs, and contaminated data.

MethodLossEstimatesUse when
Quantile regressionPinball at τThe conditional τ-quantilePrediction intervals; asymmetric costs; you need the tail, not the average
Huber regressionHuberA robust conditional meanOutliers you can't clean but shouldn't ignore
RANSACConsensus on inliersFit on the inlier subsetHeavy contamination (>20% bad points) with a clear inlier structure
Theil-SenMedian of pairwise slopesVery robust slopeSmall data, high contamination; expensive above a few thousand rows
Quantile regression gives you intervals for free

Fit at τ = 0.05 and τ = 0.95 and you have a 90% prediction interval that adapts to the input — wider where the data is noisy, narrower where it isn't. That's something a constant ±1.96σ band cannot do. Two cautions: quantiles fitted independently can cross (the 95th below the 5th somewhere), so check monotonicity or use a method that enforces it; and the coverage is only as good as the model, which is exactly the gap conformal prediction closes with a distribution-free guarantee (§16.3).

Likely interview questions
ConceptualWhat is quantile regression and when would you use it?

It minimises the pinball loss at level τ, which recovers the conditional τ-quantile rather than the mean. Three uses: prediction intervals that adapt to the input (fit at 0.05 and 0.95); asymmetric costs, where over- and under-prediction aren't equally bad — the optimal τ is c_under/(c_under+c_over); and robustness, since the median (τ=0.5) is insensitive to outliers. Cautions: independently fitted quantiles can cross, and the coverage is only as reliable as the model — conformal prediction gives you a distribution-free guarantee instead.

DesignYou need prediction intervals. Quantile regression, bootstrap, or conformal?

Depends what guarantee you need. Quantile regression is cheap and gives adaptive, heteroscedasticity-aware intervals, but coverage relies on the model being right. Bootstrap captures uncertainty in the parameters but not the irreducible noise, so it typically under-covers for a new observation unless you add the residual distribution back. Conformal prediction gives a finite-sample, distribution-free coverage guarantee under exchangeability and wraps any model — which is why it's my default when the interval carries a real commitment (§16.3). The strongest practical answer is usually conformalised quantile regression: adaptive width from the quantile model, guaranteed coverage from the conformal wrapper.

Part 6 of 17
Distance & Probability Models
kNN, Naive Bayes, LDA/QDA, SVM margins and the kernel trick

6.1 k-Nearest Neighbours ⭐

Almost never the production answer, and almost always a good interview question — because it isolates distance, scaling and the bias-variance dial with nothing else in the way.

interactive The k dial is a bias-variance dial
—train accuracy
—test accuracy
—gap

Real kNN, computed live over a 96 × 40 grid. Two things to try. k = 1: train accuracy is exactly 1.000 (every point is its own nearest neighbour) while test accuracy is much lower — the purest possible demonstration of overfitting. Then stretch x₂: as the scale grows, distance is dominated by one feature and the boundary degenerates into stripes. Nothing about the data changed — only the units.

The mechanics, and the costs

PropertyDetailConsequence
Lazy learningTraining just stores the dataTraining is free; inference is O(n·p) per query — the opposite cost profile to every other model, and usually disqualifying in production
Scaling mandatoryThe prediction is a distanceA feature in larger units dominates entirely — you end up doing 1-D kNN on whichever column has the biggest numbers
kThe bias-variance dialk=1: zero training error, maximum variance. k=n: the majority-class baseline. Rule of thumb √n, but tune it
Weightingweights='distance'Closer neighbours count more — smooths the boundary without raising k as much
Index structuresKD-tree, ball-treeHelp in low dimensions only; above roughly 15–20 features they degrade to brute-force scanning (§2.7)
Tie-breakingEven k in binary problemsUse odd k, or distance weighting, to avoid arbitrary ties
kNN still earns its place in three situations

(1) As a baseline on small, low-dimensional, well-scaled data — it's non-parametric, so it captures arbitrary boundaries with no assumptions. (2) As a recommendation neighbourhood — “customers similar to you also bought” is literally kNN, and the interpretability of “here are the five nearest examples” is a real feature. (3) As an imputation method (KNNImputer), where the same locality logic is exactly what you want. What it isn't is a scalable classifier for wide tabular data.

Likely interview questions
Very commonHow does kNN work, and why is scaling mandatory?

Store the training set; to predict, find the k nearest rows by some distance and take their majority vote or mean. Scaling is mandatory because the prediction is a distance computation — a feature measured in larger units dominates it entirely, so income in pounds swamps age in years and you're effectively doing 1-D nearest neighbour on income. k is a pure bias-variance dial: k=1 has zero training error and maximum variance; k=n is the majority-class baseline. It also suffers most from the curse of dimensionality, and its cost profile is inverted — free training, expensive inference.

ConceptualWhy does k = 1 always give 100% training accuracy?

Because every training point is its own nearest neighbour — distance zero — so it predicts its own label perfectly, by construction. That's why training accuracy is a completely uninformative metric for kNN, and it's the cleanest illustration in all of ML of why you must evaluate out-of-sample. The corollary is a nice diagnostic: if someone reports impressive training accuracy for a kNN model, they haven't understood the model.

DesignWould you ever deploy kNN in production?

Rarely as a classifier, because inference is O(n·p) per query — you carry the entire training set into production and pay for it on every request, which is the opposite of what you want. But yes in three shapes: as a recommendation neighbourhood (with an ANN index like HNSW to make it fast); as a baseline during development; and as KNNImputer inside a pipeline. If someone proposes it as the main model on wide tabular data, I'd point at latency, memory, and the curse of dimensionality, and suggest a GBM instead.

6.2 Naive Bayes ⭐

A model built on an assumption that is essentially always false, which nonetheless classifies well. The interesting question — and the one asked — is why.

VariantAssumes each feature is…Use for
GaussianNBContinuous, Gaussian within each classSmall tabular problems; a fast sanity baseline
MultinomialNBA countText with BoW/TF-IDF — see the NLP guide
BernoulliNBBinary presence/absenceShort text; binary indicator features
ComplementNBA count, with an imbalance correctionImbalanced text classification — often beats MultinomialNB there
CategoricalNBCategoricalPurely categorical tabular data
Likely interview questions
Very commonWhy does Naive Bayes work despite a false independence assumption?

Because classification needs the correct argmax, not correct probabilities. Correlated features are counted as independent evidence, so their effect is multiplied and the posterior is driven toward 0 or 1 — but the class ordering usually survives, and ordering is all a classifier needs. Consequences to state: it is badly calibrated and overconfident, so never use its predict_proba in an expected-value calculation without calibration. Add Laplace smoothing so an unseen feature-class pair doesn't zero the entire product, and compute in log space to avoid numerical underflow.

Deep diveWhat exactly does "conditional independence" mean here — and is it different from independence?

Very different, and it's the crux. Naive Bayes assumes P(x₁,x₂|y) = P(x₁|y)·P(x₂|y) — the features are independent given the class, not marginally. Two features can be strongly correlated overall while being nearly independent within each class, in which case the assumption is fine. The assumption fails when features remain correlated after conditioning on the class — which is the usual case with, say, duplicated or highly redundant columns, and it's why removing near-duplicate features can noticeably improve a Naive Bayes model.

PracticalWhy is Laplace smoothing necessary?

Because the model multiplies per-feature likelihoods, a single zero destroys the whole product: if a category never co-occurred with a class in training, P(xⱼ|y) = 0 makes the entire posterior zero regardless of how much evidence the other features provide. Additive (Laplace/Lidstone) smoothing adds α to every count so nothing is ever exactly zero. It's the same idea as the smoothing in target encoding (§3.5) — pull small-sample estimates toward a prior — and α is a genuine hyperparameter worth tuning, not a formality.

6.3 LDA & QDA ⭐

Worth knowing mostly for one question — LDA vs PCA — but the classifier itself has a nice property: it is the generative counterpart to logistic regression, and comparing them illuminates both.

LDA and logistic regression fit the same boundary shape differently

Both produce a linear decision boundary. LDA gets there generatively — model each class as a Gaussian with shared covariance, then apply Bayes' rule — while logistic regression gets there discriminatively, optimising the conditional likelihood directly. Consequence: when the Gaussian assumption roughly holds, LDA is more data-efficient (it's the §4.7 small-sample argument); when it doesn't, logistic regression is more robust because it never made the assumption. LDA is also more sensitive to outliers, since they distort the covariance estimate.

Likely interview questions
Very commonLDA vs PCA — what's the difference in objective?

PCA is unsupervised and maximises total variance; it never sees the labels, so it can discard exactly the direction that separates the classes if that direction happens to be low-variance. LDA is supervised and maximises the ratio of between-class scatter to within-class scatter, giving at most k−1 components for k classes. Both are linear projections; only one is trying to help your classifier. Practical note: LDA-as-preprocessing is fitted on training data only, exactly like any other learned transform.

ConceptualLDA vs QDA — when would you choose each?

LDA assumes a shared covariance across classes → linear boundary, few parameters, more data-efficient. QDA gives each class its own covariance → quadratic boundary, far more parameters (k·p(p+1)/2), and it needs substantially more data per class to estimate them stably. Choose QDA when you have plenty of data per class and evidence that class covariances genuinely differ (visibly different cluster shapes); otherwise LDA, whose extra bias buys a large variance reduction. Regularized discriminant analysis interpolates between them if you want to tune it.

Deep diveLDA and logistic regression both give a linear boundary. What's the difference?

How they get there. LDA is generative: model P(x|y) as Gaussian with shared covariance, model P(y), apply Bayes' rule. Logistic regression is discriminative: model P(y|x) directly by maximising the conditional likelihood. When the Gaussian assumption holds, LDA is more efficient — it converges to good performance with less data, the §4.7 argument. When it doesn't (skewed features, outliers, categorical inputs), logistic regression is more robust because it never made that assumption. LDA also gives you a supervised projection for free, which logistic regression doesn't.

6.4 Support Vector Machines — the margin ⭐

Start with the geometry, because everything else — the dual, the kernel, C — is a consequence of it.

Among all hyperplanes that separate the classes, the SVM picks the one with the largest margin — the greatest distance to the nearest point of either class. The intuition for why that generalises: a boundary sitting in the widest possible gap is the least likely to be flipped by a slightly different sample.

Likely interview questions
Very commonWhat is the margin, and why maximise it?

The margin is the distance from the decision boundary to the nearest training point of either class — 2/‖w‖ for a canonical hyperplane. Maximising it means choosing the boundary sitting in the widest possible gap, which is intuitively the least likely to be flipped by a slightly different sample, and formally gives a generalisation bound that depends on the margin rather than the dimensionality. Maximising 2/‖w‖ is equivalent to minimising ½‖w‖², which turns it into a convex quadratic program with a unique solution.

ConceptualWhat are support vectors, and why do they matter?

The training points that lie exactly on the margin boundaries (plus, in the soft-margin case, those violating them) — the ones with non-zero dual coefficients. They matter because they alone determine the solution: delete every other training point and refit, and you get the identical boundary. That gives the model a sparsity no other classifier here has, keeps prediction cheap (you only evaluate kernels against support vectors), and is why the generalisation bound scales with their number rather than with the feature count — which is what makes mapping into an infinite-dimensional space via a kernel a safe thing to do.

6.5 Soft margin and C

Real data isn't separable. The soft margin allows violations and charges for them — and C sets the price.

CPenalty for violationsMarginSupport vectorsBias / variance
LargeExpensive — few violations toleratedNarrowFewLow bias, high variance — can overfit badly
SmallCheap — many violations toleratedWideManyHigh bias, low variance — can underfit

Note the connection back to §4.4: the SVM objective ½‖w‖² + C·Σξᵢ is exactly a regularized loss — ‖w‖² is an L2 penalty and Σξᵢ is the hinge loss. So C is the inverse regularization strength, which is why sklearn uses the same letter in LogisticRegression. Small C = strong regularization, the opposite convention to alpha.

C and gamma interact — tune them jointly

With an RBF kernel, gamma controls how far a single training example's influence reaches (large gamma = tight, wiggly boundaries) while C controls violation tolerance. They pull in overlapping directions, so tuning one then the other finds a poor optimum — search them jointly on a log-spaced 2-D grid, which is the classic textbook example of why a grid over a 2-D space is sometimes genuinely appropriate (§11.4). And scale your features first, or gamma's meaning changes per feature.

Likely interview questions
Very commonWhat does C do in an SVM?

It sets the price of violating the margin. Large C makes violations expensive, so the optimiser prefers a narrow margin that classifies training points correctly — low bias, high variance, prone to overfitting. Small C tolerates violations, giving a wider margin and a smoother boundary — higher bias, lower variance. Structurally, the objective ½‖w‖² + C·Σξᵢ is an L2 penalty plus hinge loss, so C is the inverse regularization strength — small C means strong regularization, the opposite convention to alpha.

PracticalHow do you tune C and gamma?

Jointly, on a log-spaced 2-D grid — typically C ∈ [10⁻², 10³] and gamma ∈ [10⁻⁴, 10¹] — because they interact: high gamma with high C gives a wildly overfitted boundary, and tuning them sequentially finds a poor optimum. Scale features first or gamma's meaning varies per feature; sklearn's gamma='scale' default at least adapts to feature variance. And be aware of the cost: SVM training is roughly O(n²)–O(n³), so a full grid on a large dataset is genuinely expensive — which is an argument for random or Bayesian search (§11.4).

6.6 The kernel trick ⭐⭐

The topic where candidates most often recite “it maps to a higher dimension” without being able to say where in the maths that happens. It happens in the dual.

interactive The kernel trick, watched happening

In one dimension the two classes are interleaved and no threshold separates them. Add a second coordinate x² and a straight line does. That's the idea — and the “trick” is that the SVM's dual objective only ever needs inner products ⟨φ(x), φ(x′)⟩, which a kernel K(x,x′) computes directly.

Where exactly the kernel enters

The primal optimises over w, which lives in the feature space — so if φ maps to a million dimensions, w has a million components and you cannot store it. The Lagrangian dual instead optimises over one multiplier αᵢ per training point, and the objective depends on the data only through inner products:

max Σαᵢ − ½ΣΣ αᵢαⱼ yᵢyⱼ ⟨xᵢ, xⱼ⟩   subject to   0 ≤ αᵢ ≤ C, Σαᵢyᵢ = 0

Replace ⟨xᵢ, xⱼ⟩ with K(xᵢ, xⱼ) and you are optimising in the feature space without ever constructing a vector in it. Prediction is the same: f(x) = Σ αᵢyᵢK(xᵢ,x) + b, summed only over support vectors. That substitution is the entire trick — and being able to point at the exact term is what separates a real answer from a memorised one.

KernelFormulaImplied feature spaceWhen
Linear⟨x,x′⟩The original spaceHigh-dimensional sparse data (text) — fast, and often enough
Polynomial(γ⟨x,x′⟩+r)ᵈAll monomials up to degree dExplicit interaction terms; sensitive to d
RBF / Gaussianexp(−γ‖x−x′‖²)Infinite-dimensionalThe default. gamma sets the influence radius
Sigmoidtanh(γ⟨x,x′⟩+r)—Rarely; not PSD for all parameters, so it can misbehave
Mercer's condition, briefly

Not any function of two arguments is a valid kernel. It must produce a positive semi-definite Gram matrix for every finite set of points — Mercer's condition — because that is exactly what guarantees it corresponds to an inner product in some feature space. If it doesn't, the optimisation is no longer convex and the geometric story collapses. This is the practical reason the sigmoid kernel is rarely used: it isn't PSD for all parameter choices.

Likely interview questions
Very common⭐ Explain the kernel trick. Where exactly does the kernel enter?

In the dual. The primal optimises over w, which lives in the feature space and may be enormous or infinite. The Lagrangian dual optimises over one multiplier per training point and depends on the data only through inner products ⟨xᵢ,xⱼ⟩. Substituting K(xᵢ,xⱼ) for that term gives you the geometry of the mapped space without ever constructing φ(x) — and prediction, f(x) = Σαᵢyᵢ K(xᵢ,x) + b, is the same substitution. With the RBF kernel the implied space is infinite-dimensional, which is only safe because the generalisation bound depends on the margin and the number of support vectors, not on dimensionality.

Deep diveWhy does the dual exist at all — what's wrong with the primal?

Nothing, if you stay in the original space — a linear SVM is usually solved in the primal, which is why LinearSVC scales far better than SVC(kernel='linear'). The dual matters for two reasons. First, it's the only formulation that admits kernels, because it's the one where the data appears solely as inner products. Second, the dual has n variables while the primal has p+1, so the dual is preferable when p ≫ n and the primal when n ≫ p. The KKT conditions also give the support-vector characterisation directly: points with αᵢ = 0 are irrelevant to the solution.

GotchaCan you use kernels with models other than SVMs?

Yes — anywhere the algorithm can be written to touch the data only through inner products. Kernel ridge regression, kernel PCA (§9.6), Gaussian processes, and kernel k-means all exist. The catch is always the same: you need the n × n Gram matrix, which is O(n²) memory and O(n³) to decompose, so these methods stop being practical in the tens of thousands of rows. The workaround is random feature approximations (Nyström, random Fourier features) that approximate the kernel with an explicit low-dimensional map — which is how kernel methods scale in practice.

6.7 When to still use these in 2026

The honest positioning question. All four models in this part have been largely displaced on tabular data — and each still has a defensible niche.

ModelDisplaced becauseStill the right answer when
kNNO(n·p) inference; curse of dimensionality; needs scalingRecommendation neighbourhoods (with an ANN index); imputation; a quick non-parametric baseline; when “here are the 5 most similar cases” is the deliverable
Naive BayesIndependence assumption; badly calibratedVery little data; extremely high-dimensional sparse text; when you need a model in ten seconds; streaming updates (it's trivially incremental)
LDAGaussian + shared-covariance assumptionsSmall data with roughly Gaussian classes; as a supervised dimensionality reducer; when you want a generative model you can sample from
SVMO(n²)–O(n³) training; no native probabilities; needs scalingHigh-dimensional sparse features where LinearSVC is excellent and very fast; small-to-medium data with a clear margin; when you want a max-margin rule rather than a probability
The SVM probability trap

SVMs produce a signed distance, not a probability. Setting probability=True in sklearn runs Platt scaling with an internal 5-fold cross-validation — which makes fitting roughly 5× slower, can produce predict_proba that disagrees with predict (they're derived differently), and is often still poorly calibrated. If you need probabilities, that's a strong argument for using logistic regression or a GBM with explicit calibration instead.

Likely interview questions
Very commonWhen would you still choose an SVM in 2026?

Three cases. High-dimensional sparse features — a linear SVM on text is excellent and LinearSVC is extremely fast, because it solves the primal and scales roughly linearly. Small-to-medium data with a clear margin, where the max-margin inductive bias genuinely helps. And when you want a decision rule rather than a probability. Otherwise gradient boosting wins on tabular data: it trains faster, needs no scaling, handles mixed types and missing values natively, and gives usable probabilities. I'd also flag that probability=True is a trap — it runs an internal 5-fold Platt calibration that's slow and often still poorly calibrated.

DesignYou have 2 million rows and want to try an SVM. What do you do?

Don't use SVC — kernel SVM training is roughly O(n²)–O(n³) and 2M rows is far past practical. Options: use LinearSVC or SGDClassifier(loss='hinge'), which solve the primal and scale near-linearly; approximate the kernel with Nyström or random Fourier features followed by a linear model, which gets most of the RBF benefit at linear cost; or subsample to fit a kernel SVM and check whether it beats the linear version at all. Honestly though, at 2M rows on tabular data I'd expect LightGBM to be both faster and better, and I'd say so.

Part 7 of 17
Decision Trees
Splits, impurity, regression trees, pruning, failure modes, the importance trap

7.1 How a tree is built ⭐⭐

Everything in Part 8 is made of these. If you cannot compute an information gain by hand, the ensembles conversation will not go well.

interactive Find the split — Gini, entropy and information gain, live
—parent impurity
—left child
—right child
—information gain

Everything is computed exactly: Gini = 1 − Σpᵢ², Entropy = −Σpᵢ log₂ pᵢ, and gain = H(parent) − Σ(nᵢ/n)·H(childᵢ). Drag the threshold and watch the gain curve; the tree's algorithm simply evaluates every candidate threshold on every feature and takes the maximum. Switch criteria and notice how little the chosen split moves — which is the honest answer to “Gini or entropy?”

The algorithm, precisely
