  1. At the current node, for every feature and every candidate threshold, split the rows into left and right.
  2. Compute the weighted child impurity Σ(nᵢ/n)·H(childᵢ) and subtract it from the parent's impurity to get the gain.
  3. Take the split with the highest gain. If no split beats the stopping criteria, make this node a leaf and predict the majority class (or the mean).
  4. Recurse on each child, with only that child's rows.

Two properties fall straight out of that description and are constantly asked about. It is greedy — it takes the best split now and never revisits it, so the tree it produces is not the globally optimal tree (finding that is NP-hard). And it is axis-aligned — every split is a threshold on a single feature, which is why a diagonal boundary costs a staircase of splits (§7.6).

Likely interview questions
Very commonHow does a decision tree choose a split?

Greedily and exhaustively. At each node it scans every feature and every candidate threshold, computes the impurity decrease H(parent) − Σ(nᵢ/n)H(childᵢ), and takes the maximum — then recurses on each child with only that child's rows, stopping when a criterion is hit. Two properties to volunteer: it's greedy, so it never revisits an earlier split and the resulting tree isn't globally optimal (that's NP-hard); and it's axis-aligned, so every boundary is a threshold on one feature at a time.

Deep diveWhat are the "candidate thresholds", and how many are there?

For a continuous feature, the candidates are the midpoints between consecutive distinct sorted values — at most n−1 per feature, so the naive split search is O(n·p) per node after sorting. That cost is why modern implementations use histogram binning: LightGBM, XGBoost's hist method and sklearn's HistGradientBoosting pre-bin each feature into ~256 buckets and only consider bin boundaries, which turns the per-node cost into O(bins·p) and is the single biggest reason those libraries are fast (§8.6).

ConceptualWhy is the tree not globally optimal?

Because the algorithm is greedy: it picks the split with the highest immediate gain and never reconsiders. A split with modest gain now might enable two excellent splits below it, and the greedy algorithm will never find that path — the horizon effect. Finding the globally optimal tree is NP-hard, so exhaustive search isn't an option at any realistic size. In practice it matters less than it sounds, because ensembles make individual trees' myopia irrelevant — which is a large part of why we ensemble rather than trying to build one perfect tree.

7.2 Split criteria ⭐

Gini, entropy, information gain and gain ratio — with the honest answer about which to use.

CriterionFormulaRange (binary)Notes
Gini impurity1 − Σpᵢ²0 to 0.5Probability that two randomly drawn items from the node have different labels. sklearn's default; cheaper, no logarithm
Entropy−Σpᵢ log₂ pᵢ0 to 1Bits needed to encode the class. Penalises impure nodes slightly more aggressively
Information gainH(parent) − Σ(nᵢ/n)H(childᵢ)—The reduction, using either measure. This is what's maximised
Gain ratioIG / SplitInfo—C4.5's correction for the high-cardinality bias — normalises by how many ways the split partitions the data
Log loss / deviance−Σ y log p—Available in sklearn as criterion='log_loss'; equivalent to entropy for classification

Gini is the first-order Taylor approximation of entropy around the uniform distribution, which is why they behave so similarly — a fact worth knowing if someone pushes on the difference.

Gini or entropy? The honest answer

They almost always choose the same splits and produce trees of nearly identical accuracy — empirical studies put the disagreement at around 2% of splits. Gini is cheaper (no logarithm) and is sklearn's default; entropy penalises impure nodes marginally more. Saying “in practice it doesn't matter — I'd spend the tuning budget on max_depth and min_samples_leaf instead” is a better answer than inventing a difference, and it's what an experienced practitioner would actually say.

Likely interview questions
Very commonGini vs entropy — does it matter?

Almost never. Gini = 1 − Σpᵢ² is the probability two random items from the node have different labels; entropy = −Σpᵢlog₂pᵢ is the bits needed to encode the class. They pick the same split roughly 98% of the time — Gini is in fact the first-order Taylor approximation of entropy near uniform. Gini is cheaper (no logarithm) and is the default. The right answer is that it doesn't matter and the tuning budget belongs on depth and leaf size instead.

Deep diveWhat is gain ratio and what problem does it solve?

Plain information gain is biased toward high-cardinality features: a feature with a unique value per row splits the data into perfectly pure singleton nodes and scores maximum gain, while being useless. C4.5's gain ratio divides the gain by SplitInfo — the entropy of the partition sizes themselves — which penalises splits that shatter the data into many small pieces. Modern implementations mostly handle this differently: binary splits only, plus min_samples_leaf. But the underlying bias never fully goes away, and it's the root cause of the feature-importance trap in §7.7.

7.3 Regression trees

Same algorithm, different impurity — and one consequence that decides whether you can use trees on a trending time series at all.

For regression the criterion is variance reduction: the impurity of a node is its MSE about the node mean, and the split maximises MSE(parent) − Σ(nᵢ/n)·MSE(childᵢ). The leaf predicts the mean of its rows. Swap in MAE and the leaf predicts the median — the same mean-vs-median distinction as §4.1, and sklearn exposes it as criterion='absolute_error' (much slower, because the median can't be updated incrementally the way a mean can).

A regression tree outputs a step function — and cannot extrapolate

Because every prediction is a leaf mean, the output is piecewise constant: it can never produce a value outside the range of the training target, and beyond the training range of a feature it simply returns the nearest leaf's constant. For a trending series that is fatal — a model trained on 2024 data will predict 2024 levels forever. The fixes are to detrend/difference first, model the residual with a tree and add the trend back, or use a hybrid with a linear component. This is the single most important practical limitation of tree models (§10.5).

Likely interview questions
ConceptualHow does a regression tree differ from a classification tree?

Only in the impurity measure and the leaf prediction. Classification uses Gini or entropy and predicts the majority class; regression uses variance / MSE reduction and predicts the leaf mean. Switch the criterion to absolute error and the leaf predicts the median instead — the same mean-vs-median choice as any other loss, and much slower to fit because medians can't be updated incrementally. Everything else — greedy search, axis-aligned splits, recursion — is identical.

Gotcha⭐ Can a decision tree extrapolate?

No. Every prediction is a leaf constant, so the output is bounded by the range of the training target and is flat beyond the training range of any feature. A tree trained on house prices from £100k–£500k will never predict £800k, and a tree trained on a rising time series will predict the last level forever. That makes tree models a poor fit for trending targets without preprocessing — detrend or difference first, model the residual, add the trend back — or use a hybrid with a linear component. It's the main structural reason a linear model can still beat a GBM on a forecasting problem.

7.4 Controlling complexity ⭐

A fully-grown tree has near-zero training error and enormous variance. Every hyperparameter here is a way of stopping that — and each controls a genuinely different thing.

ParameterStops growth when…Notes
max_depthThe node is d levels downThe blunt, effective knob — tune it first. Caps interactions at depth d
min_samples_splitA node has too few rows to consider splittingPrevents splits on tiny samples
min_samples_leafA split would leave a child below the minimumUsually the most useful — it bounds the variance of every prediction, because no leaf estimate is based on fewer than that many rows
max_leaf_nodesThe tree hits a leaf budgetGrows best-first rather than depth-first — the same idea as LightGBM's leaf-wise growth (§8.6)
min_impurity_decreaseThe best split's gain is below a thresholdDirect control on the gain shown in the §7.1 widget
max_features—Considers a random subset of features per split. Mostly a Random Forest device (§8.3), but it also regularizes a single tree
ccp_alpha—Post-pruning by cost-complexity — see §7.5
class_weight—Re-weights impurity calculations; how you make a tree cost-sensitive
Depth caps interaction order

A useful reframing: a tree of depth d can express interactions among at most d features on any single path. max_depth=1 (a stump) is a purely additive model with no interactions at all; max_depth=3 allows three-way interactions. That's why boosting with shallow trees works so well — you're fitting an additive model of low-order interactions, which is a good inductive bias for tabular data and is the connection to GAMs (§14.2).

Likely interview questions
PracticalWhich tree hyperparameter would you tune first, and why?

max_depth for a single tree — it's the bluntest and most effective control, and it has a clean interpretation: depth d caps the interaction order at d. Then min_samples_leaf, which I'd argue is actually the more useful one on noisy data because it bounds the variance of every leaf estimate rather than just the shape of the tree. For a Random Forest the priority inverts: leave depth unbounded and control the model with min_samples_leaf and max_features, because the averaging handles the variance (§8.3).

ConceptualWhat's the difference between min_samples_split and min_samples_leaf?

min_samples_split is a precondition on the parent: don't even consider splitting a node with fewer than this many rows. min_samples_leaf is a constraint on the children: reject any split that would leave a child below the minimum. The second is stronger and more useful, because a node with 100 rows passes min_samples_split=20 and can still produce a 99/1 split whose tiny leaf is pure noise — exactly what min_samples_leaf prevents. If I could set only one, it'd be min_samples_leaf.

7.5 Pruning

Pre-pruning is cheap and myopic; post-pruning is principled and slower. The distinction is a standard question with a satisfying answer.

Why this section is really about Part 8

A single tree needs careful pruning because its variance is enormous. The insight behind ensembles is that you can instead let trees stay high-variance and average that variance away — which is why in a Random Forest you often leave max_depth=None entirely and control the model with min_samples_leaf and max_features. Pruning matters most in exactly the case where you're shipping a single tree for interpretability.

Likely interview questions
ConceptualPre-pruning vs post-pruning — which is better?

Pre-pruning (early stopping via depth, leaf size, minimum gain) is fast and needs one pass, but it's myopic: a split with poor immediate gain might be the only route to two excellent splits below it, and you'll never find out. Post-pruning (cost-complexity, ccp_alpha) grows the full tree then removes subtrees that don't justify their leaves, so it sees the whole picture — at the cost of building a large tree first. Post-pruning is generally better for a single tree; pre-pruning is what everyone actually uses inside ensembles, because there the myopia is averaged away.

PracticalHow do you choose ccp_alpha?

Use cost_complexity_pruning_path, which returns the finite sequence of α values at which the pruned tree changes — because the pruning path is a nested sequence, there are only so many distinct trees. Then cross-validate over just those α values and pick the best, or apply the one-standard-error rule and take the smallest tree within one SE of the optimum. That's a cheaper and better-posed search than tuning max_depth over an arbitrary grid, and it's a nice thing to know because most people have never used it.

7.6 Strengths and failure modes ⭐

Three failure modes worth being able to draw, and a strengths list that explains why trees became the base learner for everything in Part 8.

Likely interview questions
Very commonWhy is a single deep tree high-variance?

Because splits are chosen greedily and hierarchically: moving a handful of rows can flip the root split, and everything below it then changes completely. A fully-grown tree also drives training error to near zero by isolating individual points, so it's fitting noise by construction. That instability is exactly the property bagging exploits — average many high-variance, low-bias trees and the variance falls while the bias stays put (§8.2).

ConceptualWhat are the strengths of trees that made them the base of every winning tabular model?

No scaling, because splits use rank order. Mixed types handled natively. Interactions captured automatically — you don't have to specify them, which is exactly what linear models need feature engineering for. Missing values handled by a learned default direction. Robust to feature outliers, since an extreme value is just "the largest". And interpretable at small depth. The weakness — high variance — is precisely the one that averaging fixes, which is why bagging and boosting on trees works so well while bagging on, say, linear models buys almost nothing.

GotchaWhy do trees struggle with a diagonal decision boundary?

Because every split is axis-aligned — a threshold on one feature — so a diagonal boundary must be approximated by a staircase, which costs many splits and therefore lots of data and depth. The giveaway in practice is a tree that needs surprising depth on what looks like a simple problem. Two fixes: rotate the feature space (a PCA or a learned linear combination can make the boundary axis-aligned), or engineer the combination directly — if you know the boundary is roughly x₁ + x₂ = c, giving the model x₁ + x₂ as a feature turns many splits into one. Oblique-split trees exist but are rarely used in practice.

7.7 The feature-importance trap ⭐⭐

One of the most reliable senior filters in the whole subject. Quoting feature_importances_ without qualification is a specific, recognisable tell.

The default feature_importances_ on a sklearn tree or forest is mean decrease in impurity (MDI): for each feature, the total impurity reduction it produced across all splits, weighted by the rows reaching those nodes. It is free — it was computed while fitting — and it has two documented biases.

Bias 1 Cardinality — it favours features with many distinct values
Mechanism
A continuous or high-cardinality feature offers many more candidate split points, so it has more chances to reduce impurity by luck. A binary feature offers one.
Demonstration
Add a column of pure random noise with many distinct values to any dataset and it will rank as an important feature. Everyone should run this once — it takes four lines and permanently changes how you read an importance plot.
Bias 2 It is computed on training data
Mechanism
MDI measures impurity reduction achieved while fitting, so a feature the model overfitted to scores highly — even if it contributes nothing out of sample.
Consequence
The importances describe how the model was built, not what actually predicts. Those are different questions and the distinction is the whole point of §14.3.
And permutation importance is not a free lunch either

Permutation importance on held-out data is the right default — it measures the actual metric drop when a column is shuffled, on data the model didn't train on. But it has its own failure: with correlated features, permuting one leaves its information available through the other, so both look unimportant while jointly being essential. It also evaluates the model on unrealistic rows created by the shuffle. Three methods, three different questions — which is exactly the framing §14.3 develops.

Likely interview questions
Very common⭐ Why is impurity-based feature importance misleading? What do you use instead?

Mean decrease in impurity has two documented biases. It favours high-cardinality and continuous features, because more candidate split points means more chances to reduce impurity by luck — add a column of pure noise with many distinct values and it will rank as important. And it's computed on training data, so it rewards features the model overfitted to. It describes how the model was built, not what actually predicts. Use permutation importance on held-out data instead, which measures the real metric drop when a feature is shuffled — then state its own caveat: correlated features mask each other, so both can look unimportant while jointly being essential.

DebugYour top feature by importance is the customer ID. What's happening?

Two possibilities, and I'd check both. The MDI bias: an ID has thousands of distinct values, so it offers thousands of split points and accumulates impurity reduction by chance — it can rank high while being useless. Genuine leakage: IDs are often assigned sequentially, so an ID encodes time, and if the target rate drifted over time the model has learned a temporal shortcut that will not generalise forward one day. The test that distinguishes them: compute permutation importance on held-out data — if it's ~zero, it's the cardinality bias; if it's large, it's leakage. Either way, drop the ID.

ConceptualIs feature importance a causal statement?

No, and this is the most consequential misuse. Importance measures how much the model uses a feature, which reflects predictive association — including through proxies, confounders and consequences of the target. num_collection_calls is enormously important for predicting default and reducing collection calls will not reduce default. If someone intends to act on the explanation, they need a causal design, not an importance ranking (§16.4). What importance is good for: debugging, sanity-checking, leakage detection, and generating hypotheses worth testing properly.

Part 8 of 17
Ensembles & Gradient Boosting
Bagging, Random Forest, AdaBoost, gradient boosting, XGB/LGBM/CatBoost, stacking

8.1 Why ensembles work ⭐

Combining models helps only under one condition, and naming that condition — with the formula — is what separates a real answer from “more models is better”.

The variance formula that explains everything

Average M estimators, each with error variance σ² and average pairwise correlation ρ. The variance of the average is:

Var(ensemble) = ρσ² + (1 − ρ)σ²/M

Read it carefully. The second term vanishes as M grows — that's the benefit of adding models. The first term does not: ρσ² is a floor you cannot get below no matter how many members you add. So ρ is the ceiling on how much ensembling can help, and every design decision in bagging and Random Forest is an attempt to push ρ down.

The one-liner that gets asked constantly

Bagging attacks variance; boosting attacks bias. Bagging trains high-variance, low-bias learners in parallel on different bootstrap samples and averages, which shrinks variance while leaving bias roughly unchanged. Boosting trains weak, high-bias learners sequentially, each correcting the previous ensemble's residual error, which drives bias down — and can drive variance up, which is why boosting overfits with too many rounds and bagging does not.

Likely interview questions
Very commonWhy do ensembles work at all?

Because averaging M estimators with error variance σ² and average pairwise correlation ρ gives ensemble variance ρσ² + (1−ρ)σ²/M. The second term vanishes as M grows; the first doesn't. So the members must be individually better than chance and mutually decorrelated — and ρ is the ceiling on how much ensembling can help. That formula explains every design decision downstream: why RF randomises features, why stacking prizes diversity over individual strength, and why averaging ten seeds of the same model buys almost nothing.

Conceptual⭐ Bagging vs boosting — what does each reduce, and why?

Bagging trains high-variance, low-bias learners in parallel on bootstrap samples and averages them, so it reduces variance — directly, via the formula above — while leaving bias roughly where it was. Boosting trains weak, high-bias learners sequentially, each fitted to the current ensemble's errors, so systematic error shrinks: it reduces bias, and can increase variance, which is why it overfits with too many rounds and needs early stopping. That difference also explains their base learners: bagging uses deep trees (already low-bias), boosting uses shallow ones (deliberately high-bias).

8.2 Bagging ⭐

Bootstrap aggregating: sample with replacement, fit in parallel, average. Simple enough that the interesting questions are all about the bootstrap itself.

interactive Watch variance divide as trees are added
—avg single-tree MSE
—ensemble MSE
—avg pairwise corr ρ
—rows out of bag

Real depth-3 regression trees fitted to real bootstrap samples. Drag the tree count and watch ensemble MSE fall while the average individual tree's MSE stays put — that gap is variance reduction, measured. Then toggle feature subsampling off to see ρ rise and the benefit shrink: that is precisely the difference between plain bagging and a Random Forest.

The bootstrap, and the 63.2%

A bootstrap sample draws n rows with replacement from n rows. The probability a given row is never picked is (1 − 1/n)ⁿ → 1/e ≈ 0.368. So about 63.2% of rows appear at least once, and about 36.8% are left out — the out-of-bag set for that tree. That single fact is a standard derivation question and the basis of OOB error (§8.3).

Bagging helps unstable learners, and barely touches stable ones

Bagging reduces variance, so its benefit is proportional to how much variance the base learner has. Deep trees are extremely unstable ⇒ bagging transforms them. Linear regression is stable ⇒ bagging it buys almost nothing, because each bootstrap fit is nearly identical and ρ ≈ 1. That's a good test of whether someone understands the mechanism rather than the recipe: “would you bag a linear model?” — no, and you should be able to say why in one sentence.

Likely interview questions
Deep diveShow that ~63.2% of rows appear in a bootstrap sample.

Each of the n draws misses a given row with probability (1 − 1/n), and the draws are independent, so the row is missed entirely with probability (1 − 1/n)ⁿ. As n → ∞ that converges to e⁻¹ ≈ 0.368. Therefore about 63.2% of rows appear at least once and 36.8% are out of bag. The consequence: every tree has a free, unbiased-ish validation set — the rows it never saw — which is what OOB error uses (§8.3).

GotchaWould you bag a linear regression?

No, and the reason is the mechanism. Bagging reduces variance, and its benefit scales with how unstable the base learner is. Linear regression is stable — fit it on ten bootstrap samples and you get ten nearly identical models, so ρ ≈ 1 and the variance formula says the ensemble is no better than a single fit. Deep trees are the opposite: a few rows change and the root split flips, so bagging transforms them. The general rule: bag unstable, low-bias learners; bagging a stable or high-bias learner is wasted compute.

8.3 Random Forest & out-of-bag error ⭐⭐

Random Forest is bagging plus one extra idea — and that extra idea is the whole reason it works better. It is also the part of the answer candidates most often omit.

HyperparameterEffectGuidance
n_estimatorsMore trees ⇒ lower varianceMore is never worse, only slower — this is not a regularization knob. Stop when OOB error plateaus
max_featuresThe decorrelation dial√p classification, p/3 regression. Lower ⇒ more decorrelation, more individual bias. The single most impactful RF parameter
max_depthIndividual tree capacityUsually leave unbounded — the averaging handles the variance
min_samples_leafSmooths leaf estimatesThe knob to reach for on noisy data
bootstrapSample rows with replacementSet False and you lose OOB entirely — and you're building Extra Trees' row strategy without its split strategy
Extra TreesRandom split thresholds tooMore variance reduction, slightly more bias, noticeably faster (no threshold search)
“Can you overfit a Random Forest?” — the two-clause answer

Adding trees does not overfit. The ensemble converges as M grows; it doesn't degrade. So n_estimators is a compute budget, not a regularization knob. But a forest can absolutely overfit: fully-grown trees on noisy data will happily memorise label noise, and averaging reduces variance without removing that memorisation. The fix is therefore min_samples_leaf and max_features, not fewer trees. Contrast with a GBM, which overfits readily with too many rounds — hence early stopping.

Likely interview questions
Very common⭐ How does Random Forest differ from plain bagging? What is OOB error?

RF adds random feature subsetting at each split (max_features). Without it, a dominant feature is chosen at the root of every tree and the trees end up highly correlated — and correlation is the ceiling on what averaging can achieve (§8.1). Feature subsetting forces structural diversity, which is the entire improvement. OOB error: each bootstrap omits ~36.8% of rows, so every row can be scored by the trees that never saw it, giving a validation estimate for free without holding anything out — particularly valuable on small datasets.

Very commonCan you overfit a Random Forest by adding trees?

No — the ensemble converges rather than degrading, so n_estimators is a compute budget and more is never worse. But the forest can still overfit: deep unpruned trees on noisy data memorise label noise, and averaging reduces variance without removing that memorisation. Control it with min_samples_leaf and max_features, not with fewer trees. That contrast with boosting — which does overfit with too many rounds and needs early stopping — is the follow-up they're usually fishing for.

ConceptualIs OOB error a valid substitute for cross-validation?

Usually a good approximation, with caveats. It's genuinely free and roughly comparable to leave-one-out CV, which makes it very attractive on small data. But: it's slightly pessimistic, because each row is predicted by only ~37% of the trees rather than the full ensemble; it's only available with bootstrap=True; and critically, it uses random row assignment, so it inherits every problem random splitting has — it will be optimistic under grouping or temporal structure just like random CV (§3.6). For grouped or time-series data I'd use a proper grouped/time CV instead.

ConceptualWhat are Extra Trees and when would you use them?

Extremely Randomized Trees add a second source of randomness: instead of searching for the best threshold on each candidate feature, they pick thresholds at random and take the best among those. That decorrelates trees further (lower ρ, more variance reduction) at the cost of slightly more bias per tree, and it's noticeably faster because there's no threshold search. Use them when you have plenty of trees, noisy data where the "optimal" threshold is largely noise anyway, or when training time matters. They also, by default, use the whole dataset rather than bootstrapping.

8.4 AdaBoost

The ancestor. Worth knowing not for its own sake but because framing it as a special case of gradient boosting is a strong answer.

AdaBoost maintains a weight per training example. Each round it fits a weak learner (classically a stump), computes its weighted error, assigns the learner a vote α = ½ln((1−err)/err), then increases the weights of misclassified examples and decreases the rest. The final prediction is the weighted vote.

AdaBoost is gradient boosting with exponential loss

The re-weighting scheme isn't an arbitrary heuristic — it falls out of forward stagewise additive modelling with the exponential loss L = exp(−y·F(x)). Saying that reframes two separate-looking algorithms as one, and it also explains AdaBoost's known weakness: exponential loss grows very fast for large negative margins, so AdaBoost is unusually sensitive to label noise and outliers — mislabelled points get their weights pushed up round after round until they dominate.

Likely interview questions
ConceptualHow does AdaBoost work, and how does it relate to gradient boosting?

It maintains per-example weights: each round fits a weak learner on the weighted data, gives it a vote based on its weighted error, then up-weights the misclassified examples so the next learner focuses on them. Final prediction is the weighted vote. The connection worth making: this is exactly gradient boosting with the exponential loss exp(−y·F(x)) under forward stagewise additive modelling — the re-weighting is the gradient. Framing it that way turns two algorithms into one idea, and immediately explains AdaBoost's weakness: exponential loss blows up on large negative margins, so it's very sensitive to label noise.

8.5 Gradient boosting ⭐⭐

A top-five interview question. The answer that lands is one sentence: each new tree is fitted to the negative gradient of the loss with respect to the current predictions.

interactive Boosting, one tree at a time
—train MSE
—test MSE
—best round (early stop)
—mean |residual|

Genuine gradient boosting on squared loss with depth-2 regression stumps, fitted live. Two experiments. ν = 1.0: the fit locks on fast and test error climbs early — overfitting. ν = 0.05: slow but the test curve is flatter and bottoms out lower. That is the learning-rate × n_estimators trade-off in one picture, and why “lower the learning rate and add trees” is the standard move.

Likely interview questions
Very common⭐ Explain gradient boosting. What exactly is each new tree fitted to?

Start from a constant prediction. Each round, compute the negative gradient of the loss with respect to the current predictions — the pseudo-residuals — fit a shallow tree to those, and add it scaled by the learning rate: Fₘ = Fₘ₋₁ + ν·hₘ. It's gradient descent in function space. For squared loss the negative gradient is the ordinary residual, which is why textbooks say "fit to the residuals" — but saying negative gradient is what generalises it to log loss, Poisson, quantile and any differentiable objective. AdaBoost is the special case with exponential loss.

ConceptualWhy does gradient boosting use shallow trees when Random Forest uses deep ones?

Because they're attacking different things. Boosting reduces bias by adding many weak learners, so each one should be deliberately high-bias, low-variance — a shallow tree (depth 3–6 typically) contributes a small correction without adding much variance. Bagging reduces variance, so its members should be low-bias, high-variance — deep trees, whose instability is exactly what averaging removes. Depth also caps interaction order (§7.4), so shallow boosting trees make the ensemble an additive model of low-order interactions, which is a good inductive bias for tabular data.

PracticalHow do the learning rate and number of trees interact?

They trade off almost directly: halve ν and you need roughly twice as many rounds for the same effective complexity. A smaller learning rate with more trees generally reaches a better optimum — each tree commits less, so the ensemble explores the loss surface more carefully — at the cost of training time. Because of that coupling, don't tune them independently: fix a modest ν (0.05–0.1), let early stopping choose the number of rounds, and only at the very end consider dropping ν further and refitting. Early stopping is itself a form of regularization (§4.5).

8.6 XGBoost vs LightGBM vs CatBoost ⭐⭐

The most reliably-asked comparison in tabular ML. Answer with mechanisms, then a selection rule, then the honest caveat that once tuned they are usually within noise of each other.

XGBoost 3.4LightGBM 4.7CatBoost 1.2
OptimisationSecond-order (Newton): gradients and Hessians, giving a closed-form optimal leaf weightGradient-based, histogram binningGradient-based, ordered boosting
Tree growthLevel-wise (leaf-wise available via grow_policy)Leaf-wise (best-first)Symmetric / oblivious — the same split across a whole level
Signature tricksExplicit λ, α, γ in the objective; sparsity-aware learned default direction for NaNGOSS (keep large-gradient rows, subsample small-gradient ones) + EFB (bundle mutually exclusive sparse features)Ordered target statistics for categoricals; permutation-based to avoid target leakage
CategoricalsSupported; historically encode yourselfNative categorical splitsBest-in-class, zero manual preprocessing
Missing valuesLearned default direction per splitSameSame
Inference speedFastFastVery fast — oblivious trees vectorise beautifully
Reach for it whenMaximum control, best-understood recipe, widest ecosystemVery large data, tight training budgetMany high-cardinality categoricals, limited tuning time
Monotonic and interaction constraints

All three libraries support monotonic constraints — forcing the prediction to be non-decreasing (or non-increasing) in a given feature, enforced at split time. This is how you inject a business or regulatory rule (“risk must not fall as debt rises”) into a boosted model, and it is close to mandatory in credit and insurance. As §4.5 notes, it's also a strong regularizer that often improves held-out performance. Interaction constraints are the related tool for “these features may not interact”.

Likely interview questions
Very common⭐ XGBoost vs LightGBM vs CatBoost — the real differences, and how do you choose?

XGBoost: second-order (Newton) approximation using gradients and Hessians, so leaf values and split gains come from a closed form; explicit λ/α/γ regularization; sparsity-aware default direction for missing values; level-wise growth by default. LightGBM: leaf-wise growth plus GOSS (keep large-gradient rows, subsample the rest) and EFB (bundle mutually exclusive sparse features) — fastest at scale, native categoricals. CatBoost: ordered boosting and ordered target statistics to eliminate the prediction shift from naive target encoding; symmetric oblivious trees for very fast inference; strong defaults. Choice: high-cardinality categoricals + little tuning time ⇒ CatBoost; very large data ⇒ LightGBM; control and ecosystem ⇒ XGBoost. And once tuned, they're usually within noise of each other.

Deep diveWhat is leaf-wise vs level-wise growth, and what's the risk of leaf-wise?

Level-wise expands every node at a given depth before descending — balanced trees, predictable cost, and it splits some nodes that gain little. Leaf-wise always expands the single leaf with the largest loss reduction, so it reaches a lower loss with fewer leaves and is faster and often more accurate. The risk: it grows very deep down one branch and overfits small or noisy datasets. Control with num_leaves and min_data_in_leaf — and note the classic misconfiguration of setting max_depth while leaving num_leaves at default, which gives a far more complex model than intended.

Deep diveWhat problem does CatBoost's ordered boosting solve?

The prediction shift caused by target leakage in naive target statistics. If a row's categorical encoding and its residual are computed using its own label, training residuals are systematically biased and the model is over-optimistic on data it has seen — the same failure as non-cross-fitted target encoding (§3.5), but occurring inside the boosting loop. Ordered boosting computes each row's statistics and residuals from only the rows preceding it in a random permutation, using several permutations so early rows aren't starved of data. It's the algorithmic version of out-of-fold encoding, which is why CatBoost needs no manual categorical preprocessing.

Deep diveWhat are GOSS and EFB?

LightGBM's two speed tricks. GOSS (Gradient-based One-Side Sampling): rows with large gradients are under-fitted and informative, so keep all of them; rows with small gradients are already well-fitted, so randomly subsample them and up-weight the survivors to keep the gradient estimate unbiased. You get most of the information from a fraction of the rows. EFB (Exclusive Feature Bundling): in sparse data many features are mutually exclusive (never non-zero together — think one-hot columns), so they can be bundled into a single feature without losing information, reducing the effective feature count. Together they're why LightGBM is dramatically faster on large sparse data.

ConceptualWhat are symmetric/oblivious trees and why does CatBoost use them?

An oblivious tree uses the same split condition across an entire level — every node at depth 2 tests the same feature and threshold. That makes the tree a perfectly balanced binary structure, so evaluating it is just computing an index into a leaf array: extremely fast, branch-free inference that vectorises well. It's also a strong regularizer, since the tree has far fewer degrees of freedom than a free-form one. The trade-off is expressiveness per tree — CatBoost compensates by using more trees, and the net result is competitive accuracy with notably fast prediction, which matters in latency-bound serving (§15.3).

8.7 Tuning a GBM ⭐

Giving an order rather than a list of parameters is what makes this answer sound like experience rather than documentation.

StepWhat you tuneWhy this order
1Fix a modest learning rate (0.05–0.1); let early stopping choose n_estimatorsThese two are coupled, so pinning one and deriving the other removes a whole dimension from the search
2Tree complexity: max_depth / num_leaves, min_child_weight / min_data_in_leafThe biggest lever on the bias-variance balance
3Sampling: subsample, colsample_bytreeCheap variance reduction and speed; also decorrelates trees
4Regularization: lambda (L2), alpha (L1), gamma (min split gain)Fine-tuning once the structure is right
5Lower the learning rate, refit with more roundsThe final squeeze — usually worth a small gain for a large time cost

Use random or TPE search over log-uniform ranges, inside the CV loop (§11.4). And check the obvious things first: is the objective right for the target (§5.8), are the categoricals handled natively, is early stopping actually monitoring the metric you care about rather than the default?

Early stopping needs a validation set that isn't your test set

If early stopping monitors the same data you later report on, the reported score is optimistic — the stopping round was selected using it. Inside cross-validation this needs care: either use a nested holdout carved from each training fold, or accept that the CV score is slightly optimistic and confirm on a final untouched test set. It's a small effect, but it's the same selection bias that makes nested CV necessary (§11.3), and interviewers who ask about early stopping are often probing exactly this.

Likely interview questions
Very commonHow do you tune a GBM? Give me your order of operations.

(1) Fix a modest learning rate (0.05–0.1) and let early stopping pick the number of rounds — those two are coupled, so pinning one removes a search dimension. (2) Tree complexity: max_depth/num_leaves and min_child_weight/min_data_in_leaf — the biggest lever. (3) Sampling: subsample, colsample_bytree. (4) Regularization: lambda, alpha, gamma. (5) Optionally lower the learning rate and refit with more rounds. Random or TPE search over log-uniform ranges, inside the CV loop. And before any of it: check the objective matches the target's distribution.

DesignWhat are monotonic constraints and when have you needed them?

They force the model's output to be non-decreasing (or non-increasing) in a given feature, enforced at split time so no split can violate the direction. You need them when a business or regulatory rule demands it — risk must not fall as debt rises; premium must not fall as claim history worsens — and they make the model dramatically easier to defend to a regulator or a domain expert. The underrated second benefit: they're a strong regularizer that eliminates a huge part of the hypothesis space using real domain knowledge, so on small or noisy data they often improve held-out performance rather than costing it.

8.8 Stacking, blending & voting ⭐

Stacking has exactly one hard part, and it is a leakage trap: the meta-learner must be trained on out-of-fold predictions.

Likely interview questions
Very commonHow does stacking work, and what's the leakage trap in it?

Base models' predictions become features for a meta-learner. The trap: those meta-features must be out-of-fold — each row's base prediction must come from a model that never saw that row. Train the base models on all the data and predict the same data, and you've handed the meta-learner in-sample fit, so it learns to trust whichever base model overfits hardest and the ensemble is calibrated to a fiction. Keep the meta-learner simple (regularized linear), prize diversity over individual strength, and be honest that stacking rarely survives a production review on latency and maintenance grounds.

DesignWould you ship a stacked ensemble?

Usually no, and I'd say why rather than just declining. It multiplies latency by the number of base models, multiplies the retraining and monitoring surface (every base model can drift independently), makes debugging a specific bad prediction genuinely hard, and typically buys a fraction of a point that won't survive the practical-significance test (§11.7). Where I would: offline batch scoring with no latency constraint and a genuinely valuable margin — or as a diagnostic, because if stacking helps a lot it tells me my base models are making different mistakes, which is information worth having even if I then ship one model.

8.9 Sample weights & cost-sensitive learning

The cheapest way to encode business costs into a model — and, in modern scikit-learn, no longer awkward to route through a pipeline.

MechanismWhereEffect
sample_weightfit()Per-row importance in the loss — the general tool: recency weighting, confidence weighting, cost weighting, survey weights
class_weight='balanced'Estimator paramInverse-frequency weights; equivalent to oversampling without synthetic rows
scale_pos_weightXGBoost / LightGBMThe same idea for binary imbalance, as a single ratio
Cost matrix + thresholdPost-hocOften better — leaves the probabilities calibrated and moves only the decision (§12.7)
Metadata routingset_config(enable_metadata_routing=True), set_fit_request()Makes sample_weight travel correctly through Pipeline and cross-validation
A currency check that will date you

If you say “scikit-learn can't pass sample_weight through a Pipeline, so I write a manual loop over folds”, you are describing a library from several versions ago. Metadata routing has been broadly available since 1.4 and was expanded through 1.7 — including routing through Pipeline and through bagging ensembles' predict* methods. Also worth knowing: weighting the positive class up decalibrates the output probabilities, so if you need real probabilities downstream, prefer tuning the threshold instead.

Likely interview questions
DesignHow do you make a model cost-sensitive when a false negative costs 20× a false positive?

Two routes, and I'd prefer the second. Class weights / sample_weight bake the cost into the loss so the model optimises the weighted objective directly — but this decalibrates the probabilities, so anything downstream that uses predict_proba is now wrong. Threshold tuning leaves the model and its probabilities intact and moves only the decision: with a calibrated model the cost-optimal threshold is around c_FP/(c_FP+c_FN) = 1/21 ≈ 0.048. That's cheaper, reversible, easier to explain, and separates the modelling from the policy — which matters when the cost ratio changes next quarter.

PracticalGive a use for sample_weight that isn't about class imbalance.

Recency weighting — weight recent rows more heavily so the model adapts to drift without discarding history entirely, which is a lighter-touch alternative to a rolling training window (§15.6). Others: label confidence, where human-verified labels get weight 1 and heuristic ones get 0.3; survey/design weights, where rows represent different population counts; and economic value, weighting each row by the revenue at stake so the model optimises pounds rather than counts. That last one often changes the model materially and is rarely tried.

Part 9 of 17
Unsupervised Learning
k-means, hierarchical, DBSCAN/HDBSCAN, GMM, PCA, t-SNE/UMAP, anomalies

9.1 k-means ⭐⭐

Asked about far more than it is used. Know the algorithm, its three assumptions, and why the seed changes the answer.

interactive Run Lloyd's algorithm step by step
0iterations
—inertia
—silhouette
—points reassigned

Real Lloyd iterations with a real k-means++ seeding routine and a genuinely computed silhouette. Try the bad seed a few times: it converges to a visibly worse local optimum with higher inertia. That is exactly why n_init exists and why k-means++ is the default — the objective is non-convex, so the starting point changes the answer.

The algorithm and its three assumptions

Lloyd's algorithm: initialise k centroids; assign each point to its nearest centroid; update each centroid to the mean of its assigned points; repeat until assignments stop changing. Each step can only reduce inertia (within-cluster sum of squares), so it always converges — to a local optimum.

AssumptionWhat breaks when it fails
Clusters are roughly sphericalElongated or ring-shaped clusters get carved arbitrarily — k-means will cut a ring into wedges
Clusters have similar varianceA tight cluster next to a diffuse one: the diffuse one gets split and the tight one absorbs its neighbours
Clusters have similar size (count)Inertia is a sum, so a large cluster dominates the objective and a small one gets swallowed
Plus: Euclidean distance is meaningful⇒ scale-sensitive (§3.4) and degraded in high dimensions (§2.7)
Plus: every point belongs somewhereThere is no noise label — outliers are forced into a cluster and drag its centroid
k-means++ is not a minor detail

Random initialisation can place two centroids inside the same true cluster, and Lloyd's algorithm has no mechanism to fix that — it converges to a genuinely bad local optimum. k-means++ seeds centroids one at a time, choosing each with probability proportional to its squared distance from the nearest existing centroid, so they start spread out. It gives an O(log k) approximation guarantee in expectation, and combined with n_init (multiple restarts, keep the lowest inertia) it makes k-means reliable in practice. The widget above lets you see the failure directly.

Likely interview questions
Very common⭐ How does k-means work, and what are its assumptions?

Lloyd's algorithm: initialise centroids (k-means++), assign each point to its nearest centroid, recompute centroids as the means, repeat until assignments stabilise. It minimises inertia — within-cluster sum of squares — which is non-convex, so the seed changes the result, hence n_init. Assumptions: clusters are roughly spherical, of similar variance and similar size, and Euclidean distance is meaningful — so it's scale-sensitive and degrades in high dimensions. Plus every point must belong to a cluster: there's no noise label, so outliers drag centroids.

ConceptualWhy does k-means always converge, and does it converge to the right answer?

It always converges because each step can only reduce inertia — the assignment step reassigns points to closer centroids, the update step moves each centroid to the mean, which is the inertia-minimising point for that assignment — and there are finitely many possible assignments, so it must terminate. But it converges to a local optimum, not the global one, because the objective is non-convex. That's exactly why n_init (multiple restarts) and k-means++ seeding exist, and why "different results each run" is expected behaviour rather than a bug.

GotchaWhy does k-means fail on concentric rings?

Because it assigns by distance to a centroid, and the centroid of a ring is at its centre — the same place as the centroid of the inner circle. So the two clusters are indistinguishable to the objective, and k-means will instead cut both rings into radial wedges, which is the lower-inertia solution. It isn't failing to optimise; it's optimising a criterion that doesn't match the structure. The right tool is a density-based method (DBSCAN/HDBSCAN, §9.4), or a spectral method that clusters in a transformed space.

9.2 Choosing k ⭐

Every method here has a caveat, and the complete answer includes the non-technical half.

MethodWhat it measuresCaveat
Elbow on inertiaWhere added clusters stop reducing WCSS muchInertia always falls with k, and the elbow is often absent or ambiguous — the most-taught and least-reliable method
Silhouette(b−a)/max(a,b) per point: separation vs cohesionFavours spherical, well-separated clusters — i.e. it rewards the shape k-means assumes. O(n²) distances
Gap statisticInertia vs that of uniform random reference dataPrincipled; needs many reference samples, so it's slow
Davies-BouldinAverage similarity between each cluster and its most similar oneLower is better; same spherical bias
Calinski-HarabaszBetween-cluster vs within-cluster dispersion ratioTends to increase with k; compare shapes, not raw values
BIC / AIC (via GMM)Likelihood penalised by parameter countThe most principled option — but requires a probabilistic model (§9.5)
StabilityHow consistent assignments are across bootstrap resamplesUnderused and genuinely informative — an unstable k is a wrong k
The honest half of the answer

k is usually a business constraint. How many segments can the marketing team actually build campaigns for? How many risk tiers does the pricing system support? How many groups can an analyst meaningfully name? Giving the technical methods and then saying “in practice I'd narrow to a plausible range statistically and let the business pick within it, because a mathematically optimal 17 segments that nobody can act on is worth less than a defensible 5” is the complete answer.

Likely interview questions
Very commonHow do you choose k?

Technically: the elbow on inertia (subjective and often absent), the silhouette score, the gap statistic, Davies-Bouldin, Calinski-Harabasz, and — most principled — BIC via a GMM. I'd also check stability: re-run on bootstrap samples and see whether assignments are consistent, because an unstable k is a wrong k. And the honest half: k is usually a business decision — how many segments can actually be acted on. I'd narrow to a plausible range statistically and let the business choose within it.

GotchaWhy can't you just pick the k that minimises inertia?

Because inertia is monotonically decreasing in k — it reaches exactly zero when k = n, with every point its own cluster. So minimising it always selects the most degenerate solution. That's the entire reason for the elbow heuristic (look for diminishing returns rather than the minimum) and for penalised criteria like BIC that explicitly charge for parameters. It's the clustering analogue of R² always increasing with more features (§5.5), and the fix is the same: penalise complexity or use held-out evidence.

9.3 Hierarchical clustering

Gives you every k at once, in the form of a tree you can cut at any height — which is genuinely useful for exploration.

LinkageDistance between clustersProduces
SingleClosest pairLong, chained clusters; can follow non-convex shapes but suffers from chaining — one bridge point merges two real clusters
CompleteFarthest pairCompact, roughly equal-diameter clusters; sensitive to outliers
AverageMean pairwise distanceA compromise; the usual default outside Ward
WardIncrease in within-cluster variance from mergingThe common choice. Minimises the same quantity as k-means, so it gives similar, compact clusters — and requires Euclidean distance

Cost is the limiting factor: agglomerative clustering is O(n²) in memory for the distance matrix and O(n²log n) or worse in time, so it stops being practical in the tens of thousands of rows. Divisive (top-down) variants exist but are rarer.

Likely interview questions
ConceptualWhen would you use hierarchical clustering over k-means?

Three cases. When you want every k at once — the dendrogram lets you cut at any height and inspect the nesting, which is far better for exploration than refitting k-means at each k. When the data has a genuine hierarchy (taxonomies, org structures, product categories). And when you want to use a non-Euclidean distance like Gower for mixed types (§2.6), which most linkages support but Ward doesn't. The blocker is always size: it's O(n²) memory, so past tens of thousands of rows you need k-means or a sampled approach.

Deep diveWhat is the chaining effect in single linkage?

Single linkage merges the two clusters whose closest pair is nearest, so a thin bridge of intermediate points can chain two genuinely distinct clusters into one — the algorithm follows the chain rather than seeing the gap. It's the reason single linkage can find elongated, non-convex shapes (a real strength, similar in spirit to DBSCAN) and also why it's fragile to noise: one badly-placed point merges everything. Complete and Ward linkage don't chain, at the cost of preferring compact, roughly spherical clusters.

9.4 DBSCAN & HDBSCAN ⭐

Density-based clustering — the answer when clusters aren't spherical, when you don't know k, and when you want “this point is noise” to be a valid output.

Why DBSCAN fails on varying density — and what HDBSCAN does

DBSCAN uses a single global eps. If one cluster is dense and another sparse, no single value works: small eps shatters the sparse cluster into noise, large eps merges the dense ones together. HDBSCAN removes eps entirely — it builds a hierarchy across all density levels (a minimum spanning tree on mutual reachability distance), then extracts the clusters that persist most stably across that hierarchy. That's why it's the sensible modern default for exploratory clustering, and it needs essentially one parameter (min_cluster_size) that has an interpretable meaning.

Likely interview questions
Very commonk-means vs DBSCAN vs hierarchical — pick one for a given problem.

k-means for large data with roughly spherical, similarly-sized clusters and a k you can justify — it's O(nkd) per iteration and scales. DBSCAN when clusters are arbitrarily shaped, you don't know k, and you want noise labelled as noise rather than forced into a cluster — but it struggles with varying density, which is what HDBSCAN fixes and why HDBSCAN is my default for exploration. Hierarchical/Ward when you want a dendrogram you can cut at any level, or a non-Euclidean distance, and n is small enough for O(n²). And GMM when you want soft assignments and elliptical clusters.

PracticalHow do you choose eps for DBSCAN?

The standard heuristic: compute each point's distance to its k-th nearest neighbour (with k = min_samples), sort those distances descending, and plot them — the knee of that curve is a reasonable eps, because it's where distances start growing rapidly, i.e. where you leave dense regions. Set min_samples from domain knowledge (a common rule of thumb is 2·dim). Honestly though, if you find yourself agonising over eps, that's the signal to use HDBSCAN, which eliminates the parameter by considering all density levels at once.

9.5 Gaussian mixtures and EM ⭐

The probabilistic generalisation of k-means: soft assignments, elliptical clusters, and a likelihood you can use for model selection.

A GMM models the data as a mixture of k Gaussians with weights πₖ, means μₖ and covariances Σₖ. It is fitted by EM:

  • E-step: compute each point's responsibility γᵢₖ ∝ πₖ·N(xᵢ | μₖ, Σₖ) — a soft assignment summing to 1 across clusters.
  • M-step: re-estimate πₖ, μₖ, Σₖ as responsibility-weighted averages.

Each iteration cannot decrease the likelihood, so it converges — again, to a local optimum, so multiple restarts matter. k-means is the limiting case of a GMM with spherical, equal covariances and responsibilities hardened to 0/1, which is a satisfying connection to be able to state.

covariance_typeShapeParameters per component
sphericalCircular, one variance1 — closest to k-means
diagAxis-aligned ellipsep
tiedSame ellipse shape for all componentsp(p+1)/2 shared — the LDA assumption (§6.3)
fullArbitrary ellipse per componentp(p+1)/2 each — most flexible, most data-hungry
The GMM's real advantage: BIC

Because a GMM is a probabilistic model, it has a likelihood — so you can select k (and the covariance type) with BIC or AIC, which penalise the likelihood by parameter count. That is a genuinely principled model-selection criterion rather than a heuristic like the elbow, and it's the single strongest argument for reaching for a GMM when “how many clusters?” actually matters. The other advantage: soft assignments — “this customer is 70% segment A, 30% segment B” is often more useful and more honest than a hard label.

Likely interview questions
Deep diveDerive the EM update for a Gaussian mixture, at a high level.

E-step: given current parameters, compute each point's responsibility for each component, γᵢₖ = πₖN(xᵢ|μₖ,Σₖ) / Σⱼ πⱼN(xᵢ|μⱼ,Σⱼ) — the posterior probability that point i came from component k. M-step: re-estimate parameters as responsibility-weighted statistics: πₖ = Σᵢγᵢₖ/n, μₖ = Σᵢγᵢₖxᵢ/Σᵢγᵢₖ, and Σₖ the weighted covariance. Each iteration maximises a lower bound on the log-likelihood, so the likelihood cannot decrease — which guarantees convergence to a local optimum.

ConceptualHow does a GMM relate to k-means?

k-means is a limiting case of a GMM: take spherical covariances, all equal, and shrink the variance toward zero — then the responsibilities harden to 0/1 and the EM steps become exactly Lloyd's assign-and-update. So a GMM generalises k-means in three ways: soft assignments instead of hard, elliptical clusters instead of spherical, and a likelihood that lets you use BIC for model selection. The cost is more parameters (especially with full covariance) and therefore more data needed.

9.6 PCA ⭐⭐

Two questions dominate: why must you scale first, and how do you choose the number of components. The widget answers the first one by demonstration.

interactive PCA — and what happens if you forget to scale
—PC1 explained var.
—PC2 explained var.
—PC1 angle

The covariance matrix and its eigenvectors are computed exactly (closed form for 2×2). Set the mode to raw and stretch x₁: PC1 swings to align with it and its explained-variance share races toward 100% — not because x₁ is more informative, but because it is measured in smaller units. Switch to standardised and the axes stop moving.

What PCA actually computes

Centre the data, then find the direction v maximising the variance of the projection vᵀx. That variance is vᵀΣv, and maximising it subject to ‖v‖ = 1 gives the top eigenvector of the covariance matrix Σ, with the eigenvalue equal to the variance along it. Subsequent components are the next eigenvectors, orthogonal to those before. Equivalently — and this is how it's actually computed — they are the right singular vectors of the centred data matrix, because X = UΣVᵀ ⇒ XᵀX = VΣ²Vᵀ. SVD is preferred because forming XᵀX squares the condition number (§5.1).

Choosing the number of componentsMethodNote
Explained variance thresholdSmallest k with cumulative ratio ≥ 0.90/0.95Most common; the threshold is arbitrary
Scree plot elbowWhere eigenvalues level offSame subjectivity as the k-means elbow
Downstream CVTreat n_components as a hyperparameter in the pipelineThe right answer when PCA feeds a supervised model
Kaiser criterionKeep components with eigenvalue > 1 (on standardised data)Crude; tends to over-retain
Parallel analysisCompare eigenvalues against random dataMore principled, less common
PCA is unsupervised — and that's a risk

PCA maximises variance, which has nothing to do with your target. A low-variance direction can be the one that separates your classes, and PCA will happily discard it — which is exactly the LDA contrast in §6.3. So using PCA before a classifier is a bet that variance and signal align; validate it by cross-validating n_components against downstream performance rather than against explained variance. And relatives worth naming: TruncatedSVD/LSA works on sparse matrices without centring them (so it doesn't destroy sparsity), Kernel PCA for non-linear structure, and NMF for non-negative parts-based factors that are often far more interpretable.

Likely interview questions
Very common⭐ Explain PCA. Why must you scale first? How do you choose the number of components?

PCA finds orthogonal directions of maximum variance — the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix, equivalently the right singular vectors of the centred data matrix, with eigenvalues giving the variance along each. Scaling: variance carries units, so an unscaled feature measured in smaller units dominates the first component purely by measurement convention rather than by information content. Components: cumulative explained-variance threshold, the scree elbow, or — best when PCA feeds a supervised model — cross-validate n_components against downstream performance. Caveat to add: components are linear mixtures of every feature, so interpretability is limited, and PCA is unsupervised so it can discard the direction that matters.

Deep diveShow PCA's equivalence to the SVD of the centred data matrix.

Write the centred data as X = UΣVᵀ. Then XᵀX = VΣᵀUᵀUΣVᵀ = VΣ²Vᵀ, which is exactly an eigendecomposition of (n−1) times the sample covariance matrix. So the right singular vectors V are the principal components, and the eigenvalues are σᵢ²/(n−1). Why it matters practically: computing the SVD of X directly is numerically better than forming XᵀX, which squares the condition number — the same argument as in §5.1 for least squares.

DesignWould you use PCA before a gradient boosting model?

Usually no. PCA gives you dense linear combinations of every feature, which destroys two things a GBM is good at: interpretability (a split on "0.3·age − 0.7·income + …" means nothing to anyone) and its ability to handle features individually, including missing values and monotonic constraints. GBMs also aren't hurt by correlated features or moderate dimensionality the way distance-based methods are. Where PCA does help before a GBM: genuinely huge feature counts where training time is the binding constraint, or dense embedding blocks that you want to compress before mixing with tabular columns.

9.7 t-SNE, UMAP and the trap ⭐

One caveat here should be volunteered unprompted, because it separates people who have read about t-SNE from people who have used it.

Likely interview questions
Very common⭐ PCA vs t-SNE vs UMAP — and what's the trap with t-SNE plots?

PCA is linear, deterministic, reversible and safe as a preprocessing step. t-SNE and UMAP are non-linear, stochastic visualisation tools. The trap: in a t-SNE plot, distances between clusters and the sizes of clusters are not meaningful — it optimises a neighbour-probability KL divergence that weights near pairs heavily and effectively ignores far ones, and the layout depends strongly on perplexity. UMAP preserves more global structure and is much faster, but is still stochastic. Never say "these clusters are similar because they're close on the plot".

DesignCan you use UMAP output as features for a classifier?

With real care. Three problems. It's stochastic, so the embedding isn't reproducible without fixing seeds and it changes if you refit. It's unsupervised and non-parametric in spirit — you must use the fitted transformer's transform on new data, and doing that correctly inside a pipeline (fitted on training folds only) is essential or you've leaked. And it discards information that the classifier might have used. If the goal is dimensionality reduction for a supervised model, PCA inside the pipeline is safer and LDA is more targeted; if the goal is a picture for humans, UMAP is excellent and shouldn't be feeding a model at all.

9.8 Anomaly detection ⭐

The hard part is never the algorithm. It is that you usually have no labels, so you cannot evaluate — which changes how you should design the whole system.

MethodIdeaStrength / weakness
z-score / MahalanobisDistance from the centreFast, interpretable; assumes a (multivariate) Gaussian
Isolation ForestAnomalies need fewer random splits to isolateScales well, few assumptions, no distance metric needed — the practical default
LOFLocal density relative to neighboursFinds local anomalies a global method misses; needs a neighbourhood size; poor in high dimensions
One-Class SVMBoundary around the normal regionSensitive to ν and γ; expensive; often outperformed by IForest
AutoencoderReconstruction errorGood for high-dimensional structured signals; needs enough clean data to learn "normal"
Three distinctions that make this answer senior

(1) Novelty vs outlier detection: novelty detection trains on clean data and flags anything new; outlier detection assumes the training data is already contaminated. Scikit-learn's API distinguishes them, and choosing the wrong one silently changes what “normal” means. (2) The contamination parameter is a prior you are asserting, not something the data tells you — and it directly sets your alert volume, so it's a business decision dressed as a hyperparameter. (3) If you have labels, use a classifier. Anomaly detection is what you do when you cannot frame it as highly-imbalanced classification; framing it that way when you can is throwing away supervision.

Likely interview questions
Very commonHow would you detect anomalies with no labels?

Isolation Forest as the default — anomalies require fewer random splits to isolate, it scales well, needs no distance metric and makes few assumptions. LOF when anomalies are local (unusual relative to their neighbourhood rather than globally extreme). Mahalanobis for a fast Gaussian baseline, and an autoencoder for high-dimensional structured signals. Then the three things that matter more than the algorithm: contamination is a prior you're asserting and it sets your alert volume; novelty vs outlier detection are different settings; and if you have any labels, use a classifier instead.

DesignHow do you evaluate an anomaly detector with no labels?

You can't, directly — and saying so plainly is the right answer. What you can do: have a human review the top-k flagged cases and measure precision-at-k, which is expensive but real; check stability across time windows and resamples (a detector whose flagged set changes completely week to week isn't measuring anything); use proxy labels if any exist (confirmed incidents, refunds, manual escalations), even if partial and biased; and inject synthetic anomalies of known types to measure recall on those, while being explicit that it only covers the failure modes you thought of. In production I'd instrument the review outcome so labels accumulate and the problem gradually becomes supervised.

9.9 Association rules & matrix factorization

Still asked in retail and e-commerce interviews, and the metric that matters is the one people forget.

Likely interview questions
ConceptualSupport, confidence and lift — which matters and why?

Support is how often the itemset occurs — it prunes the search space but says nothing about association. Confidence is P(consequent | antecedent), which looks convincing and is misleading on its own: if 40% of all baskets contain milk, then 40% confidence for {bread}→{milk} means bread told you nothing. Lift divides confidence by the base rate, so lift = 1 means independence, > 1 a genuine positive association, < 1 substitutes. Lift is the one that actually detects a relationship — and it's the one people omit.

GotchaWhat's the difference between explicit and implicit feedback in matrix factorization?

Explicit feedback is a stated preference — a star rating — where a missing entry genuinely means "unknown" and you fit only the observed ones. Implicit feedback is behaviour: views, clicks, purchases. The critical difference is that a zero is not a negative — not buying something usually means you never saw it. So implicit methods (ALS with confidence weighting, BPR) fit all entries but weight observed interactions with high confidence and unobserved ones with low confidence, rather than treating absence as dislike. Getting that backwards is the classic implicit-feedback mistake.

Part 10 of 17
Beyond Plain Supervised Learning
Few labels, multi-label, ordinal, survival, ranking, time series

10.1 Learning with few labels ⭐

“You have 500 labels and need 10,000” is a standard senior question. The good answer is a ladder, not a technique — and it starts by questioning the premise.

Question the premise first

Before proposing techniques, ask: does the model actually need 10,000 labels? A strong regularized baseline on 500 labels with proper cross-validation might already clear the bar. And ask what the label quality is — 500 carefully-adjudicated labels beat 10,000 noisy ones, because label noise caps achievable performance (§4.6) and inter-annotator agreement is your accuracy ceiling (§16.7). Candidates who go straight to semi-supervised methods have skipped the two cheapest options.

Likely interview questions
Very common⭐ What would you do with 500 labels and a need for 10,000?

First question the premise — a strong regularized baseline on 500 labels with honest CV might clear the bar, and 500 well-adjudicated labels beat 10,000 noisy ones. Then a ladder: active learning to spend the next labels where uncertainty is highest, with a diversity/core-set term so you don't label 500 near-duplicates; weak supervision (labelling functions plus a label model) if domain rules exist; pseudo-labelling with a clean held-out set to catch confirmation bias; transfer from a related task; a cheaper proxy label; and — often correct — buy the labels, with clear guidelines and an inter-annotator agreement check, because that agreement rate is your ceiling. Also worth naming: TabPFN-style models are strongest exactly in this small-data regime (§16.1).

GotchaWhen does pseudo-labelling make things worse?

When the model's confident predictions are systematically wrong — it then trains on its own mistakes and reinforces them, which is confirmation bias. It's most dangerous when the unlabelled pool has a different distribution from the labelled one (so the model is confidently extrapolating), or when classes are imbalanced (the majority class gets pseudo-labelled disproportionately, worsening the imbalance). Guards: keep a clean human-labelled validation set that never receives pseudo-labels, add them gradually with a high confidence threshold, and check per-class rates rather than overall accuracy.

DesignWhy does uncertainty sampling alone fail?

Because the most uncertain points are often near-duplicates of each other — one ambiguous region generates hundreds of similarly-uncertain examples, and labelling 500 of them teaches the model almost nothing beyond what the first 20 did. It also over-selects outliers and mislabelled points, which are uncertain for the wrong reason. The fix is to combine uncertainty with a diversity or core-set criterion so the selected batch covers the input space, and to select in batches with an explicit redundancy penalty rather than greedily one at a time.

10.2 Multi-label and ordinal targets

Two target shapes that are routinely mis-framed as multi-class, throwing away information in both cases.

Target shapeWrong framingRight framingMetric
Multi-label — several labels per rowMulti-class softmax (forces exactly one)Per-label sigmoid (binary relevance); classifier chains if labels are dependentPer-label F1, macro/micro-F1, Hamming loss, subset accuracy
Ordinal — ordered categoriesMulti-class (throws away the order)Ordinal models (cumulative logit), or a chain of binary "≥ k" classifiers; or regression + thresholdsQuadratic weighted kappa, MAE on the ordinal scale
Multi-output regressionIndependent models per outputShared representation, or a model with native multi-output supportPer-output plus an aggregate
Hierarchical labelsFlat multi-classLevel-by-level classifiers, or a hierarchical lossHierarchical precision/recall
Why treating ordinal as multi-class is a real loss

With categories poor / fair / good / excellent, multi-class treats predicting “poor” when the truth is “excellent” as exactly as wrong as predicting “good” — it has no notion that some errors are worse than others. That both wastes information during training and makes your metric meaningless. Ordinal models exploit the ordering; at minimum, use quadratic weighted kappa or MAE on the ordinal scale so the metric knows that near-misses are better than far ones.

Likely interview questions
ConceptualMulti-label vs multi-class — how do they differ in practice?

Multi-class assigns exactly one label from k options, so a softmax is appropriate and the probabilities sum to 1. Multi-label allows any subset, so you use per-label sigmoids (binary relevance) and the probabilities don't sum to anything. Consequences: metrics differ (per-label F1, Hamming loss, subset accuracy rather than plain accuracy), thresholds are per-label, and if labels are dependent — "cat" makes "animal" certain — binary relevance ignores that and classifier chains or a hierarchical structure captures it. Using softmax on a multi-label problem silently forces mutual exclusivity that doesn't exist.

DesignYour target is a 1–5 satisfaction rating. Classification or regression?

Neither, strictly — it's ordinal. Multi-class classification throws away the ordering (predicting 1 when the truth is 5 counts the same as predicting 4). Plain regression assumes the gaps are equal and the scale is interval, which is rarely true for satisfaction ratings — the step from 4 to 5 isn't the same as 2 to 3. Best options: an ordinal model (cumulative logit), or a chain of binary "is it ≥ k?" classifiers whose outputs you combine. If I do use regression, I'd threshold the output and report quadratic weighted kappa, which penalises distant errors more — that's the standard metric for exactly this situation.

10.3 Survival analysis ⭐

The trigger phrase is “when will this happen?” rather than “will it happen?” — and the giveaway in the data is that some rows simply haven't had the event yet.

Why labelling censored rows as 0 biases everything

A customer who joined last month and hasn't churned is not the same as one who has been around three years and hasn't churned — but binary labelling calls both “0”. The model then learns that recent tenure predicts staying, which is an artefact of your snapshot date rather than a property of customers. It also makes the label depend on when you extracted the data, so refreshing the dataset changes labels for the same rows. That is the concrete reason survival framing exists.

Likely interview questions
DesignWhat is censoring and why does it matter?

Right-censoring means you know only that the event hadn't occurred by the end of observation — the subject may fail tomorrow or never. Treating those rows as negatives is wrong twice: it conflates "survived three years" with "joined last month", so the model learns that short tenure predicts staying, which is an artefact of your snapshot; and it makes the labels depend on when you pulled the data, so refreshing changes labels retroactively. Survival methods handle it correctly — Kaplan-Meier for the marginal curve, Cox proportional hazards for covariate effects, or XGBoost's survival objectives if you want a GBM.

ConceptualWhat does the Cox model assume, and how would you check it?

Proportional hazards: the ratio of hazards between any two subjects is constant over time, so covariates shift the hazard multiplicatively but don't change its shape. It's semi-parametric — the baseline hazard is left unspecified, which is why it's so widely applicable. Check it with Schoenfeld residuals (they should show no trend against time), or by plotting log(−log(S(t))) curves per group and confirming they're roughly parallel. If it fails, options are: stratify on the offending variable, add a time-varying coefficient, or switch to an AFT model or a survival forest, neither of which needs proportional hazards.

10.4 Ranking & recommendation ⭐

Ranking is not classification with a sort. The loss knows about order, and the metrics know about position.

Likely interview questions
ConceptualPointwise, pairwise, listwise — what's the difference?

Pointwise predicts a relevance score per item independently, so it's just regression or classification and ignores that ranking is relative. Pairwise learns which of two items should rank higher (RankNet), which captures relativity but treats all pairs equally regardless of position. Listwise optimises a whole-list objective directly — LambdaMART is the classical workhorse, weighting each pair's gradient by how much swapping them would change nDCG, so it focuses effort on the top of the list. In practice LambdaMART on a GBM is still extremely strong for tabular ranking.

ConceptualWhy nDCG rather than precision@k?

Because precision@k is blind to order within the top k — putting the relevant items at ranks 1–3 or at ranks 8–10 gives the identical score, yet the user experience is completely different. nDCG discounts each item's gain by 1/log₂(rank+1) and normalises by the ideal ordering, so rank 1 is worth roughly 3× rank 8, and it also supports graded relevance rather than just binary. Use MRR instead when there's essentially one right answer and all you care about is where it lands.

DesignWhy is recommendation split into candidate generation and ranking?

Latency and cost. You cannot score ten million items per request with an expensive model, so a cheap, high-recall retrieval step narrows the catalogue to ~1,000 candidates (embedding ANN search, co-occurrence, popularity, business rules), and only then does an expensive high-precision ranker score those. A third re-ranking stage applies diversity, freshness and business constraints on the final ~10. The design consequence worth stating: the ranker can never recover an item the retriever missed, so retrieval recall is the ceiling on the whole system — and it's the stage people under-invest in.

10.5 Time series as supervised learning ⭐

Framing a forecast as a supervised problem is straightforward. The two things that trip people up are the feature set and the fact that trees cannot extrapolate.

Feature familyExamplesNote
Lagsy[t−1], y[t−7], y[t−28]The backbone. Choose lags from the ACF/PACF and domain seasonality
Rolling statisticsMean/std/min/max over 7, 28, 91 daysMust be computed with a shift — a window ending at t includes y[t] and leaks
CalendarDay-of-week, month, holiday, days-to-holiday, paydayCyclically encoded where appropriate (§13.3)
Fourier termssin/cos(2πkt/P) for k = 1…KSmooth seasonality with far fewer parameters than dummies; handles multiple periods
ExogenousPrice, promotion, weather, competitor activityThe main reason ML beats classical methods — but they must be known in advance for the forecast horizon
Series identitySKU, store, category embeddings or target-encoded IDsWhat makes a global model work across many series
Trees cannot extrapolate — the single biggest gotcha in ML forecasting

A GBM's prediction is a leaf constant, so it is bounded by the training target range (§7.3). On a series with a genuine trend, a model trained on 2024 data will predict 2024 levels forever, and the error grows without bound as you forecast further out.
