Three fixes: detrend or difference the target and model the residual; use a hybrid (linear trend + GBM on residuals); or include time as a feature only if you're confident the trend continues — which is usually a bad bet. This is the most common reason a "simple" classical model beats a GBM on a forecasting task.

Likely interview questions
Very common⭐ ML or ARIMA for forecasting?

Many related series with shared structure and exogenous drivers (10,000 SKUs, promotions, prices, holidays) ⇒ a global gradient boosting model on lag, rolling, calendar and Fourier features usually wins, mostly because it can learn across series and use covariates that classical univariate methods can't. A single short series ⇒ classical methods (ETS, ARIMA, seasonal-naive) are hard to beat and far easier to explain. And the constraint that decides many real cases: trees can't extrapolate, so a trending series needs detrending, differencing, or a hybrid with a linear component.

DebuggingYour rolling-mean feature gives 0.99 R² in backtest and fails live. Why?

Almost certainly the rolling window includes the current value. A 7-day mean computed as rolling(7).mean() at time t contains y[t] itself, so the feature is a smoothed copy of the target — spectacular in backtest, unavailable at forecast time. The fix is a shift: rolling(7).mean().shift(1), and more generally shift by the full forecast horizon, since at t you're predicting t+h and may not even have y[t] yet given reporting lag. This is temporal leakage (§3.7) in its most common concrete form.

ConceptualDirect vs recursive multi-step forecasting?

Direct: train a separate model for each horizon h, each predicting y[t+h] from features at t. No error accumulation, but h models to train and maintain, and each sees less structure. Recursive: one model predicting one step ahead, fed its own prediction as the next lag. One model, any horizon — but errors compound step by step, and the model is being applied to inputs (its own predictions) that don't look like its training inputs. Direct is the safer default for short fixed horizons; recursive is fine for a few steps. There's also a hybrid ("DirRec") that retrains at each step.

10.6 Forecast validation & metrics ⭐⭐

More forecasting projects go wrong here than anywhere else — a random split on time-series data produces a number that means nothing.

MetricWhat it doesWatch out
MAE / RMSEAbsolute error in target unitsNot comparable across series of different scale
MAPEPercentage errorUndefined/explodes near zero; asymmetric — over-prediction caps at 100%, under-prediction doesn't, so optimising it biases forecasts low
sMAPESymmetric variantBetter, still unstable near zero
MASEMAE ÷ MAE of seasonal-naiveScale-free and comparable across series — the one to use with many SKUs; < 1 means you beat the naive baseline
Pinball lossQuantile forecastsThe right metric when you forecast intervals rather than points; report coverage too
WAPE / weighted MAEError weighted by volumeOften the closest to the business quantity in retail
Likely interview questions
Very common⭐ How do you cross-validate time series data? What are purging and embargo?

Walk-forward / rolling-origin: train on everything up to time t, test on the window after it, then roll the origin forward — with an expanding or sliding window. Never a random split. Purging removes training samples whose label horizon overlaps the test window: if a label is observed 30 days after its features, a training row from just before the boundary has a label that partly occurs during the test period. Embargo additionally drops a buffer immediately after the test window before training resumes, so serial correlation and feature reporting latency can't leak backwards. Without both, you get an optimistic score and a production surprise.

Very commonWhen does MAPE break? What do you use instead?

Two failures. It's undefined and explodes as the actual approaches zero — fatal for intermittent demand, where many periods are genuinely zero. And it's asymmetric: over-prediction error is bounded at 100% while under-prediction is unbounded, so optimising MAPE systematically biases forecasts low. Use sMAPE (better, still unstable near zero) or — the right answer for many series at different scales — MASE, which divides by the seasonal-naive error, is scale-free and comparable across series, and has the useful property that < 1 means you beat the naive baseline. For volume-weighted business impact, WAPE is often closest to what people actually care about.

DesignYou're forecasting 10,000 SKUs. One model or 10,000?

One global model, almost certainly. It learns patterns shared across series (weekly seasonality, promotion response, holiday effects) so short-history and sparse SKUs borrow strength from the rest, and it's one artefact to train, monitor and deploy rather than 10,000. Give it series identity features (SKU, category, store) so it can specialise. Per-series models make sense only for a small number of high-value, long-history, idiosyncratic series — and a common good answer is a hybrid: global model for the long tail, bespoke treatment for the top 50 SKUs by revenue. Evaluate with MASE so results are comparable across the whole catalogue.

Part 11 of 17
Model Selection & Validation
The CV family, nested CV, hyperparameter search, curves, slices, honest comparison

11.1 The cross-validation family ⭐⭐

You met the splitters in §3.6. This is how you use them to produce a number you can defend — and what each one costs.

Likely interview questions
Very common⭐ Explain k-fold cross-validation. When is stratification necessary?

Partition into k folds; for each, train on k−1 and evaluate on the held-out one; average the k scores and — importantly — report the standard deviation too. Every row is tested exactly once, which gives a lower-variance estimate than a single hold-out. Stratify whenever the target is imbalanced or n is small, so no fold ends up with very few (or zero) positives, which destabilises both training and the metric. Add: stratification is orthogonal to grouping and to time, so it does not protect you from either (§3.6).

GotchaIs leave-one-out the most accurate form of CV?

No — that's a common misconception. LOO is nearly unbiased (each model trains on n−1 rows, almost the full dataset) but has high variance, because the n training sets are almost identical, so the n error estimates are highly correlated and averaging them removes little noise. It's also n model fits. 5- or 10-fold usually gives a lower-variance estimate at a fraction of the cost, which is why they're the standard. LOO earns its place mainly when n is tiny and you can't afford to hold anything out.

11.2 Choosing k

k itself trades bias against variance, and knowing which direction each goes is a neat two-sentence answer.

kTraining set per foldBias of the estimateVariance of the estimateCost
Small (k=2,3)Much smaller than the full dataPessimistic — models trained on less data perform worseLower (folds share less training data)Cheap
k=5 or 1080–90% of the dataSmallModerateThe standard compromise
k=n (LOO)n−1 rowsNearly unbiasedHigh — training sets almost identical, so errors are correlatedn fits

The practical rule: 5 or 10, and use repeated k-fold if the fold-to-fold spread is large relative to the difference you're trying to detect. With very small datasets, prefer repeated stratified k-fold over LOO.

Likely interview questions
ConceptualHow does the choice of k affect the bias and variance of the CV estimate?

Small k means each model trains on much less data, so it under-performs the model you'll actually ship — the estimate is pessimistically biased. Large k (up to LOO) trains on nearly the full data so bias is small, but the k training sets overlap almost completely, so the fold errors are highly correlated and averaging them removes little noise — high variance, plus k model fits. 5 or 10 is the standard compromise. If the fold spread is large relative to the effect you're measuring, use repeated k-fold rather than increasing k.

11.3 Nested cross-validation ⭐⭐

A favourite senior question precisely because most candidates have read about it and never done it. The key insight is why a tuned CV score is not an estimate.

How much optimism are we talking about?

It scales with how many settings you tried and how noisy each estimate is. On a large dataset with 20 settings, the bias may be a fraction of a point and nested CV isn't worth the compute. On a small dataset with 500 settings and a high-variance metric, the flat-CV score can be optimistic by several points — enough to change a shipping decision. So the honest answer to “do you always use nested CV?” is “no — I use it when the dataset is small or the search is large, and otherwise I rely on a test set I touch once.”

Likely interview questions
Very common⭐ What is nested cross-validation and why does it exist?

Tuning hyperparameters on the same CV you report gives an optimistically biased estimate — the reported score is the maximum over many noisy estimates, so it's inflated even if every setting were genuinely equally good. Nested CV puts hyperparameter selection in an inner loop run separately inside each outer training fold, so no outer test fold ever influences selection. Cost: k_outer × k_inner fits. What it estimates is subtle: the performance of the whole procedure including tuning, not of one model — so you don't get "the best hyperparameters" from it, you get an honest number and then refit.

DesignDo you always use nested CV?

No, and being able to say when it's unnecessary is part of the answer. The optimism scales with how many settings you tried and how noisy each fold estimate is. On a large dataset with a modest search, the bias is often a fraction of a point and the k×k cost isn't justified. On small data with a large search, it can be several points — enough to change a decision. My default is a single held-out test set touched exactly once, with nested CV reserved for small datasets, large searches, or when the number itself is the deliverable (a paper, a regulatory submission).

11.4 Hyperparameter search ⭐

The search space usually matters more than the search algorithm. But the algorithm question gets asked, so here is the picture that answers it.

interactive Grid vs random search — the Bergstra & Bengio result
—grid · distinct values tried
—random · distinct values tried
—grid · best score found
—random · best score found

The response surface here depends almost entirely on one of the two hyperparameters — which is the empirically usual situation. With a budget of 16, a 4×4 grid tries only 4 distinct values of the parameter that matters; random search tries 16. That is the whole Bergstra & Bengio argument, and it gets stronger as dimensions grow.

StrategyHow it worksReach for it when
Grid searchExhaustive product of values2–3 parameters with genuinely few sensible values — e.g. the C/gamma grid for an SVM (§6.5)
Random searchSample from distributionsThe sane default — better per unit compute when few parameters matter
Bayesian / TPESurrogate model + acquisition function (Optuna)Expensive evaluations, many parameters. Note it behaves like random search until its model warms up
Successive halving / HyperbandStart many trials cheaply, kill the losers, escalate survivorsHalvingRandomSearchCV — excellent when a cheap fidelity (fewer trees, less data) predicts the full one
Population-based / evolutionaryMutate and select over a populationRarely worth it for classical ML; more common in deep learning
Early stoppingStop a single fit when validation stallsAlways, for boosting and NNs — orthogonal to the search itself
Search spaces beat search algorithms

Use log-uniform distributions for learning rates, regularization strengths and anything spanning orders of magnitude — a uniform sample over [0.0001, 1] puts 90% of its mass above 0.1, which is almost never where the answer is. Bound the space with domain knowledge instead of searching absurd regions. Seed the sampler for reproducibility. Prune unpromising trials. And the rule that matters most: tune inside the CV loop, never on the test set — otherwise §11.3 applies.

Likely interview questions
Very commonGrid vs random vs Bayesian search — which and why?

Random is the sane default: with a fixed budget it probes far more distinct values of the parameters that actually matter (the Bergstra & Bengio result), and the advantage grows with dimensionality since a grid's coverage per axis falls as B^(1/d). Grid only for two or three parameters with genuinely few sensible values. Bayesian/TPE when each evaluation is expensive — noting it behaves like random search until its surrogate warms up. Successive halving/Hyperband when a cheap fidelity predicts the full one. And the real lesson: the search space matters more than the algorithm — log-uniform ranges, bounded by domain knowledge, tuned inside the CV loop.

PracticalWhy log-uniform for a learning rate?

Because what matters is the order of magnitude, not the linear value — 0.001 and 0.01 are as different from each other as 0.01 and 0.1, but a uniform sample over [0.0001, 1] puts about 90% of its draws above 0.1 and would barely explore the small end at all. Log-uniform sampling gives equal probability to each decade, which matches how the parameter actually behaves. The same applies to regularization strengths, C, gamma, and anything else spanning orders of magnitude. Getting this wrong is a much bigger error than choosing the wrong search algorithm.

11.5 Learning & validation curves ⭐

The two diagnostic plots that turn “the model isn't good enough” into a specific next action.

Plotx-axisAnswers
Learning curveTraining-set sizeDo I have a bias or variance problem? Will more data help? (§4.6)
Validation curveOne hyperparameterIs my search range even right? Where is the optimum, and is the curve flat around it?
A flat validation curve is information, not a failure

If performance barely changes across two orders of magnitude of a hyperparameter, that parameter doesn't matter for this problem — stop tuning it, fix it at a sensible value, and spend the budget elsewhere. Conversely, if the optimum is at the edge of your search range, your range is wrong and you should extend it. Both readings are more actionable than the best-score number that a search returns, and neither is visible from the search output alone.

Likely interview questions
PracticalWhat's the difference between a learning curve and a validation curve?

A learning curve plots train and validation error against training-set size, and answers "do I have bias or variance, and will more data help?" A validation curve plots them against one hyperparameter, and answers "is my search range right and where is the optimum?" They're complementary: the learning curve tells you whether to buy data or change the model; the validation curve tells you whether you're even searching in the right region. Two readings worth stating: a flat validation curve means the parameter doesn't matter here, and an optimum at the edge of the range means your range is wrong.

11.6 Slice analysis ⭐

An aggregate metric tells you whether something is wrong. Slice analysis tells you what — and it is the single highest-yield diagnostic in applied ML.

Likely interview questions
DebuggingYour overall metric is fine but users are complaining. Where do you look?

Slices. An aggregate is a weighted average, so a small segment can be badly broken while barely moving the headline — and small segments are often the important ones: new customers, a new market, a new channel, a protected group. I'd cut by time period, tenure, geography, channel, device, value band and data source, and look at both the metric and the sample size per slice. This is also where Simpson's paradox shows up (§2.5). I'd then automate the slice report so it runs with every evaluation, because this is exactly the failure a single number is designed not to show you.

11.7 Comparing models honestly ⭐

“Your model is 0.4% better. Is it better?” is a question about statistics and judgement, and the good answer contains both.

Likely interview questions
Very common⭐ Your model is 0.4% better. Is it better?

Three checks. Statistical: compare paired across the same folds or the same test rows, report a bootstrap CI on the difference (resampling indices once and scoring both models on the same resample), and use a paired permutation test or the corrected resampled t-test — plain t-tests over CV folds are anti-conservative because training sets overlap. Selection: if this is the best of 40 variants, part of that 0.4% is luck. Practical: what does it cost in latency, complexity, retraining and explainability? A 0.4% gain that adds a service dependency usually isn't worth shipping — and saying that is the senior half of the answer.

GotchaTwo models' confidence intervals overlap. Does that mean no significant difference?

No — that's a common inferential error. Overlapping marginal intervals can coexist with a paired difference whose interval excludes zero, because pairing removes the variation the two models share (same rows, same folds, same difficulty). The correct procedure is to bootstrap the difference directly: resample indices once, score both models on that resample, take the difference, repeat. If that interval excludes zero, the difference is real — regardless of what the marginal intervals look like.

Deep diveWhy are plain t-tests over CV folds problematic?

Because the fold results aren't independent — every pair of training sets in k-fold CV overlaps in about (k−2)/(k−1) of the data, so the fold-level differences are positively correlated. A standard t-test assumes independence, so it underestimates the variance and is anti-conservative: it declares significance far too often. Fixes: Nadeau & Bengio's corrected resampled t-test, which inflates the variance estimate to account for the overlap; a paired permutation test, which makes no independence assumption; or repeated CV with the correction applied.

Part 12 of 17
Metrics, Thresholds & Imbalance
Confusion matrix, ROC vs PR, averaging, thresholds, calibration, imbalance

12.1 The confusion matrix ⭐⭐

Everything in this part is derived from four numbers. Being fluent in that derivation is what lets you answer any metric question from first principles.

interactive Move the threshold, watch every metric move with it
True positives—
False positives—
False negatives—
True negatives—
—accuracy
—precision
—recall
—F1
—ROC-AUC
—PR-AUC

All six numbers computed exactly from 4,000 simulated scores. Three experiments. (1) Drop the base rate to 2% and watch accuracy stay above 0.97 at every threshold while precision collapses. (2) Compare ROC-AUC and PR-AUC as the base rate falls. (3) Notice that ROC-AUC and PR-AUC don't change at all when you move the threshold — they are threshold-free, which is exactly why neither tells you what your deployed system will do.

Everything derived from four cells

MetricFormulaReads as
Accuracy(TP+TN)/nFraction correct — useless under imbalance
Precision (PPV)TP/(TP+FP)Of what we flagged, how much was real?
Recall / TPR / sensitivityTP/(TP+FN)Of what was real, how much did we catch?
Specificity / TNRTN/(TN+FP)Of the negatives, how many did we leave alone?
FPRFP/(FP+TN) = 1 − specificityThe ROC x-axis — normalised by the negative count, which is why it flatters imbalance
F1 / F-β(1+β²)PR/(β²P+R)Harmonic mean; β > 1 favours recall, β < 1 favours precision
MCCCorrelation between predicted and true labelsUses all four cells; robust under imbalance where F1 is not
Balanced accuracy(TPR + TNR)/2Accuracy with class sizes ignored
Cohen's κAgreement corrected for chanceAlso the annotator-agreement measure (§16.7)
F1 ignores true negatives — MCC doesn't

F1 is the harmonic mean of precision and recall, both of which are computed without ever touching TN. That's usually what you want (TN is enormous and uninformative under imbalance), but it means F1 can look identical for two very different classifiers, and it's asymmetric — swap which class you call positive and F1 changes. MCC uses all four cells, is symmetric, and gives a more honest single number on imbalanced problems. Worth naming when someone asks for "one metric".

Likely interview questions
Very common⭐ Accuracy is 95% and the model is useless. Explain.

Ask for the base rate. If 95% of rows are negative, predicting "negative" for everything scores 95% and catches nothing — accuracy has become a majority-class detector. Report instead the confusion matrix at the deployed threshold, per-class recall, and PR-AUC. There's a second failure worth adding: accuracy is blind to the cost asymmetry between a false positive and a false negative, so even on balanced data it's the wrong objective whenever the two errors cost different amounts.

ConceptualPrecision vs recall — a business example where each dominates.

Precision dominates when acting is expensive or damaging: blocking a legitimate payment (lost sale + support contact), sending an enforcement letter, or opening a fraud case that costs an analyst 20 minutes. Recall dominates when missing is catastrophic: cancer screening, safety recalls, AML compliance, security alerts. The framing to use: precision is "what happens when we act", recall is "what happens when we miss" — and the threshold (§12.7) is the dial that buys one with the other, so the real question is always which error the business can afford.

Deep diveWhen would you use MCC instead of F1?

When you want a single honest number on an imbalanced problem. F1 is the harmonic mean of precision and recall, neither of which uses true negatives — so F1 is asymmetric (swap which class is "positive" and it changes) and can be identical for classifiers that behave very differently. MCC is essentially the correlation between predicted and true labels, uses all four cells, is symmetric, and returns 0 for a random or constant classifier regardless of the class balance. That last property makes it much harder to game than F1 or accuracy.

12.2 Precision, recall and F-β ⭐

The trade-off is mechanical: moving the threshold buys one with the other. What's not mechanical is choosing where to sit.

F-β lets you state that preference numerically: F_β = (1+β²)·P·R/(β²P + R). Setting β = 2 weights recall roughly 4× more than precision (β² = 4); β = 0.5 does the reverse. The clean way to choose β is from the cost ratio — if a miss costs 4× a false alarm, β = 2 is the corresponding F-measure.

Why the harmonic mean rather than the arithmetic

The harmonic mean is dominated by the smaller value. A classifier with precision 1.0 and recall 0.01 has an arithmetic mean of 0.505 — flattering — but an F1 of about 0.02. That's the point: F1 refuses to reward a model that achieves one at the total expense of the other, which is exactly the degenerate behaviour a threshold at an extreme produces. Being able to explain why harmonic is a small but reliable differentiator.

Likely interview questions
ConceptualWhy is F1 a harmonic mean rather than an arithmetic one?

Because the harmonic mean is dominated by the smaller value, so it refuses to reward a model that maximises one metric at the total expense of the other. Precision 1.0 with recall 0.01 gives an arithmetic mean of 0.505 but an F1 of ~0.02 — which correctly reflects that the model is useless. Since moving the threshold to an extreme trivially maximises either precision or recall alone, a mean that punishes imbalance between them is the only sensible single summary.

DesignHow do you choose β in F-β?

From the cost ratio. β² is roughly how many times more you weight recall than precision, so if a false negative costs 4× a false positive, β = 2 is the matching measure. In practice I'd rather skip F-β entirely and go straight to expected cost: assign real currency values to FP and FN, and choose the threshold that minimises total cost (§12.7). F-β is a useful summary when you need one number for comparison, but it's a proxy for the cost calculation, and if you can do the calculation directly you should.

12.3 ROC-AUC vs PR-AUC ⭐⭐

The most-asked metrics question, and it has a structural explanation that most candidates don't give.

interactive ROC-AUC flatters, PR-AUC doesn't
—ROC-AUC
—PR-AUC
—PR baseline (= base rate)
—lift over baseline

The classifier is exactly as good at every setting — the score distributions never change, only the mix. Drag from 50% down to 1% and watch ROC-AUC stay essentially flat while PR-AUC falls off a cliff. The reason is structural: the ROC's x-axis is the false-positive rate, normalised by a huge negative count, so a flood of false positives barely registers.

The structural explanation

ROC plots TPR against FPR. FPR is FP/(FP+TN) — divided by the total number of negatives. Under 1:1000 imbalance, going from 100 false positives to 1,000 moves FPR from 0.0001 to 0.001: visually nothing. But precision, TP/(TP+FP), is divided by the number of alerts, so the same change is devastating. That is the whole difference: ROC normalises by a quantity you don't care about; PR normalises by the one you do.

ROC-AUCPR-AUC / Average Precision
AxesTPR vs FPRPrecision vs Recall
Random baselineAlways 0.5, regardless of balanceThe base rate — so 0.30 means very different things at 2% vs 40% prevalence
Under imbalanceFlattering — barely movesReflects what the alert queue will feel
InterpretationP(random positive ranks above random negative)Roughly the average precision across recall levels
Use whenRoughly balanced; you care about ranking generally; comparing across datasets with different prevalencePositives are rare; you care about the top of the ranking
Says about calibrationNothingNothing
Likely interview questions
Very common⭐ ROC-AUC vs PR-AUC — when do you prefer which?

ROC-AUC plots TPR against FPR and summarises ranking quality well when classes are roughly balanced. Its weakness under imbalance is structural: FPR divides by the total negative count, so going from 100 to 1,000 false positives on a 1:1000 problem moves it from 0.0001 to 0.001 — visually nothing. PR-AUC plots precision against recall, and precision divides by the number of alerts, so the same change is devastating. ROC normalises by a quantity you don't care about; PR normalises by the one you do. Prefer PR-AUC when positives are rare. And note its baseline is the base rate, not 0.5 — plus neither says anything about calibration.

Very commonWhat does ROC-AUC actually mean, probabilistically?

It's the probability that a randomly chosen positive is scored above a randomly chosen negative — P(score(x⁺) > score(x⁻)), with ties counted as a half. It equals the normalised Mann-Whitney U statistic. Two consequences follow directly: it's threshold-free, so it tells you nothing about the deployed operating point; and it's invariant to any monotone transform of the scores, which is why Platt scaling changes the probabilities completely and leaves AUC untouched (§12.8).

GotchaCan you compare PR-AUC across two datasets?

Not directly, because the baseline differs — a random ranker achieves PR-AUC equal to the base rate, so 0.30 on a 2% prevalence problem is a 15× lift and excellent, while 0.30 on a 40% prevalence problem is worse than random. Report PR-AUC alongside the base rate, or report the lift over baseline. ROC-AUC is comparable across prevalence (its baseline is always 0.5), which is one of the few genuine arguments in its favour — but that same property is exactly what makes it flattering on the imbalanced problem itself.

12.4 Multi-class averaging ⭐

“F1 = 0.84” is an incomplete claim in a multi-class setting. Which averaging you used changes the number and the meaning.

AveragingHowDominated byReport it when
MicroPool TP/FP/FN across all classes, then computeFrequent classesYou care about overall correct predictions. In single-label multi-class, micro-F1 = accuracy
MacroCompute per class, then average unweightedNothing — every class counts equallyRare classes matter as much as common ones — the usual choice when imbalance is meaningful
WeightedPer class, averaged by supportFrequent classesYou want per-class detail but a support-weighted summary; mostly reproduces micro
SamplesPer row, then averaged—Multi-label only (§10.2)
Why micro-F1 = accuracy in single-label multi-class

Every prediction is either correct (one TP) or wrong — in which case it contributes exactly one FP to the predicted class and one FN to the true class. So summed across classes, ΣFP = ΣFN, which makes micro-precision = micro-recall = ΣTP/n = accuracy — and the harmonic mean of two equal numbers is that number. Being able to derive it in two sentences is a satisfying answer to a question that usually gets a shrug.

Likely interview questions
Very commonMicro vs macro F1 — which do you report?

Micro pools TP/FP/FN across classes, so it's dominated by frequent classes — and in single-label multi-class it equals accuracy exactly. Macro averages per-class F1 with equal weight, so a rare class counts as much as a common one; that's what you report when small classes matter, which under imbalance they usually do. Weighted averages by support and mostly reproduces micro. The real answer: report the one matching the decision, say which one it is, and show the per-class breakdown — the aggregate hides exactly the failure you need to see.

Deep diveProve that micro-F1 equals accuracy in single-label multi-class.

Every prediction is either right or wrong. A correct prediction contributes one TP. An incorrect one contributes exactly one FP (to the class predicted) and exactly one FN (to the true class). Summing over classes therefore gives ΣFP = ΣFN = number of errors. Micro-precision is ΣTP/(ΣTP+ΣFP) and micro-recall is ΣTP/(ΣTP+ΣFN), which are equal, and both equal ΣTP/n = accuracy. The harmonic mean of two identical numbers is that number, so micro-F1 = accuracy. Note it relies on single-label: in multi-label it no longer holds.

12.5 Regression metrics ⭐

Same principle as classification: pick from the decision. Is a 10-unit error twice as bad as a 5-unit error, or four times?

MetricOptimises / penalisesUse whenWatch out
RMSEThe mean; large errors quadraticallyBig misses are disproportionately costlyOutlier-sensitive; in target units, which is good for communication
MAEThe median; linear penalty“Typical error” is the business quantityNot differentiable at zero (rarely a practical issue)
RMSLERelative error; punishes under-prediction moreTargets spanning orders of magnitudeRequires non-negative targets
MAPEPercentage errorCommunicating to a business audienceUndefined/explodes near zero; asymmetric — biases forecasts low (§10.6)
MASEError ÷ seasonal-naive errorComparing across many series of different scaleNeeds a defined seasonal period
PinballA specific quantilePrediction intervals; asymmetric costsReport coverage alongside it
R² / adjusted R²Variance explainedCommunicating fitAlways rises with features; test R² can be negative; not comparable across datasets (§5.5)
RMSE vs MAE, stated as a decision

If the cost of an error grows faster than linearly — a stock-out that cascades, a structural failure — RMSE matches the business and you should optimise squared loss. If cost grows roughly linearly and you have outliers you cannot clean, MAE matches it. And note the consequence for the model, not just the report: optimising MSE fits the conditional mean, optimising MAE fits the conditional median (§4.1). On a right-skewed target those are materially different numbers, so this choice changes the predictions themselves.

Likely interview questions
Very commonRMSE vs MAE — what does each optimise?

Minimising squared error fits the conditional mean; minimising absolute error fits the conditional median — so on a right-skewed target they give materially different predictions, not just different scores. RMSE penalises large errors quadratically (right when costs grow super-linearly) and is outlier-sensitive; MAE is robust and reports "typical error". Choose from the decision: is a 10-unit error twice as bad as a 5-unit error, or four times? And keep the metric consistent with the training loss — reporting MAE while optimising MSE means you're measuring something you didn't ask the model to do.

GotchaYour RMSE looks fine but the business says the model is wrong. What might be happening?

Several possibilities worth checking in order. The error is concentrated in a slice that matters — high-value customers, recent periods — and the aggregate hides it (§11.6). The mean isn't the quantity they act on: if they need a typical value or a safety margin, RMSE's mean-seeking behaviour is systematically wrong for them and MAE or a quantile is right. The scale differs across the range: 10% error is fine on large values and disastrous on small ones, which RMSE weights the opposite way. Or the errors are biased in one direction — RMSE doesn't distinguish over- from under-prediction, so I'd plot residuals against fitted and check for systematic bias.

12.6 Ranking metrics

Short section, one idea: position matters, and only some metrics know it.

Likely interview questions
ConceptualPrecision@k vs nDCG vs MRR — when does each apply?

Precision@k when you only care whether relevant items are in the top k and order within it doesn't matter — a grid of results all visible at once. nDCG when position matters and relevance is graded: it discounts gain by 1/log₂(rank+1) and normalises by the ideal ordering, so rank 1 is worth ~3× rank 8. MRR when there's essentially one right answer and all you care about is how far down it is — question answering, navigational search. Default to nDCG for feeds and recommendations; it's the one that matches how people actually consume a ranked list.

12.7 Choosing a threshold ⭐⭐

0.5 is a default, not a decision. It is the right threshold only when false positives and false negatives cost the same and the classes are balanced — which is almost never.

Likely interview questions
Very common⭐ How do you choose a decision threshold?

Not 0.5 — that's a default, correct only when classes are balanced and both errors cost the same. Three legitimate sources: a cost matrix (minimise expected cost; for a calibrated model the optimum is near c_FP/(c_FP+c_FN)); an operating constraint ("analysts can review 200 cases a day" fixes alert volume and therefore t); or a guarantee (the lowest t meeting a contractual precision floor, then report the recall you get). Tune it on a validation set — TunedThresholdClassifierCV does this with CV — never on test, and consider abstention for low-confidence cases.

Deep diveWhy is the cost-optimal threshold c_FP/(c_FP+c_FN)?

At probability p, acting costs (1−p)·c_FP in expectation (you pay for a false positive when the case is negative); not acting costs p·c_FN. You should act when acting is cheaper: (1−p)c_FP < p·c_FN, which rearranges to p > c_FP/(c_FP + c_FN). So with FP = £8 and FN = £120, the threshold is 8/128 ≈ 0.0625. The crucial precondition: this only holds if p is a genuine calibrated probability — which is why calibration (§12.8) isn't an optional refinement but a prerequisite for cost-based decisions.

DesignWould you use different thresholds for different customer segments?

Sometimes, and it needs care. It's legitimate and often optimal when the cost structure genuinely differs by segment — reviewing a high-value transaction is worth more analyst time, so a lower threshold there maximises expected value. It's legally fraught when the segment correlates with a protected attribute, because per-group thresholds are an explicit use of that attribute and are prohibited in several jurisdictions even when they improve outcomes (§14.8). My rule: segment by cost or capacity, never by a protected characteristic or an obvious proxy, and document the justification.

12.8 Calibration ⭐⭐

Among the cases you scored 0.7, roughly 70% should be positive. If they aren't, every expected-value calculation downstream is wrong — including the threshold you just derived.

interactive Reliability diagram — miscalibrate it, then fix it
—ECE
—Brier score
—log loss
—ROC-AUC

Platt scaling is fitted by real gradient descent on a one-parameter-pair logistic model; isotonic regression is a real pool-adjacent-violators implementation. Two things to notice. ROC-AUC does not move under Platt scaling — it's a monotone transform, so the ranking is untouched while the probabilities change completely. And with a small calibration set, isotonic overfits: its ECE looks good while its log loss gets worse.

Likely interview questions
Very common⭐ What is calibration, how do you measure it, and how do you fix it?

A model is calibrated if, among cases predicted at p, a fraction p are actually positive. Measure with a reliability diagram, ECE Σ(nᵦ/n)|acc(b) − conf(b)|, and the Brier score. Fix with Platt scaling (a sigmoid on the log-odds — parametric, works with little data), isotonic regression (non-parametric, more flexible, needs more data and overfits on small calibration sets), or Venn-Abers. Always fit on held-out data. The 2026 nuance: verify it helped on a proper scoring rule — a recent benchmark found Platt and isotonic can degrade strong tabular models. And it matters because cost-based thresholds (§12.7) are only valid if p is real.

Very commonWhich models are typically miscalibrated, and in which direction?

Well-regularized logistic regression is usually close to calibrated — it optimises log loss, a proper scoring rule, so calibration is what it's minimising. Random Forests are under-confident at the extremes: averaging many trees pulls predictions away from 0 and 1, because reaching a prediction of 1.0 requires every tree to agree. Boosted trees are typically over-confident, since boosting drives margins up. Naive Bayes is wildly overconfident because it double-counts correlated evidence (§6.2). SVMs have no probabilities natively. Rule: check with a reliability diagram, never assume.

Deep divePlatt vs isotonic — how do you choose?

Platt fits a two-parameter sigmoid to the log-odds — parametric, so it works with a few hundred calibration points, but it can only apply a sigmoid-shaped correction and will fail if the miscalibration has a different shape. Isotonic fits a free monotone step function via pool-adjacent-violators — it can correct any monotone distortion, but with too little data it interpolates noise and overfits, which shows up as good ECE and worse log loss. Rule of thumb: isotonic above ~1,000 calibration points, Platt below. And with either: fit on held-out data, and measure whether it helped on a proper scoring rule rather than assuming.

GotchaDoes calibration change your AUC?

Not for Platt scaling, and not for any strictly monotone transform — ROC-AUC depends only on the ranking, and a monotone map preserves the order of every pair. That's a useful sanity check: if AUC changes after Platt scaling, something is wrong with your implementation. Isotonic can change AUC very slightly, because it produces ties where the step function is flat, and tied scores are handled differently in the AUC calculation. The broader point: calibration and discrimination are independent axes — a model can rank perfectly and be badly calibrated, or be well-calibrated and rank poorly.

12.9 Imbalanced classification ⭐⭐

There is a correct order of operations, and reaching for SMOTE first is the single most common wrong answer in classical ML interviews.

Metrics under imbalance

Never accuracy. Report PR-AUC / average precision, per-class recall, and an F-β aligned to your costs. Be explicitly wary of ROC-AUC's optimism — the §12.3 widget shows exactly why. And always show the confusion matrix at the threshold you intend to deploy, because that is the only artefact that tells the business how many cases land in the queue tomorrow.

Likely interview questions
Very common⭐ How do you handle class imbalance? Give me your order of operations.

(0) Characterise it — 1:10 or 1:10,000? separated or overlapping? (1) Tune the decision threshold on a strong baseline: cheapest experiment, no new failure modes, frequently sufficient on its own. (2) Class weights / scale_pos_weight: no synthetic rows, no leakage risk — but it decalibrates, so recalibrate if you use the probabilities. (3) Only then resampling — SMOTE, under-sampling, Tomek links, BalancedRandomForest — always inside the pipeline. Throughout: PR-AUC, per-class recall, cost-aligned F-β. Never accuracy.

Very commonWhat's wrong with applying SMOTE before the train-test split?

It leaks. Synthetic minority points are interpolated between real rows, and some of those real rows end up in validation — so validation rows are partly reconstructions of training data and the model is effectively tested on things it has seen. You get an excellent CV score and a production collapse. The fix is structural rather than a judgement call: split first, and put the resampler inside the pipeline so it's refitted on each training fold only — which is exactly what imblearn's Pipeline exists for (sklearn's won't do it, because it applies transforms at predict time too).

GotchaWhen is SMOTE actively harmful?

When classes overlap or labels are noisy. Interpolating between two minority points that sit near or inside the majority region manufactures synthetic examples right on the boundary, which pushes the boundary into majority territory and inflates false positives. It also amplifies a single mislabelled minority point into a whole neighbourhood of fake ones. In high dimensions the interpolation is even less meaningful (§2.7). On clean tabular data, inverse-frequency weighting gives near-identical results while being simpler and leak-proof — which is why it's step 2 and SMOTE is step 3.

DesignFraud at 0.1% prevalence. Walk me through your approach.

First, characterise: 1:1000, and fraud is heterogeneous rather than a single tight cluster. Metric: PR-AUC plus precision-at-the-review-capacity, never accuracy or ROC-AUC alone. Model: a GBM with scale_pos_weight, but I'd start by checking whether threshold tuning alone on an unweighted model suffices. Threshold from capacity — if analysts review 200 cases/day, that fixes the alert volume and everything else follows. Validate with a time-based split, because fraud patterns drift. Then the two things people forget: calibrate if the probability feeds an expected-value decision, and plan for the feedback loop — blocked transactions never reveal their true label, so I'd hold out a small exploration slice (§15.7).

Part 13 of 17
Feature Engineering & Selection
Numeric, datetime, text and geo features, selection, pipelines, feature stores

13.1 Why feature engineering still matters ⭐

A model can only use structure you expose. On tabular data that single sentence explains why feature work routinely beats model choice — even in 2026.

The counter-argument you'll hear is “deep learning does automatic feature extraction”, and it's true for images, audio and text — modalities with strong local structure that a convolution or attention layer can exploit. Tabular data has no such structure: columns have no spatial or sequential relationship, so there's nothing for an architecture to discover generically. The structure is semantic — that debt and income should be divided, that a timestamp implies a business calendar — and semantics come from you.

Likely interview questions
ConceptualDoesn't deep learning make feature engineering obsolete?

For images, audio and text — largely yes, because those modalities have strong local structure (spatial, spectral, sequential) that convolutions and attention exploit generically. Tabular data has no such structure: columns have no inherent adjacency, so there's nothing for an architecture to discover from the geometry. The structure that matters is semantic — that debt should be divided by income, that a timestamp implies a business calendar — and that comes from domain knowledge. Even tabular foundation models (§16.1) benefit from well-constructed features; they change the modelling baseline, not the value of exposing real structure.

13.2 Numeric features ⭐

Ratios, differences and group aggregates carry most of the value. Transformations matter mainly for linear models.

TechniqueExampleWhy it helps
Ratiosdebt/income, amount/avg_amount_30dOften more predictive than either input — it encodes a comparison the model would otherwise have to learn from a 2-D interaction
Differencesnow − last_login, price − category_medianRecency and deviation-from-normal are the two most reusable signals in tabular ML
Group aggregatesmean / max / std / count per customer, merchant, dayGives a row context it doesn't have alone — and is the most common source of temporal leakage (§3.7)
Transformationslog, sqrt, Box-Cox / Yeo-JohnsonTames skew for linear models; does nothing for trees
BinningUniform, quantile, supervised (tree-based)Injects non-linearity into a linear model; usually loses information for a GBM
Clipping / winsorizingCap at the 1st/99th percentileBounds the influence of extremes without deleting rows
Interactions & splinesPolynomialFeatures, SplineTransformerHow a linear model gets what a tree gets for free
The fraud-features answer, organised

Structure it as entity × window × statistic. Transaction-level: amount, currency, hour (cyclically encoded), channel, merchant category, is-the-country-new. Card/customer aggregates over 1h / 24h / 7d / 30d: count, sum, max, std, distinct merchants, distinct countries, velocity (count this hour ÷ average hourly count). Deviation features: amount ÷ customer's 30-day median, geo-distance since last transaction ÷ elapsed time. Merchant-side: cross-fitted chargeback rate, relationship age. Graph-ish: cards seen on this device. Then close with the constraint that makes it real: every one of these must be computable inside the ~150 ms budget and must be point-in-time correct.

Likely interview questions
Very common⭐ Walk me through feature engineering for a transaction fraud model.

Organise by entity × window × statistic. Transaction: amount, hour (cyclically encoded), channel, merchant category, is-new-country. Card/customer aggregates over 1h/24h/7d/30d: count, sum, max, std, distinct merchants, distinct countries, velocity ratios. Deviation: amount ÷ 30-day median, geo-distance ÷ elapsed time. Merchant: cross-fitted chargeback rate, relationship age. Device/graph: cards per device. Then the constraints that make it a real answer: every feature must fit the ~150 ms budget and be point-in-time correct, and aggregates must never be computed over the full history at training time.

ConceptualWhy does a ratio like debt/income beat giving the model both columns?

Because a ratio is a multiplicative interaction, and neither a linear model nor a shallow tree gets there cheaply. A linear model literally cannot represent a ratio without you constructing it. A tree can approximate it, but only with a staircase of axis-aligned splits — it needs many splits and therefore many rows to learn what one column states directly (§7.6). Providing it is pure inductive bias: you're telling the model something true about the domain that it would otherwise have to discover from data it may not have enough of.

GotchaWhen does binning a continuous feature help, and when does it hurt?

Helps for linear models, where it's a cheap way to capture non-linearity without specifying its shape — and in regulated settings, where binned "scorecard" features are easier to explain and to constrain. Hurts for trees and GBMs, which already choose their own thresholds optimally: pre-binning throws away resolution and can only lose information. It also creates discontinuities at bin edges that are hard to defend ("£49,999 and £50,001 get different treatment"). If I want non-linearity in a linear model, I'd usually prefer splines, which are smooth and don't have edge artefacts.

13.3 Datetime features ⭐

The one people get wrong most often, and the fix is a single line of trigonometry.

interactive Why cyclical encoding — 23:00 and 00:00 are one hour apart
—distance, raw integer
—distance, sin/cos
—true clock distance (h)

Both distances computed exactly. The raw integer encoding says 23:00 and 00:00 are the furthest apart pair on the clock; the sin/cos encoding says they're adjacent, which is the truth. This matters for every distance- and linear-based model — and even for trees, which would otherwise need two separate splits to express “late night”.

Likely interview questions
Very commonHow do you encode a datetime? Why cyclical encoding?

Extract components (hour, day-of-week, day-of-month, month, week-of-year), add domain flags (holiday, business day, days-to-next-holiday), and add time-since-last-event recency features, which are consistently among the strongest in churn and fraud. Use cyclical encoding — sin(2πh/24) and cos(2πh/24) — because on a raw integer scale 23 and 0 are the furthest apart values when they're actually one hour apart. Two traps: be explicit about timezone/DST, and never feed the raw absolute timestamp, or the model memorises a period rather than a pattern.

GotchaDo trees need cyclical encoding?

Less than linear or distance-based models, but it still helps. A tree can express "hour ≥ 22 or hour ≤ 5" — but only with two separate splits on different branches, so it needs more depth and more data to learn what one sin/cos pair states directly. Giving it both the raw integer and the cyclical pair costs two columns and lets it choose. The models where cyclical encoding is essential rather than helpful are anything using a distance (kNN, k-means, RBF-SVM) or a linear coefficient, where hour 23 and hour 0 would otherwise be maximally far apart.

DebuggingYour model works in backtest and degrades every month after deployment. What datetime mistake might explain it?

Most likely you fed absolute time — a raw timestamp, an epoch integer, or a monotonically increasing ID that proxies for it. The model then learns "recent rows behave like X", which is true within the training window and meaningless beyond it: every prediction after deployment is an extrapolation past the largest value the tree ever saw, so it just returns the last leaf (§7.3). The fix is to use relative time features (time-since-event, day-of-week, seasonality) and never the absolute index, and to validate with a time-based split which would have caught it before launch.

13.4 Text & geospatial on a tabular row

Two modalities that show up as columns in an otherwise-tabular problem, each with a standard ladder of options.

ModalityCheapMiddleExpensive
TextLength, word count, has-keyword flags, punctuation ratio, is-all-capsTF-IDF + TruncatedSVD to a few dozen dimsSentence embeddings — but a 384-dim block among 20 tabular columns usually needs reduction to be useful to a GBM. See the NLP guide
GeospatialCountry, region, postcode prefixDistance to points of interest; geohash prefixes at several precisionsCluster the coordinates and use cluster ID + distance-to-centroid; spatial joins to demographic data
Raw latitude and longitude are bad features

A tree splitting on latitude carves the world into horizontal bands, which almost never matches anything real, and it cannot express “near this city” without many splits. Better: distance to relevant points (city centre, nearest branch, nearest competitor), geohash prefixes at a few precisions (which give hierarchical categorical regions), or cluster IDs from k-means on coordinates. And note that postcode is a proxy for protected attributes in many jurisdictions (§14.8), so its use needs a fairness review rather than just a performance check.

Likely interview questions
DesignYou have a free-text description column in an otherwise tabular problem. What do you do?

Ladder up only as far as the value justifies. Start cheap: length, word count, keyword flags, punctuation/caps ratios — these often capture most of the signal in short operational text and cost nothing. Then TF-IDF plus TruncatedSVD down to 20–50 dimensions, which plays well with a GBM. Only then embeddings, and if I use them I'd reduce dimensionality first, because a 384-dim dense block alongside 20 tabular columns will dominate the split search and dilute the tabular signal. Whatever I choose gets fitted inside the pipeline — a TF-IDF vocabulary is learned from data, so fitting it before the split is contamination (§3.7).

GotchaWhy are raw latitude and longitude poor features?

Because axis-aligned splits on lat/long carve the map into rectangles that almost never correspond to anything meaningful, and expressing "within 5km of this city" needs many splits. Better representations: distance to relevant points of interest (which encodes the actual mechanism), geohash prefixes at several precisions (hierarchical categorical regions the model can use directly), or cluster IDs from clustering the coordinates plus distance to the centroid. And a governance point: postcode and fine-grained location are strong proxies for protected attributes, so their use needs a fairness review, not just a performance check.

13.5 Feature selection ⭐

The interesting question is not how to select but why — and the honest answer is usually not accuracy.

Selection is part of the model

Choosing features by looking at the whole dataset — including validation rows — and then cross-validating is textbook train-test contamination. The selection has already seen the labels it will be scored against, so the CV score is optimistic, sometimes dramatically so when p ≫ n. Feature selection must be fitted inside the CV loop, exactly like a scaler or an imputer, which in practice means it lives in the Pipeline.

Likely interview questions
Very commonFilter vs wrapper vs embedded feature selection.

Filter scores each feature independently of any model (correlation, chi², ANOVA F, mutual information) — fast and scalable, but blind to interactions, so a feature useless alone but valuable in combination gets dropped. Wrapper repeatedly refits a model on subsets (forward/backward, RFE/RFECV) — accounts for the actual model and interactions, but is expensive and can overfit the selection itself. Embedded gets selection as a by-product of fitting (L1, tree importances, boosting gain) — the practical default, but it inherits the model's biases (§7.7). Whichever I use: it's fitted inside the CV loop.

Very commonWhy would you drop features that improve accuracy?

Because accuracy isn't the only cost. Each feature carries serving latency (a fetch, a join), acquisition cost (a paid third-party call), drift and monitoring surface, leakage risk, maintenance burden, and sometimes regulatory exposure as a proxy for a protected attribute. A feature worth 0.002 AUC and £0.30 per prediction is a bad trade at any volume. Being able to make that argument explicitly — and to have actually done it — is one of the clearest signals of production experience.

Deep diveWhat is Boruta and when would you use it?

Boruta is an all-relevant selection method rather than a minimal-optimal one. It creates shadow features — random shuffles of each real column — trains a Random Forest, and keeps any feature whose importance significantly exceeds the best shadow feature's, repeating with statistical tests. The distinction matters: most methods find a minimal set sufficient for prediction, which arbitrarily drops one of every correlated pair. Boruta finds every feature carrying signal, which is what you want for understanding the problem or for downstream causal work — not necessarily for building the leanest production model.

13.6 Pipelines in production ⭐

The Pipeline is not a convenience — it is the unit that makes leakage structurally impossible and makes training and serving the same code.

PracticeWhy
ColumnTransformer + PipelineThe unit of everything learned from data — refitted per fold, serialised as one object
Custom transformersBaseEstimator + TransformerMixin; implement get_feature_names_out so downstream explanations stay readable
set_output(transform="pandas")Keeps column names through the pipeline — essential for SHAP and for debugging
handle_unknownServe-time categories will include levels not seen in training. Decide the behaviour explicitly rather than crashing
Feature versioningChanging a feature's definition silently invalidates every model trained on the old one — version the definition, not just the code
Latency budget per featureWhat can be computed inline at request time versus precomputed and looked up (§15.3)
Likely interview questions
PracticalWhy put everything in a Pipeline rather than transforming the data first?

Three reasons. Correctness: cross-validation refits the whole pipeline per fold, so scalers, imputers, encoders and selectors are fitted on training data only — leakage becomes structurally impossible rather than a discipline you have to remember (§3.7). Deployment: the pipeline serialises as one object, so serving applies exactly the transforms that training used — no second implementation to drift (§15.4). Tuning: preprocessing hyperparameters (imputation strategy, encoder settings, n_components) become searchable alongside model hyperparameters, which is often where the real gains are.

DesignWhat happens when a categorical level appears at serve time that wasn't in training?

Whatever you decided in advance — and if you didn't decide, it throws and takes down the endpoint. Options: handle_unknown='ignore' (all-zeros one-hot, i.e. treated as the baseline), 'infrequent_if_exist' (mapped to the rare-category bucket, which is usually the most sensible), or an explicit unknown level created at training time by grouping rare categories. I'd also monitor the unknown rate as a data-quality signal — a spike means an upstream vocabulary changed, which is one of the most common production incidents (§15.5).

13.7 Feature stores & point-in-time correctness ⭐⭐

The deepest form of the leakage question: reconstructing what a feature's value was at prediction time, rather than what it is now.

Likely interview questions
Very common⭐ What is a feature store and what problem does point-in-time correctness solve?

A feature store is a shared, versioned system for computing, storing and serving features so that training and inference use the same definitions. Point-in-time correctness is the hard part it exists for: when you build a training row for March, the feature values must be the values that existed in March, not today's. Joining today's lifetime_spend onto a March label leaks six months of the future into the row — CV looks great, production doesn't. The mechanism is an as-of join against a time-versioned feature history. The sibling problem it solves is training/serving skew: one code path instead of two implementations that silently diverge.

DesignDo you always need a feature store?

No — it's infrastructure, and infrastructure has a cost. You need one when: multiple models share features, features are computed from streams, you have genuine real-time serving with precomputed aggregates, or point-in-time correctness is hard to get right by hand. You don't need one for a single batch-scored model whose features come from one warehouse query — there, a well-tested shared transformation module and a disciplined as-of join do the same job for a fraction of the complexity. The principles (one definition, point-in-time joins, versioning) are non-negotiable; the product is optional.

Deep diveHow would you implement a point-in-time join yourself?

Keep feature values in an event-sourced table with a validity timestamp: (entity_id, feature_name, value, valid_from), appending rather than updating. Then the training join is an as-of join — for each label row with timestamp t, take the most recent feature row with valid_from ≤ t − latency, where latency accounts for how long the value takes to become observable (a value stamped at t but only landing in the warehouse at t+2h is not available at t). Pandas has merge_asof; in SQL it's a lateral join or a window function. The subtle part is that latency, not just the timestamp — which is exactly what the purge/embargo gap encodes in validation (§10.6).

Part 14 of 17
Interpretability & Fairness
Glass-box models, three importances, PDP/ICE/ALE, LIME, SHAP, counterfactuals, fairness

14.1 The interpretability taxonomy

Three axes. Knowing which box a technique sits in is most of the vocabulary you need — and it makes the rest of this part navigable.

AxisOption AOption B
WhenIntrinsic — the model is readable by construction (linear coefficients, a shallow tree, a GAM/EBM)Post-hoc — explain a fitted black box afterwards (SHAP, LIME, PDP)
ScopeGlobal — how does the model behave overall?Local — why this prediction?
CouplingModel-specific — TreeSHAP, coefficients, decision pathsModel-agnostic — permutation importance, PDP/ALE, LIME, KernelSHAP
Interpretability vs explainability vs justifiability

Three different words for three different requirements. Interpretability: a human can follow the mechanism (a shallow tree). Explainability: a post-hoc account of a decision that is approximately faithful (SHAP). Justifiability to a regulator: a documented, reproducible, auditable reason that satisfies a legal standard — which is a process requirement, not a plot. Knowing you legally need the third in credit, insurance, hiring and healthcare is what turns this from an academic topic into a design constraint.

Likely interview questions
ConceptualGlobal vs local interpretability — when do you need each?

Global answers "how does this model behave overall?" — needed for model validation, governance sign-off, checking it hasn't learned something absurd, and communicating with stakeholders. Local answers "why this prediction?" — needed for adverse-action notices, customer disputes, analyst triage, and debugging individual failures. They need different tools (PDP/ALE and global importance vs SHAP/LIME/counterfactuals), and a common mistake is presenting a global summary when someone asked a local question, or vice versa.

14.2 Intrinsically interpretable models ⭐

The option people forget: instead of explaining a black box, use a model that doesn't need explaining. On tabular data this costs less accuracy than you'd expect.

ModelWhat you can read off itCaveat
Linear / logistic regressionA coefficient per feature — sign, magnitude, odds ratioStandardise first, and beware multicollinearity flipping signs (§5.4)
Shallow decision treeA literal rule path for every predictionOnly readable to ~depth 4; unstable across refits (§7.6)
GLM with splinesA smooth per-feature curveGenuinely underrated — non-linear and readable
GAM / EBMOne shape function per feature (plus chosen pairwise terms), all plottableCompetitive with GBMs on tabular data, and interpretable by construction. ExplainableBoostingMachine
RuleFitA sparse set of if-then rules with weightsReadable, but rule sets get long quickly
Scorecard (binned + linear)Points per attribute band — the credit-industry standardDeliberately coarse; the trade-off is accepted for defensibility
EBMs deserve to be named

An Explainable Boosting Machine is a GAM fitted by cyclic gradient boosting: it learns a separate shape function per feature (plus a small number of chosen pairwise interactions), so the model is exactly the sum of curves you can plot — no approximation, no post-hoc explanation. On many tabular benchmarks it lands within a point or two of an unrestricted GBM. Mentioning it when someone asks “how do you get interpretability?” is a genuinely strong answer because it sidesteps the SHAP-caveat conversation entirely.

Likely interview questions
DesignYou need an interpretable model for a regulated use case. What do you build?

I'd try intrinsic interpretability before post-hoc explanation, because explaining a black box is an approximation and a regulator can challenge the approximation. In order: a regularized logistic regression or GLM with splines and monotonic constraints, which gives coefficients you can put in an adverse-action notice; or an EBM/GAM, which is exactly a sum of per-feature shape functions you can plot and is usually within a point or two of a GBM on tabular data. If accuracy genuinely demands a GBM, I'd add monotonic constraints (which are both a regularizer and a compliance artefact) and pair it with SHAP plus the caveats — but I'd quantify the accuracy gap first, because it's often smaller than assumed.

ModernWhat is an EBM and why is it interesting?

An Explainable Boosting Machine is a GAM fitted by cyclic gradient boosting: it boosts on one feature at a time, producing a separate shape function per feature plus a small number of automatically-selected pairwise interactions. Because the model is the sum of those curves, the explanation is exact rather than approximate — you plot the function and that's the model. It's interesting because it lands close to unrestricted GBMs on many tabular benchmarks, so it largely dissolves the accuracy-vs-interpretability trade-off that the SHAP conversation exists to manage.

14.3 The three feature importances ⭐⭐

They are not three implementations of one idea. They answer three different questions, and the point of the question is whether you know that.

interactive Correlated features break every importance method
—x₁ importance
—x₂ importance
—drop both together
—x₀ (uncorrelated)

Real permutation importance: a ridge model is fitted, then each column is shuffled on held-out data and the increase in MSE is measured. Slide the correlation to 0.98 and watch both correlated features drop toward zero individually — while removing them together still destroys the model. Neither is redundant; the method just cannot see joint contribution. SHAP has a version of the same problem.

Likely interview questions
Very common⭐ Three kinds of feature importance — how do they differ?

Impurity/gain (MDI): how much this feature reduced impurity while the tree was built — free, but biased toward high-cardinality and continuous features and computed on training data. Permutation: how much the held-out metric degrades when the column is shuffled — measures what you actually care about and works for any model, but correlated features mask each other and shuffling creates unrealistic rows. SHAP: how this prediction is divided among features — local and globally aggregable, additive, expensive, with correlation problems of its own. They answer three different questions and can rank features differently while all being correct.

DebuggingTwo features you know matter both show near-zero permutation importance. What's happening?

They're almost certainly correlated with each other. Permutation shuffles one column at a time, so when you scramble x₁ the model simply reads the same information from x₂ and the metric barely moves — and vice versa. Both look unimportant while jointly being essential, which the widget above demonstrates directly. Diagnostics: compute a correlation matrix alongside any importance ranking; try grouped permutation (shuffle correlated features together); or use conditional permutation, which respects the correlation structure. And note SHAP is not immune — it splits credit between correlated features in ways that are equally hard to interpret causally.

14.4 PDP, ICE and ALE ⭐

Three ways to plot “what does the model do as this feature changes?” — and one of them can be actively misleading on its own.

interactive PDP hides what ICE reveals

The underlying model is y = β·x·(segment) + …: raising x helps one segment and hurts the other by the same amount. The PDP is their average and is essentially flat — read alone, it says “this feature does nothing.” The ICE curves show two opposite fans. Set the interaction to zero and the two views agree, which is exactly when a PDP is safe to trust on its own.

PlotShowsFails when
PDPThe average marginal effect: vary the feature, hold others at their observed values, average the predictionsInteractions (opposite effects cancel) and correlation (it evaluates the model on combinations that don't exist — 25 years of tenure at age 19)
ICEOne curve per instance — the same computation without averagingCluttered with many rows; use a sample plus the centred variant (c-ICE)
ALEAccumulated local effects: computes differences within small windows of the feature and accumulates themHarder to explain; less familiar. But it is the correlation-robust answer
The rule: look at ICE before trusting a PDP

A flat PDP means one of two very different things — the feature genuinely doesn't matter, or it matters enormously in opposite directions for different subgroups. Only the ICE plot distinguishes them, and the second case is often the more important finding. Modern PartialDependenceDisplay can draw both together (kind="both"), so there is no reason not to.

Likely interview questions
Very common⭐ PDP vs ICE vs ALE — what does each show?

PDP shows the average marginal effect of a feature — but it averages over instances, so it hides heterogeneity, and it evaluates the model on unrealistic combinations when features are correlated. ICE plots one curve per instance, revealing exactly that hidden heterogeneity: if half your population responds positively and half negatively, the PDP is flat and the ICE plot shows two fans. ALE computes effects within small local windows of the feature and accumulates them, so it never leaves the data manifold — the correlation-robust alternative. Rule: look at ICE before trusting a PDP, and prefer ALE when features are correlated.

Deep diveWhy does correlation break a PDP specifically?

Because the PDP algorithm fixes the feature of interest at a grid value and keeps every other feature at its observed value, then averages. With correlated features that generates rows the data-generating process would never produce — age 19 with 25 years at the employer — and the model's prediction there is an extrapolation with no meaning. The averaged curve then reflects model behaviour in regions with no data. ALE fixes this by only ever comparing predictions for points already inside a small window of the feature, so it never queries impossible combinations.

14.5 LIME

A local surrogate: fit a simple interpretable model in the neighbourhood of one prediction, and read that. Intuitive, fast — and unstable in a way you should be able to name.

LIME perturbs the instance you want to explain, gets the black box's predictions for those perturbations, weights them by proximity to the original, and fits a sparse linear model to that weighted local dataset. The coefficients are the explanation.

LIME's three weaknesses, in order of importance

(1) Instability. Run it twice on the same instance and you can get materially different explanations, because the perturbations are random. That is disqualifying for any use where the explanation is a record (an adverse-action notice). (2) The neighbourhood is a free parameter — the kernel width silently determines what "local" means and therefore the answer, with no principled way to choose it. (3) The perturbation scheme is arbitrary for tabular data, and typically samples features independently, so it evaluates the model off the data manifold — the same flaw as KernelSHAP (§14.6). In practice SHAP has largely displaced it for tabular work.

Likely interview questions
ConceptualHow does LIME work, and why would you not use it?

It perturbs the instance, gets black-box predictions for the perturbations, weights them by proximity, and fits a sparse linear surrogate to that local dataset — the coefficients are the explanation. Reasons not to use it on tabular data: it's unstable (random perturbations mean two runs can disagree, which is disqualifying when the explanation is a record); the kernel width silently defines "local" with no principled way to choose it; and the perturbation scheme samples features independently, so it queries the model off the data manifold. SHAP gives a more principled decomposition with consistency guarantees, and TreeSHAP is fast and exact for tree models — so for tabular work SHAP has largely displaced it.

14.6 SHAP ⭐⭐

The most valuable thing you can say about SHAP is what it gets wrong. Everyone can describe what it does; very few can name its failure modes.

What it is

SHAP assigns each feature the Shapley value of its contribution to a single prediction — the average marginal contribution across all possible orderings in which features could be added to the model. That construction is the unique attribution satisfying four axioms: efficiency (contributions sum to the prediction minus a base value), symmetry (equal contributors get equal credit), dummy (a feature with no effect gets zero), and additivity. Being additive and local means it aggregates cleanly into a global view.

Likely interview questions
Very common⭐ Explain SHAP. What are its assumptions and failure modes?

SHAP gives each feature the Shapley value of its contribution to a single prediction — its average marginal contribution across all orderings in which features could be added — which is the unique attribution satisfying efficiency, symmetry, dummy and additivity. Contributions sum to the prediction minus a base value, and being local and additive it aggregates into a global view. Failure modes: (1) KernelSHAP assumes feature independence when marginalising, so it queries the model on unrealistic rows off the data manifold. (2) Path-dependent TreeSHAP avoids that by using the tree's own paths, but changes the value function such that a feature with no effect can get non-zero attribution — breaking the dummy axiom. (3) With correlated features credit is split unintuitively. (4) A SHAP value is not a causal effect. Use it with correlation analysis and other diagnostics.

Deep diveWhat's the difference between TreeSHAP's interventional and path-dependent modes?

Interventional uses an explicit background dataset and breaks feature dependence deliberately — it satisfies the dummy axiom (irrelevant features get exactly zero) but evaluates the model on off-manifold combinations, so the attributions describe a hypothetical intervention rather than observed behaviour. Path-dependent follows the tree's own split structure using the training distribution, so it stays on-manifold and is faster, but the changed value function means a feature that never affects the prediction can receive non-zero credit if it's correlated with one that does. There is no mode that achieves both, and knowing that trade-off exists is more valuable than picking a side.

GotchaCan you use SHAP values to decide what to change?

No — that's the most consequential misuse. SHAP explains how the model composed a prediction, which reflects predictive association including through proxies, confounders and consequences of the target. High SHAP for num_collection_calls in a default model doesn't mean reducing collection calls reduces default. To decide what to change you need a causal quantity — an experiment, or an identification strategy (§16.4). What SHAP is good for: debugging, sanity-checking, leakage detection, per-case explanation of a decision as it was made, and generating hypotheses worth testing causally.

14.7 Counterfactuals & adverse-action notices ⭐

The most useful explanation for an end user is not an attribution — it is “what would need to change?”

AudienceWantsGive them
A data scientist debuggingMechanismSHAP, ALE, ICE, slice analysis
A stakeholderConfidence and a mental modelGlobal drivers in their language, plus one worked example
An end user who was declinedWhat to do nextA counterfactual: “had utilisation been below 40%, this would have been approved”
A regulatorA defensible, reproducible recordAdverse-action notice: standardised reason codes, model version, input snapshot, and the fairness evidence
An analyst triaging alertsSpeed and prioritisationTop-3 contributing features plus similar historical cases
What makes a counterfactual good

Four properties, and they conflict. Validity — it genuinely flips the prediction. Proximity — it changes as little as possible. Sparsity — it changes as few features as possible, because "change these seven things" is useless advice. Actionability — it only changes things the person can actually change: “be five years younger” is a valid counterfactual and an unacceptable one. That last constraint is why counterfactual generation needs a per-feature mutability specification, not just an optimiser.

Likely interview questions
Very common⭐ A regulator asks why an application was declined. What do you give them?

Not a SHAP beeswarm. An adverse-action notice: a small number of specific, plain-language, actionable reasons, derived reproducibly, tied to a recorded model version and input snapshot. In practice that means a locally faithful attribution method ranked into standardised reason codes, ideally paired with a counterfactual ("had utilisation been below 40%, this would have been approved"), plus the audit trail — model version, feature values at decision time, policy thresholds applied — and the fairness evidence. Worth adding: this requirement is often why the production model is a logistic regression or a monotonically-constrained GBM in the first place.

DesignWhat makes a counterfactual explanation good?

Four properties that trade off against each other. Validity — it actually flips the prediction. Proximity — minimal change from the original. Sparsity — few features changed, because "alter these seven things" is useless advice. And actionability — only mutable features: "be five years younger" is mathematically valid and practically insulting. That last one means counterfactual generation needs a per-feature mutability and direction specification (age immutable, income increase-only, utilisation freely changeable) rather than just an optimiser over the feature space.

14.8 Fairness ⭐⭐

The question is never “is the model fair?” It is “which fairness, and what are you giving up to get it?” — because several definitions are provably incompatible.

Document it, or it didn't happen

Model cards (intended use, out-of-scope uses, per-subgroup performance, known limitations) and datasheets for datasets (how it was collected, by whom, with what consent, what is missing) are the standard artefacts. They matter for a boring reason: they make the assumptions auditable later, which is exactly what someone will ask for when a journalist calls or a complaint escalates.

Likely interview questions
Very common⭐ Define two fairness metrics and explain why you can't satisfy all of them.

Demographic parity: equal positive-prediction rates across groups. Equal opportunity: equal true-positive rates among those who actually qualify. Also worth naming: equalised odds (equal TPR and FPR) and predictive parity (equal precision — i.e. a score means the same thing in every group). The impossibility result: when base rates genuinely differ between groups, calibration within groups and equalised odds cannot both hold except in degenerate cases — a perfect classifier or equal base rates. It's a theorem, not a tooling gap. So "make it fair" is under-specified: someone must choose which criterion, and that's a policy decision, not a modelling one.

GotchaCan't you just remove the protected attribute?

No — this is "fairness through unawareness" and it doesn't work. Proxies encode the attribute: postcode, name, device type, education history, shopping patterns, even writing style. A model with enough features will reconstruct it, and you've now lost the ability to measure disparate impact while doing nothing to prevent it.
