The correct approach is the opposite: retain the attribute for measurement (in a governed way), measure outcomes per subgroup on the deployed decision, and mitigate deliberately at whichever stage is appropriate — pre-processing, in-processing, or post-processing.

DesignYou discover a shipped model has disparate impact. What do you do?

Quantify it precisely first — per subgroup, on the deployed decision, with confidence intervals, before saying anything imprecise. Then escalate immediately with the number and the affected population, because delay is the thing that becomes indefensible later. Propose interim mitigation while a fix is built: a threshold change, human review for the affected slice, or disabling the model if the harm is serious. Then treat "which fairness criterion do we hold ourselves to" as a policy decision needing an owner outside the modelling team — legal, compliance, or the product owner — because the impossibility result means it's a value judgement, not a technical one. Finally, document the whole thing in the model card.

Part 15 of 17
Production ML Engineering
Architecture, serving, skew, drift, retraining, deployment, A/B testing, hygiene

15.1 The architecture ⭐

One rule dominates this whole level: the same feature code must serve training and inference. Almost every production ML incident traces back to a violation of it.

Likely interview questions
System design⭐ Walk me through deploying a model end to end.

Frame the decision and metric → build the offline pipeline with point-in-time-correct features → validate with a split that mimics production → choose a threshold from cost or capacity → package the whole pipeline (not just the estimator) and register it with a version and lineage → deploy in shadow to check latency and stability → canary at a few percent with guardrails → A/B test against the incumbent → full rollout with a rollback path → monitor data quality, drift, prediction distribution and eventually performance → define retraining triggers and write the runbook. The two markers of a good answer: one feature code path for training and serving, and a rollback plus an on-call playbook.

DesignWhat do you log at inference time, and why?

The full input feature vector, the raw score, the applied threshold, the final decision, the model version, and a request ID that ties back to the business event. The inputs matter most: when someone disputes a decision months later, or you're diagnosing a drift alert, reconstructing the feature vector from the warehouse gives you today's values, not what the model saw — and the difference is exactly the bug you're hunting. Input logs are also what let you compute training/serving skew (§15.4) and replay traffic against a candidate model. It's cheap, and its absence turns solvable incidents into unsolvable ones.

15.2 Batch vs real-time ⭐

One question decides it: do the features exist before the request arrives?

BatchReal-timeStreaming
When it runsOn a scheduleOn requestContinuously as events arrive
ServingPrecomputed to a key-value store — prediction is an O(1) lookupFetch features, transform, predict inlineUpdate features as events land; predict on demand
RequiresAll features knowable in advanceFeatures that only exist at request timeEvent infrastructure
Cost & complexityLowestHigher — latency budget, scaling, cold startsHighest
StalenessUp to one cycleNoneSeconds
ExampleNightly churn scores for a CRMPayment fraud, ad rankingVelocity features for fraud
Most real systems are hybrid — and that's the good answer

Precompute the expensive, slow-moving parts (customer 30-day aggregates, embeddings, segment membership) into a key-value store; compute only the genuinely request-time features inline (this transaction's amount, this session's clicks); join them at serving time. You get most of real-time's freshness at most of batch's cost and simplicity. Saying “hybrid, and here's the split” is a better answer than picking one.

Likely interview questions
System designBatch vs real-time serving — how do you decide?

One question: do the features exist before the request arrives? If yes, precompute on a schedule and write to a key-value store — prediction becomes an O(1) lookup, which is cheaper, more stable and far easier to monitor. If a feature only exists at request time (this transaction's amount, this session's behaviour), you need real-time. Secondary considerations: acceptable staleness, model cost, and the p99 budget. Most real systems are hybrid — precomputed aggregates joined with a few live features — and describing the split is a better answer than choosing one.

15.3 Serving & latency ⭐

Latency budgets are decomposed, not asserted — and you report p95/p99, not p50.

Likely interview questions
System designYou have a 150 ms end-to-end budget. How do you spend it?

Decompose it: network (~15 ms), feature fetch (usually the bottleneck — 60 ms if it's a remote store), transform (~20 ms), predict (~18 ms, and often the smallest piece), post-process (~12 ms), and keep headroom for tail latency. Then optimise in cost order: precompute what you can, cache, batch the fetches into one round trip, drop features that don't earn their fetch cost, then shrink the model, then change the serving format. And budget on p95/p99, not p50 — a p50 of 40 ms with a p99 of 900 ms means thousands of users an hour waiting a second.

PracticalWould you pickle a model for production?

It works, and I'd do it with eyes open. Three issues: it's version-coupled (unpickling with a different sklearn version can fail or, worse, silently misbehave), it's an arbitrary-code-execution vector if the file is ever untrusted, and it's Python-only. Alternatives: ONNX for a portable graph with usually faster inference, at the cost of an export step that doesn't cover every estimator; or the model's native format (Booster.save_model for XGBoost/LightGBM), which is my usual choice for GBMs because it's stable across wrapper versions. Whatever I use, the deps get pinned and there's a golden-prediction test that would catch a silent change (§15.9).

15.4 Training/serving skew ⭐⭐

The same feature computed two slightly different ways in two codebases — with nothing to alert you, because both systems individually “work”.

Skew sourceConcrete exampleDetection
Different implementationsTraining computes a 30-day mean in SQL; serving reimplements it in Python with a subtly different windowLog serving features and compare distributions against training
Different null handlingSQL AVG ignores nulls; pandas mean() does too, but the denominator differs from a hand-written sum/countSame
Timezone / boundary“Yesterday” means UTC in the warehouse and local time in the serviceCompare per-hour distributions
Data freshnessTraining used a complete day; serving sees a partial one because the ETL hasn't finishedMonitor feature completeness by hour
Schema driftAn upstream column changed type or units, only one side updatedSchema tests on both paths
Point-in-time incorrectnessTraining joined today's value onto a historical row (§13.7)The worst case — it can't be seen from serving logs at all
Why the fix is architectural, not procedural

“Be careful to implement it the same way” is not a fix — it's a hope, and it fails the first time someone changes one side. The fix is to make two implementations impossible: one shared library imported by both paths, a feature store both paths read from, or a batch job whose output the API simply looks up. Then add a skew check that logs serving features and compares their distribution against training, so if it does happen you find out in a dashboard rather than in a post-mortem.

Likely interview questions
Very common⭐ What is training/serving skew and how do you prevent it?

The training pipeline and the serving path compute the same feature differently — a different window, null handling, timezone, or rounding — so the model sees a distribution it was never trained on, and nothing alerts because both systems are individually working. Prevent it architecturally: one shared code path (a library, a feature store, or a batch job whose output the API reads), because "be careful to implement it the same way" fails the first time someone changes one side. Then add a skew check comparing logged serving features against the training distribution. Its worse sibling is point-in-time incorrectness, which serving logs can't reveal at all.

DebuggingOffline AUC 0.85, production performance clearly worse, no drift alerts. What do you check?

Skew, because drift monitors compare production to production and won't catch a training/serving mismatch. Concretely: log the actual serving feature vectors and compare each feature's distribution against the training data — a shifted mean, a different null rate, or a different cardinality on one feature usually falls out immediately. Also check feature completeness by hour (a partial-day ETL gives serving a different picture than training had), and replay a sample of production requests through the training pipeline to see whether the scores match. If the scores differ for identical inputs, it's skew; if they match, look at threshold, base rate, or label definition instead.

15.5 Monitoring & drift ⭐⭐

The highest-value idea in production ML is a negative one: not every drift alert warrants a retrain.

interactive PSI, KS and the question they can't answer
—PSI
—KS statistic
—PSI band
—action

PSI is computed exactly as Σ (aᵢ − eᵢ)·ln(aᵢ/eᵢ) over 10 quantile bins of the reference distribution, and KS as the maximum gap between the empirical CDFs. The third slider is the one that isn't in the formula: a large PSI on an unimportant feature is not an incident, and a small PSI on the feature carrying half your signal might be.

Likely interview questions
Very common⭐ How do you detect drift when labels arrive 60 days late?

Layered proxies. Input: per-feature PSI (<0.1 stable, 0.1–0.2 moderate, >0.2 significant), KS/chi-square, Jensen-Shannon and Wasserstein as smoother alternatives to KL on noisy production data — weighted by feature importance. Output: the prediction distribution and mean predicted probability, which move immediately and need no labels. Behavioural: override rate, abstention rate, analyst agreement, downstream conversion. Partial labels: any fast-resolving subset. Data quality: schema, nulls, ranges, cardinality — which in practice catches more incidents than drift statistics do. And the discipline: confirm a metric actually moved before retraining.

Very commonData drift vs concept drift — how do the responses differ?

Data/covariate drift is P(x) moving with P(y|x) stable — a new segment or channel. The model may still be valid; you might reweight, retrain on recent data, or do nothing. Concept drift is P(y|x) changing — fraudsters adapt, a recession redefines risk — and only retraining helps, possibly with new features or a new target definition. There's a third worth naming: prior/label drift, where the base rate moves, which shifts precision at a fixed threshold and is usually fixed by re-thresholding rather than retraining. Practical difference: covariate and prior drift are detectable without labels; concept drift generally is not.

DebuggingPSI = 0.35 on one feature. Do you retrain?

Not yet. PSI > 0.2 means the distribution changed significantly — it does not mean the model got worse. First: how important is that feature? A big shift on a feature contributing 1% of the signal is a log entry, not an incident. Second: did a metric actually move? Score the recent window against whatever labels have arrived, watch the prediction distribution and the override rate. Third: why did it shift — an upstream pipeline change or a genuine population change? Those have different fixes. Retraining on drifted-but-harmless data costs you churn, reproducibility and possibly performance. Not every drift alert warrants a retrain, and alert fatigue kills monitoring programmes faster than missed drift does.

15.6 Retraining triggers ⭐

Three triggers, in preference order — and one trade-off nobody mentions until it bites them.

TriggerWhen it worksRisk
Performance-triggeredLabels arrive in time to measure — the idealBy the time you can measure it, you've already been degraded for the label-delay period
Drift-triggeredThe proxy when labels are slow, with a confirmation step (§15.5)False alarms — retraining on harmless drift costs churn and reproducibility
ScheduledThe boring default that mostly worksRetrains when nothing changed; misses fast degradation between cycles
Data-volume triggered“Every 100k new labelled rows”Decouples from calendar, which suits irregular businesses
Event-triggeredA known regime change — a product launch, a policy changeRequires someone to remember to trigger it
The staleness-vs-churn trade-off

Retraining constantly sounds obviously good and isn't. Every retrain changes predictions for the same inputs, which means a customer declined today might be approved tomorrow for no reason anyone can explain; incidents become unreproducible because the model that made the decision no longer exists; and downstream thresholds calibrated to the old score distribution silently stop meaning what they meant. Against that, staleness costs accuracy. The resolution: retrain on a defensible cadence, gate every retrain behind champion/challenger comparison and a golden-set regression suite, and version every model so any past decision can be reproduced.

Likely interview questions
Very commonWhen do you retrain? What triggers it?

Three triggers in preference order: performance-triggered when labels arrive in time, drift-triggered as the proxy when they don't (with a confirmation step so you don't retrain on noise), and scheduled as the boring default that mostly works. The trade-off to name is staleness vs churn: retraining constantly makes predictions change under users for no visible reason, makes incidents unreproducible, and silently invalidates downstream thresholds calibrated to the old score distribution. So I'd gate every retrain behind champion/challenger comparison and a golden-set regression suite, and version every model so past decisions stay reproducible.

DesignRetrain on all history, or a rolling window?

Depends on whether the relationship is stable. If P(y|x) is stable and only the input mix moves, use all history — more data is better and old rows are still valid. If there's genuine concept drift, old data is actively misleading and a rolling window (or exponentially decaying sample weights, §8.9) is right. The empirical way to decide: backtest both — train on all-history and on a window, evaluate on the most recent period, and see which wins. Sample weighting is often the best of both, since it downweights rather than discarding, and the decay rate becomes a tunable parameter rather than an arbitrary cutoff.

15.7 Deployment & the feedback loop ⭐

The ladder from shadow to full rollout — and the problem that makes fraud and credit systems genuinely hard.

Likely interview questions
Very common⭐ What is the feedback-loop problem in a fraud or credit model?

The model's decisions determine the data it will be trained on next. A fraud model never observes whether the transactions it blocked were really fraud; a credit model never sees how rejected applicants would have performed (the reject inference problem). The training set becomes systematically censored, the model grows confident about a shrinking slice of the world, and offline evaluation cannot detect it because the missing data is missing from evaluation too. Mitigations: hold out a small exploration/control slice that bypasses the model, use propensity weighting on the observed data, and model the blocked population explicitly rather than dropping it.

DesignWhy bother with shadow mode if you're going to canary anyway?

Because they answer different questions and shadow is free. Shadow answers "does this survive production?" — real latency on real feature fetches, real malformed inputs, real memory at peak traffic, real distribution of missing values — none of which offline testing reproduces, and all of which are cheaper to discover when the model affects nothing. Canary answers "does it break anything when it actually decides?" — which risks real customers. Running shadow for a week catches most operational failures before any user is exposed, and it also gives you a score-distribution comparison against the incumbent, which is the best early warning that something is subtly wrong.

15.8 A/B testing a model ⭐

The statistics are standard. What makes it an ML question is everything that can invalidate the test.

Design decisionGet it rightWhat goes wrong
Randomisation unitRandomise the unit the effect acts on — usually the user, not the requestPer-request randomisation lets one user see both variants, diluting the effect and breaking independence
Sample sizeCompute it up front from the MDE, baseline rate and powerUnderpowered tests read as “no effect” when the effect exists
Primary vs guardrailOne primary metric; guardrails on latency, revenue, complaints, fairnessPicking the winning metric after the fact is p-hacking
PeekingFix the duration, or use a proper sequential testChecking daily and stopping at significance badly inflates the false-positive rate
Novelty / primacyRun at least one full business cycleEarly lift that decays; or early loss from users adapting
Network effectsCluster/geo randomisationTreatment leaks to control through the marketplace, biasing everything toward zero
Sample-ratio mismatchCheck the actual split matches the intended oneA 50/50 split that arrives 52/48 signals an assignment bug that invalidates everything
Variance reductionCUPED using pre-period dataNot using it just means a longer, more expensive test
The offline-to-online gap, stated before someone asks

Your offline metric is a proxy. A model with better AUC can lose an A/B test because it improved ranking in a region users never see, because it shifted the score distribution and the fixed threshold now behaves differently, or because the business metric depends on something the model doesn't optimise (diversity, latency, fairness of exposure). Say explicitly: “I'd confirm that the offline metric actually moves the online objective — ideally by checking historical launches — before trusting it as a launch criterion.”

Likely interview questions
System designHow do you A/B test a model? What could invalidate the test?

Randomise at the unit the effect acts on (usually the user, not the request), compute the sample size up front from the MDE and power, declare one primary metric plus guardrails (latency, revenue, complaints, fairness), and fix the duration. Invalidators: peeking and stopping at significance; novelty and primacy effects; network effects leaking treatment into control (use cluster/geo randomisation); sample-ratio mismatch, which signals an assignment bug; and choosing the winning metric after the fact. Use CUPED with pre-period data to cut variance. And state the offline-to-online gap explicitly rather than assuming better AUC means a better outcome.

Deep diveWhat is CUPED and why does it help?

Controlled-experiment Using Pre-Experiment Data. Much of the variance in an outcome metric is explained by the same user's pre-period behaviour — a heavy spender before the test is a heavy spender during it. CUPED regresses the outcome on that pre-period covariate and analyses the residual, which removes that predictable variance without biasing the treatment effect (the covariate is pre-treatment, so it can't be affected by the assignment). The practical payoff is large: variance reductions of 30–50% are common, which means the same test reaches significance in roughly half the time — or detects an effect half the size for the same duration.

GotchaYour A/B test shows treatment winning overall but losing on both mobile and desktop. What's happening?

Simpson's paradox (§2.5), and in an A/B test it almost always indicates a bug rather than a real effect — specifically a sample-ratio mismatch, where the treatment group received a different mix of mobile and desktop users than control. That means randomisation didn't work as intended, which invalidates the whole test rather than just this cut. I'd check the actual assignment ratios per segment against the intended split with a chi-square test, look for a bug in the assignment logic or in how exposure is logged, and not ship on the aggregate result until it's resolved.

15.9 Engineering hygiene

The unglamorous section that separates a system from a notebook. Interviewers ask it as “how do you make an ML pipeline reproducible?”

PracticeConcretely
Data-schema testsTypes, ranges, allowed categories, null rates, row-count bounds — run on every batch, fail loudly
Pipeline invariantsDoes fit then transform equal fit_transform? Are outputs deterministic given a seed? Does it reject unseen categories gracefully?
Golden-prediction testsA fixed set of inputs with expected outputs, checked in CI — the single cheapest way to catch a silent regression
No-network unit testsTests must not depend on a live warehouse; fixture the data
ReproducibilityPinned dependencies (a lockfile), seeded randomness, data snapshots or versioned datasets, captured environment, and lineage from a prediction back to a model, a dataset and a commit
Config over codeHyperparameters, feature lists and thresholds in versioned config, not scattered literals
Experiment trackingEvery run's params, metrics, artefacts and data version recorded automatically
DocumentationModel card, stated assumptions, known limitations, a retraining runbook and an on-call playbook — “the model is returning nulls, now what?”
Reproducibility is more than random_state

“Set the seed” is the 2018 answer. The 2026 answer is: pinned dependencies, a versioned data snapshot, captured environment, config-as-code, recorded lineage, and golden-prediction tests — because what actually breaks reproducibility is a library minor-version bump changing a default, or the upstream table having been backfilled since you trained. Seeds only control the randomness you own.

Likely interview questions
Very commonHow do you make an ML pipeline reproducible?

"Set the seed" is the 2018 answer. The full one: pinned dependencies (a lockfile, not a range), versioned data snapshots (DVC/lakeFS-style, or an immutable partition), captured environment, config-as-code for hyperparameters and thresholds, recorded lineage from a prediction back to a model, dataset and commit, experiment tracking, and golden-prediction tests in CI. What actually breaks reproducibility in practice is a library minor version changing a default, or the upstream table being backfilled after you trained — seeds only control the randomness you own.

PracticalWhat tests would you write for an ML pipeline?

Data-schema tests on every batch (types, ranges, allowed categories, null rates, row counts) — these catch more production incidents than model monitoring does. Pipeline invariants: fit-then-transform equals fit_transform; output is deterministic given a seed; unseen categories don't crash. Golden-prediction tests: a fixed set of inputs with expected outputs, checked in CI — the cheapest possible guard against a silent regression from a library bump. No-network unit tests with fixtured data so the suite runs anywhere. And a smoke test that trains on a tiny sample end-to-end, so a broken pipeline fails in seconds rather than after an hour of training.

Frontier & Senior Signal
TabPFN, uncertainty, conformal, causal inference, uplift, DML, data-centric ML

16.1 Tabular foundation models ⭐⭐

“GBDTs beat deep learning on tabular data” was a safe answer for years. As of 2026 it is genuinely contested, and knowing that — with the caveats — is the clearest currency signal in this subject.

The answer to give, near-verbatim

“Historically GBDTs, decisively. As of 2026 that's genuinely contested for small-to-medium data by tabular foundation models like TabPFN — I'd benchmark both on my own data, and I'd still default to a GBDT where I need interpretability, monotonic constraints, cheap retraining and a well-understood ops story.” That sentence shows currency, judgement and appropriate scepticism in one breath. Also be able to name the deep tabular architectures — TabNet, FT-Transformer, SAINT, TabR — and AutoGluon as the strong AutoML baseline worth beating.

Likely interview questions
Modern⭐ GBDT or deep learning for tabular data? Has that changed?

“Historically GBDTs, decisively — faster to train, less tuning, native missing-value and categorical handling. As of 2026 it's genuinely contested for small-to-medium data by tabular foundation models: TabPFN-2.5 reported a 100% win rate against default XGBoost on ≤10k rows / ≤500 features, and TabPFN-3 (May 2026) scales to 1M training rows, reporting that a single forward pass beats 8-hour-tuned GBDT baselines up to 1M rows / 200 features on TabArena and outperforms AutoGluon 1.5 'extreme' while roughly 10× faster. The caveats matter: pretrained exclusively on synthetic data, benchmarks have selection effects, and the deployment, licensing and interpretability stories are less mature. So I'd benchmark both on my own data and still default to a GBDT where I need monotonic constraints, interpretability, cheap retraining and a known ops story.”

Deep diveHow does TabPFN actually work? It doesn't train on your data?

Correct — it does in-context learning. A transformer was pretrained once, offline, on millions of synthetic tabular datasets generated from structural-causal-model priors, learning to approximate Bayesian inference over that prior. At use time your dataset is fed in as context alongside the rows you want predictions for, and the answer comes out of a single forward pass — no fitting loop, no hyperparameter search, no per-dataset optimisation. That's why it can compete with a long tuning run: the "training" already happened. The consequences to name: its inductive bias is whatever the synthetic prior encoded, and its limits (row count, feature count) are architectural rather than statistical.

DesignWould you put TabPFN in production?

Cautiously, and I'd benchmark it first because the reported results are strong enough to be worth the test. Reasons for hesitation: the model is pretrained on synthetic data, so its inductive bias is inherited rather than learned from your domain; the interpretability story is thinner than a GBM with SHAP or monotonic constraints; latency is different in kind (a forward pass carrying context, not a tree traversal); and licensing and operational maturity lag. Where I'd reach for it readily: small-data problems where a GBM is starved and tuning is unstable, and as a strong baseline to check whether my heavily-tuned model is actually earning its complexity.

16.2 Aleatoric vs epistemic uncertainty

Two kinds of “I don't know”, and they call for opposite responses.

Likely interview questions
ConceptualAleatoric vs epistemic uncertainty.

Aleatoric is irreducible noise in the process — two identical applicants can have different outcomes. More data will not reduce it; you model it, with quantile regression or a predictive distribution. Epistemic is model ignorance where data is sparse — it does shrink with more data, which is exactly what active learning targets (§10.1), and you estimate it with ensemble variance or bootstrap spread. The practical payoff: epistemic uncertainty tells you where to collect data; aleatoric tells you where to widen the interval and stop trying. Confusing them wastes either data budget or modelling effort.

16.3 Conformal prediction ⭐⭐

The cheapest way to attach a real, distribution-free guarantee to any model — and it fits on a slide.

interactive Split conformal — set α, get coverage
—target coverage
—empirical coverage
—interval width
—conformal quantile q̂

This is the complete algorithm, implemented: fit any model on a training split, compute absolute residuals on a disjoint calibration split, take the ⌈(n+1)(1−α)⌉/n empirical quantile of those residuals as q̂, and emit [ŷ − q̂, ŷ + q̂]. Coverage lands on target with no distributional assumption. Then push the drift slider and watch it break: exchangeability is the one assumption it needs.

PropertyWhat it means
Distribution-freeNo assumption about the noise distribution or the model's correctness
Model-agnosticWraps any predictor — a GBM, a neural net, a lookup table
Finite-sampleThe guarantee holds at your actual n, not asymptotically
Marginal, not conditionalCoverage holds on average over the test distribution — not for every subgroup. Easy cases get intervals that are too wide, hard cases too narrow, unless you use a normalised score
Assumes exchangeabilityCalibration and test data must be exchangeable — which breaks under drift and for time series, hence adaptive and weighted variants
Conformalised quantile regression is the practical best of both

Plain split conformal gives a constant-width band, which is wrong wherever the noise varies. Fit a quantile regression at α/2 and 1−α/2 first (adaptive width, §5.9), then conformalise its residuals — you get an interval that is both adaptive and carries the finite-sample guarantee. That combination is the answer when someone asks how you'd produce prediction intervals you can actually commit to.

Likely interview questions
Modern⭐ What is conformal prediction and what guarantee does it give?

A distribution-free, model-agnostic wrapper turning point predictions into sets or intervals with finite-sample coverage. Split conformal: fit on a training split, compute a nonconformity score (e.g. absolute residual) on a disjoint calibration split, take the ⌈(n+1)(1−α)⌉/n empirical quantile as q̂, emit ŷ ± q̂. The guarantee is marginal coverage ≥ 1−α under exchangeability of calibration and test data — which breaks under drift and for time series, hence adaptive and weighted variants. Two caveats worth volunteering: coverage is marginal, not conditional (too wide for easy cases, too narrow for hard ones unless you normalise the score), and the interval is constant-width unless you conformalise a quantile model.

DesignYou need prediction intervals. Quantile regression, bootstrap, or conformal?

Depends on the guarantee you need. Quantile regression is cheap and gives adaptive, heteroscedasticity-aware intervals, but coverage relies on the model being right. Bootstrap captures parameter uncertainty but not irreducible noise, so it typically under-covers for a new observation unless you add the residual distribution back. Conformal gives a finite-sample, distribution-free coverage guarantee and wraps any model — my default when the interval carries a real commitment. The strongest practical answer is conformalised quantile regression: adaptive width from the quantile model, guaranteed coverage from the conformal wrapper.

GotchaDoes conformal prediction work for time series?

Not out of the box, because it assumes exchangeability — that calibration and test points are drawn from the same distribution in a way that's invariant to ordering. Time series violates that by construction: there's a temporal trend, autocorrelation, and drift, so residuals from last month don't calibrate next month. The fixes are named variants: adaptive conformal inference (ACI), which updates α online based on realised coverage, and weighted conformal, which down-weights older calibration points. Knowing that exchangeability is the assumption — and that it's the only one — is what the question is testing.

16.4 Causal inference ⭐⭐

Most ML answers “what will happen?”. Most business questions are “what should we do?”. Those are different, and a correlation-trained model answers the wrong one.

ConceptWhat it isWhy it bites
Potential outcomesEach unit has Y(1) and Y(0); you observe only oneThe fundamental problem of causal inference — there is no per-row label to be right about (§16.5)
ATE / ATT / CATEAverage effect / effect on the treated / effect conditional on xCATE is what targeting needs; ATE is what an experiment reports
ConfounderCauses both treatment and outcomeMust be controlled for, or the estimate is biased
ColliderCaused by both treatment and outcomeControlling for it creates bias that wasn't there — the opposite of a confounder, and the reason "control for everything" is wrong
MediatorOn the causal path between treatment and outcomeControlling for it removes part of the effect you're trying to measure
Selection biasWho ends up in your data depends on the outcomeThe reject-inference and feedback-loop problems (§15.7)
Likely interview questions
Very common⭐ Your model predicts churn accurately. The business asks who to give a discount to. What's wrong?

The churn model answers "who will leave?", but the decision needs "who will stay because we acted?" — different quantities. The highest churn scores are dominated by lost causes who leave regardless; budget also leaks to sure things who'd have stayed; and some customers are sleeping dogs for whom the offer is a reminder to cancel, so the treatment effect is negative. You need uplift / CATE, ideally from a randomised holdout, evaluated with Qini and uplift curves rather than AUC. The general principle: a predictive model is invalid under intervention.

Deep diveWhat's a collider, and why does controlling for it hurt?

A collider is a variable caused by both the treatment and the outcome (or by two otherwise-independent causes). Confounders must be controlled for; colliders must not be — conditioning on one creates a spurious association between its causes that didn't exist in the population. The classic illustration: among hospitalised patients, two unrelated diseases appear negatively correlated, because being admitted (the collider) means you probably have at least one. This is why "control for everything you have" is wrong: adding a covariate can introduce bias as easily as remove it, and only a causal graph tells you which is which.

DesignYou can't run an experiment. What do you do?

Pick a method and state its assumption explicitly, because that's what makes the estimate reviewable. Propensity matching/IPW assumes no unmeasured confounders — strong and usually unverifiable. Difference-in-differences assumes parallel trends, which you can partially check on pre-period data. Regression discontinuity assumes continuity at the cutoff and is very credible where a real threshold exists. Instrumental variables needs relevance and the exclusion restriction. DML lets you use ML for the nuisance functions while keeping valid inference. Then run refutation tests — placebo treatments, random common causes, subset stability — because an estimate nobody tried to break isn't evidence.

16.5 Uplift modelling ⭐⭐

The concrete form of the causal argument — and the widget makes the cost of getting it wrong visible in pounds.

interactive Churn score vs uplift — who actually gets the discount?
—customers actually retained
—discounts to sure-things
—sleeping dogs woken
—net effect per 100 contacts

2,000 simulated customers, each with a true churn probability and a true treatment effect that are only weakly related — the realistic case. Switch rules at a fixed budget and read the retained count. Targeting the highest churn scores spends most of the budget on lost causes and sure things; targeting uplift spends it on persuadables. Same data, same budget, very different outcome.

Likely interview questions
Modern⭐ Explain uplift modelling. Why is AUC the wrong metric for it?

Uplift estimates the conditional average treatment effect E[y|x,treat] − E[y|x,control] — the change caused by the action, not the outcome level. Estimators: T-learner (separate models per arm), S-learner (one model with treatment as a feature), X-learner (better when arms are imbalanced), causal forests. AUC is wrong because there's no per-row label to be right about — you never observe both potential outcomes for the same person. Evaluation must be aggregate: rank by predicted uplift and compare treated vs control outcomes within score deciles, which is what the Qini curve plots.

DesignHow do you get the data to train an uplift model?

Ideally from a randomised experiment: treat a random subset, hold out a random control, and you have unbiased treated and untreated outcomes across the whole feature space. That's why mature retention programmes keep a permanent randomised holdout — it costs a little margin and it's the only thing that makes uplift estimable and measurable over time. Without randomisation you're doing observational causal inference (§16.4) with propensity weighting or DML, and you must state the no-unmeasured-confounders assumption — which is usually violated when past campaigns targeted people because they looked like churners. Recommending the holdout before the modelling is the senior move.

ConceptualWhat are sleeping dogs and why do they matter so much?

Customers whose treatment effect is negative — the retention offer reminds them the subscription exists, or the marketing email prompts an unsubscribe. They matter disproportionately because they're the one group where the campaign is worse than doing nothing, so every contact is a double loss: the cost of the offer plus a customer you'd otherwise have kept. A churn-score-ranked campaign can't distinguish them from persuadables (both may score high on risk), which is the sharpest single argument for uplift over propensity — and it's the kind of effect that only shows up if you kept a randomised control to measure against.

16.6 Double machine learning ⭐

How to use a GBM for the messy parts of a causal estimate without destroying your inference.

You want the effect of a treatment D on an outcome Y, with high-dimensional confounders X. DML fits two nuisance models with any ML method — E[Y|X] and E[D|X] — takes the residuals of each, and regresses one residual on the other. That is the Frisch-Waugh-Lovell theorem, made robust.

IngredientWhat it prevents
Neyman orthogonalityThe effect estimate is insensitive to first-order errors in the nuisance models — so a slightly wrong GBM doesn't bias the effect
Cross-fittingA row's nuisance predictions come from a model that never saw it — without this, regularization bias and overfitting contaminate the residuals
ResultA √n-consistent effect estimate with valid confidence intervals, while using flexible ML for the nuisances
Cross-fitting is the same idea as out-of-fold everything else

Notice the pattern: out-of-fold target encoding (§3.5), ordered boosting (§8.6), stacking's OOF meta-features (§8.8), and now cross-fitting in DML — all four are the same insight, that a row's derived value must come from a model that never saw that row. Spotting that as one principle rather than four tricks is exactly the kind of connection that makes an interview go well.

Likely interview questions
Deep diveWhat is double machine learning for?

Estimating a causal effect with high-dimensional confounders while still using flexible ML. Fit two nuisance models with any learner — outcome given confounders, and treatment given confounders — take the residuals of each, and regress one on the other (Frisch-Waugh-Lovell). Two ingredients make it valid: Neyman orthogonality, so small nuisance errors don't bias the effect to first order, and cross-fitting, so a row's nuisance predictions come from a model that never saw it — otherwise regularization bias contaminates the estimate. The payoff is a √n-consistent effect with valid confidence intervals while using gradient boosting for the messy parts. EconML implements it.

ConceptualWhy can't you just put the treatment in a regression with all the confounders?

You can, and with a correctly-specified linear model it's fine. The problem is when you use a flexible model to handle high-dimensional or non-linear confounding: the regularization that makes the ML model work also biases the treatment coefficient (it shrinks it along with everything else), and the model's own overfitting to the confounders contaminates the estimate. Standard inference then gives confidence intervals that are simply wrong. DML fixes both — orthogonalisation removes the first-order sensitivity to nuisance error, cross-fitting removes the overfitting contamination — which is why it exists as a separate procedure rather than "just add the controls".

16.7 Data-centric ML ⭐

One sentence carries this section: most of the remaining accuracy is in the data, not the model.

Likely interview questions
DesignYour model is stuck at 84% and the business wants 90%. What do you do?

Before touching the model: audit 200 random errors. That single hour usually tells you whether the remaining gap is label noise, a missing feature, a broken slice, or genuine difficulty — and those have completely different fixes. Then check the ceiling: what's inter-annotator agreement? If humans agree 88% of the time, 90% is not achievable and the honest answer is to say so. Then slice analysis (§11.6) to see whether the deficit is concentrated. Only after those would I look at features, and only after that at the model — because the ordering of that list is the answer.

GotchaWhen does synthetic data help and when does it hurt?

Helps for genuinely rare classes where you need more coverage of a known pattern, and for privacy-constrained sharing where the alternative is no data at all. Hurts when it fabricates structure — the generator imposes its own assumptions, the model learns them as real, and performance on genuine data doesn't improve or degrades. That's the SMOTE critique (§12.9) generalised. The non-negotiable check: train on synthetic (or augmented) data and evaluate on real held-out data. If that number doesn't improve, the synthetic data isn't helping regardless of how good it looks.

16.8 Shift, robustness & the big question ⭐

The closing section, and the one that gives you a position rather than a fact.

ShiftWhat movesResponse
Covariate shiftP(x), with P(y|x) stableImportance weighting; domain adaptation; often just retrain on recent data
Label / prior shiftP(y)Re-threshold; prior correction on the probabilities (§2.3)
Concept shiftP(y|x)Retrain — nothing else helps
Strategic / adversarialThe subjects adapt to the modelFraudsters and credit-score gamers respond to your rules — strategic classification. Prefer features that are costly to fake, and expect to retrain on a cycle
Shortcut learningNothing — you learned the wrong thingSpurious correlations that hold in training and not in deployment; stress-test with counterfactual slices
⭐ “Is classical ML dead?”

No — and the reason is worth saying carefully. Most of the world's high-value prediction problems are still tabular, latency-bound, regulated and small-data: credit, insurance, fraud, demand, pricing, clinical risk. What changed is that the baseline moved. Strong AutoML and tabular foundation models mean that getting a competent model is no longer where the difficulty is — so the job has shifted toward framing the problem, owning the data, designing the evaluation and running the deployment. That is a better answer than either “no, GBDTs still win” or “yes, LLMs do everything now”, because it is the one that is actually true.

Privacy, at a glance

Differential privacy — a formal guarantee bounded by ε, with a real accuracy cost; k-anonymity and its successors, which are weaker and defeatable by linkage; federated learning, which keeps raw data on-device but does not by itself provide privacy (gradients leak; combine it with DP). Enough to have an opinion, not enough to claim expertise — which is the right calibration for a classical ML interview.

Likely interview questions
Modern⭐ Is classical ML dead?

No. Most of the world's high-value prediction problems are still tabular, latency-bound, regulated and small-data — credit, insurance, fraud, demand, pricing, clinical risk — and none of that is going to an LLM. What changed is that the baseline moved: strong AutoML and tabular foundation models mean getting a competent model is no longer the hard part. So the job has shifted toward framing the problem, owning the data, designing the evaluation, and running the deployment — which is exactly where this whole subject spends its time. That's a more honest answer than either "GBDTs still win" or "LLMs do everything now".

Deep diveWhat is strategic classification, and where have you seen it?

When the subjects of the model adapt to it, the data distribution changes because you deployed. Credit-score gaming (opening accounts to manipulate utilisation), fraudsters probing which transaction sizes clear, SEO against a ranking model, applicants tailoring CVs to a screener. It's distinct from ordinary drift because the shift is adversarial and responsive — fixing the model provokes the next adaptation. Practical responses: prefer features that are costly to fake or causally related to the outcome rather than merely correlated; keep the exact rules non-public; expect a retraining cycle rather than a stable model; and monitor for sudden distribution changes concentrated in gameable features.
